questions.question: In which direction does the sun rise?
questions.answer: In the East

questions.question: In which direction does the sun set?

questions.question: Which way do shadows point in the morning?

questions.question: Name the parts of a district, from the biggest to the smallest.

questions.question: What is a municipality?

questions.question: What is the smallest administrative unit?

questions.question: Name any four things found on a good map.

questions.question: What is the key of a map used for?

questions.question: Why has Uganda been divided into districts?

questions.question: What is a division?

items.subject: Social Studies
subtopics: 2. Name the physical features in the syllabus and what each one is.
4. What are physical features used for?
5. What dangers come from physical features?
6. How can we keep safe near physical features?
7. How do we care for physical features?
9. How do physical features affect people?

questions.question: What are physical features?
questions.answer: Natural things found on the earth's surface that were not made by people.

questions.question: Give any four examples of physical features.
questions.answer: Any four of hills, mountains, valleys, plains, rivers, lakes, swamps, forests, rocks, islands

questions.question: Which of these is not a physical feature: a lake, a hill, a bridge, a valley?
questions.answer: A bridge — it is made by people

questions.question: What is a river?
questions.answer: Water flowing in a channel from a highland to a lake or sea

questions.question: What is a valley?
questions.answer: Low land lying between hills or mountains

questions.question: What is a plain?
questions.answer: Flat or gently sloping land

questions.question: Give any three uses of a lake.
questions.answer: Any three of fishing, water for use, transport by boat, tourism, irrigation

questions.question: Give any two uses of a swamp.
questions.answer: Any two of papyrus for mats and baskets, clay for bricks and pots, growing rice or yams, home for fish and birds

questions.question: Give any two uses of a forest.
questions.answer: Any two of timber, firewood, herbs for medicine, homes for animals, help rainfall

questions.question: Give any two dangers of a river.
questions.answer: Any two of drowning, floods, crocodiles and hippos, water-borne diseases such as bilharzia

questions.question: Give one danger of a steep mountain slope.
questions.answer: Landslides (or falling rocks, or soil erosion)

questions.question: Which disease do mosquitoes from a swamp spread?
questions.answer: Malaria

questions.question: Give any three ways of caring for a lake.
questions.answer: Any three of do not throw rubbish in it, do not fish with poison, leave plants on the banks, do not use small nets, do not bathe or wash cars at the source

questions.question: What is terracing?
questions.answer: Cutting steps across a slope to stop soil being washed away

questions.question: What is soil erosion?
questions.answer: The carrying away of soil by water or wind

questions.question: What is the difference between afforestation and deforestation?
questions.answer: Afforestation is planting trees where there were none; deforestation is cutting down trees without replacing them.

questions.question: Why do many people settle on plains?
questions.answer: Because the land is flat and easy to farm and build on, and there is usually water.

questions.question: Name one physical feature found in your own district.
questions.answer: (Your own answer — a feature really found in your district.)

questions.question: Give one use of that feature to the people of your district.
questions.answer: (Your own answer.)

questions.question: Give one way the people of your district can care for it.
questions.answer: (Your own answer.)

items.subject: Social Studies
subtopics: 2. Name the five types of vegetation.
3. What is the difference between natural and planted vegetation?
4. What are the uses of vegetation?
5. Which activities of people damage vegetation?
6. What happens when vegetation is destroyed?
7. How do we care for vegetation?

questions.question: What is vegetation?
questions.answer: All the plants growing in a place

questions.question: Name the five types of vegetation given in the syllabus.
questions.answer: Forests, swamps, shrubs, grass and crops

questions.question: What is natural vegetation?
questions.answer: Vegetation that grew on its own, without being planted by people

questions.question: What is planted vegetation?
questions.answer: Vegetation planted and cared for by people

questions.question: Give one way of telling a planted forest from a natural forest.
questions.answer: A planted forest grows in straight lines and is usually of one kind of tree.

questions.question: Give any four uses of vegetation.
questions.answer: Any four of firewood, herbs for medicine, food, oxygen, timber, shade, grazing, beauty, homes for animals, tourism

questions.question: Which gas do plants give out that people need?
questions.answer: Oxygen

questions.question: How does vegetation help rain to form?
questions.answer: Trees give off water vapour, which rises and helps clouds and rain to form.

questions.question: How do the roots of plants help the soil?
questions.answer: They hold the soil together so it is not washed or blown away.

questions.question: Name any four activities of people that destroy vegetation.
questions.answer: Any four of burning bushes, over cultivation, over grazing, deforestation, making bricks, road construction, building houses and industries

questions.question: What is deforestation?
questions.answer: Cutting down trees without replacing them

questions.question: Give any three results of destroying vegetation.
questions.answer: Any three of soil erosion, less rain, drought, wild animals lose homes, shortage of firewood and timber, strong winds, deserts forming

questions.question: What is afforestation?
questions.answer: Planting trees where there were none before

questions.question: What is reafforestation?
questions.answer: Planting trees again where they had been cut

questions.question: What is selective cutting?
questions.answer: Cutting only the mature trees and leaving the young ones

questions.question: What is over grazing?
questions.answer: Keeping too many animals on the same land so the grass is eaten down to the roots

questions.question: Give any four ways of caring for vegetation.
questions.answer: Any four of afforestation, reafforestation, selective cutting, avoiding bush burning, controlling grazing, using energy-saving stoves, gazetting forests, educating people, mulching and crop rotation

questions.question: What does it mean to gazette a forest?
questions.answer: It means the government marks it off by law as a protected reserve.

questions.question: Name one type of vegetation found in your own district.
questions.answer: (Your own answer — the vegetation really found in your district.)

questions.question: Give one way you yourself can help care for vegetation.
questions.answer: Any correct answer, for example: plant a tree at school or at home and take care of it, or never set fire to the bush.

questions.question: Give the meaning of: origin.
questions.answer: Origin: The place where a person or group of people came from.

questions.question: Give the meaning of: tribe.
questions.answer: Tribe: A group of people who have a common culture, language and history.

questions.question: Give the meaning of: clan.
questions.answer: Clan: A group of people who believe that they have a common ancestor.

questions.question: Give the meaning of: immigration.
questions.answer: Immigration: The movement of people into a place to live there.

questions.question: Give the meaning of: emigration.
questions.answer: Emigration: The movement of people out of a place to live somewhere else.

questions.question: Give the meaning of: settlement.
questions.answer: Settlement: The place where people live.

questions.question: Give the meaning of: settlement pattern.
questions.answer: Settlement pattern: The way people are spread or arranged in an area.

questions.question: Give the meaning of: occupation.
questions.answer: Occupation: The work a person does to earn a living.

questions.question: Give the meaning of: pottery.
questions.answer: Pottery: The making of things from clay.

questions.question: Give the meaning of: craft work.
questions.answer: Craft work: The making of useful or decorative things by hand.

questions.question: Give the meaning of: trading.
questions.answer: Trading: The buying and selling of goods and services.

questions.question: Give the meaning of: social activities.
questions.answer: Social activities: Activities in which people come together and interact with one another.

questions.question: Give the meaning of: way of life.
questions.answer: Way of life: How people live and carry out their daily activities.

questions.question: Give the meaning of: quality of life.
questions.answer: Quality of life: The general well-being of people.

questions.question: Give the meaning of: cooperation.
questions.answer: Cooperation: Working together to achieve a common goal.

questions.question: Who are the people in our district?
questions.answer: The people in our district are the different groups of people who live and work in the district.

questions.question: What makes up the social environment?
questions.answer: People and the things they make form the social environment.

questions.question: Mention four things made by people in our district.
questions.answer: Houses, roads, schools and markets.

questions.question: Mention three traditional legends about the origin of people in Uganda.
questions.answer: Kintu and Nambi, Labong and Gipir, and Mundu and Sera.

questions.question: Give six reasons why people move from one place to another.
questions.answer: People move to look for water, food, pasture, jobs, fertile soils and security.

questions.question: Mention six factors that influence settlement patterns.
questions.answer: Fertile soils, reliable rainfall, trade, jobs, food, security, water, roads, education and health services.

questions.question: Why do people settle in areas with fertile soils?
questions.answer: People settle in areas with fertile soils because they can grow crops well.

questions.question: Why do jobs attract people to an area?
questions.answer: Jobs give people opportunities to earn money.

questions.question: Why do people settle in peaceful areas?
questions.answer: Peaceful areas are safer places for people to live and work.

questions.question: Mention eight types of work done by people in our district.
questions.answer: Farming, fishing, pottery, brick laying, craft work, trading, teaching and office work.

questions.question: Why do people work?
questions.answer: People work to earn money and meet their needs.

questions.question: Mention five problems faced by people while doing their work.
questions.answer: Insecurity, diseases, poor roads, poor health and poverty.

questions.question: How do poor roads affect people's work?
questions.answer: Poor roads make it difficult and expensive to transport people and goods.

questions.question: How do animal diseases affect farmers?
questions.answer: Animal diseases can make animals sick or die, causing farmers to lose income.

questions.question: Mention five social activities carried out in our district.
questions.answer: Introduction ceremonies, marriages, weddings, naming ceremonies and circumcision.

questions.question: What is the importance of social activities?
questions.answer: Social activities keep families together, promote culture, unite people, promote acceptable behaviour and encourage people to work together.

questions.question: How do social activities promote culture?
questions.answer: They help people pass on their language, food, dressing, customs and traditions.

questions.question: How do social activities unite people?
questions.answer: They bring people together to celebrate, work and share experiences.

questions.question: Mention ten factors that contribute to people's way of life.
questions.answer: Work, food, security, education, diseases, unemployment, poverty, trade, transport and communication.

questions.question: How does education affect people's way of life?
questions.answer: Education gives people knowledge and skills for getting jobs and solving problems.

questions.question: How do diseases affect people's way of life?
questions.answer: Diseases make people sick, reduce their ability to work and may cause them to spend money on treatment.

questions.question: How does unemployment affect people's way of life?
questions.answer: Unemployment makes it difficult for people to earn money to meet their needs.

questions.question: Mention five things that improve people's quality of life.
questions.answer: Good education, health services, enough food, employment and good roads.

questions.question: Why should people live peacefully together?
questions.answer: To promote unity, development, cooperation and security.

questions.question: Give five ways of promoting peace in our district.
questions.answer: Respecting one another, helping one another, cooperating, obeying laws and solving disagreements peacefully.

items.subject: Social Studies
subtopics: 1. Who is a leader? Why do we need leaders?
2. Name the four groups of leaders in a district.
4. How is an election carried out?
6. How are prefects chosen at school?

questions.question: Who is a leader?
questions.answer: A person who guides, plans and organises other people

questions.question: Give any three reasons why we need leaders.
questions.answer: Any three of to keep law and order, to plan development, to settle quarrels, to speak for the people, to look after public property, to represent people to government

questions.question: Name the four groups of leaders found in a district.
questions.answer: Political, civic, religious and voluntary leaders

questions.question: Name the local council levels from the village to the district.
questions.answer: LC1 (village), LC2 (parish), LC3 (sub-county), LC4 (county), LC5 (district)

questions.question: Who is the head of the local council at the village?
questions.answer: The LC1 chairperson

questions.question: Who heads the district council?
questions.answer: The LC5 chairperson

questions.question: Who represents the President in the district?
questions.answer: The RDC

questions.question: Give the full meaning of RDC.
questions.answer: Resident District Commissioner

questions.question: Give the full meaning of CAO.
questions.answer: Chief Administrative Officer

questions.question: Give the full meaning of DISO.
questions.answer: District Internal Security Officer

questions.question: Name any three civic leaders in a district.
questions.answer: Any three of CAO, District Health Officer, District Agricultural Officer, magistrate, District Police Commander

questions.question: Name any four religious leaders.
questions.answer: Any four of bishops, priests, reverends, pastors, sheikhs, khadis

questions.question: Name any two voluntary organisations given in the syllabus.
questions.answer: Any two of UWESO, TASO, the Red Cross (Scouts and Guides also accepted)

questions.question: Give the four ways in which leaders are chosen.
questions.answer: By election, by appointment, through inheritance, and by volunteering

questions.question: Which leaders are chosen through inheritance?
questions.answer: Cultural leaders — for example a king, a chief or a clan head

questions.question: Name the steps followed in an election.
questions.answer: Registration, nomination, campaigning, voting, counting, declaring the winner, swearing in

questions.question: What is a ballot box used for?
questions.answer: For putting in the ballot papers during voting

questions.question: What is a secret ballot?
questions.answer: Voting in a way that nobody else can see whom you have chosen

questions.question: Give any four qualities of a good leader.
questions.answer: Any four of honest, fair, listens to people, keeps promises, hard-working, humble, patient, educated enough

questions.question: Give any three duties of the people towards their leaders.
questions.answer: Any three of obey the law, pay taxes, attend meetings, vote wisely, respect leaders, report wrong acts, take part in community work

items.subject: Social Studies
items.topic: How to Meet People's Needs in Our District
subtopics: 1. What are social services? Who provides them?
2. Name the types of social services.
4. What problems are met in providing social services?
5. What are the solutions to these problems?
6. How do we care for social service centres?

questions.question: What are social services?
questions.answer: Things provided to help people live well, which people cannot easily provide alone

questions.question: Who has the main responsibility of providing social services?
questions.answer: The government

questions.question: Name any three groups allowed to provide services on behalf of government.
questions.answer: Religious groups, private medical practitioners and business people

questions.question: Name any six types of social services.
questions.answer: Any six of education, medical, security, transport, water, electricity, housing, road maintenance, banking, postal and communication

questions.question: Where is the medical service found?
questions.answer: At hospitals, health centres and clinics

questions.question: Which service is provided at a police post?
questions.answer: Security (law and order)

questions.question: Name any six people who provide social services.
questions.answer: Any six of teachers, doctors, nurses, veterinary officers, police officers, army officers, drivers, carpenters, bankers, farmers, shopkeepers, local leaders, chiefs, parents

questions.question: Who provides education?
questions.answer: Teachers

questions.question: Who treats animals?
questions.answer: A veterinary officer

questions.question: What does a banker do?
questions.answer: Keeps people's money safely and lends money

questions.question: What do parents provide for their children?
questions.answer: Food, clothing, shelter, school fees, love and care

questions.question: Name any five problems met in providing social services.
questions.answer: Any five of poverty, bad weather, shortage of food, theft, corruption, irresponsibility, laziness, idleness, high population, poor attitude to work

questions.question: What is corruption?
questions.answer: The dishonest use of a position for personal gain — for example taking money meant for services

questions.question: Give one solution to poverty.
questions.answer: Any one of start income-generating work, join a savings group, work hard, learn a skill, group farming

questions.question: Give one solution to theft of school property.
questions.answer: Any one of guard the property, fence and lock the buildings, report thieves to the police

questions.question: Give one solution to a high population.
questions.answer: Any one of family planning and education, building more schools and health centres

questions.question: Give any three ways of caring for a school.
questions.answer: Any three of sweep and slash the compound, do not write on the walls, do not break desks, use the latrine properly, plant trees, report damage

questions.question: Give any two ways of caring for a borehole.
questions.answer: Any two of keep the surroundings clean, repair the handle, do not wash clothes at the source, keep animals away, fence it

questions.question: Give the steps to follow when crossing a road safely.
questions.answer: Stop · look right · look left · look right again · cross when the road is clear (use a zebra crossing where there is one)

questions.question: Name any two social service centres found in your own district.
questions.answer: (Your own answer — two centres really found in your district.)

questions.question: Give the meaning of: culture.
questions.answer: Culture: The way of life of a group of people.

questions.question: Give the meaning of: cultural identity.
questions.answer: Cultural identity: The feeling of belonging to a particular culture or community.

questions.question: Give the meaning of: language.
questions.answer: Language: A way people use to communicate with one another.

questions.question: Give the meaning of: custom.
questions.answer: Custom: A way of behaving that has been followed by a particular community for a long time.

questions.question: Give the meaning of: tradition.
questions.answer: Tradition: A belief or practice passed from one generation to another.

questions.question: Give the meaning of: cultural value.
questions.answer: Cultural value: A good belief or principle that guides people's behaviour in a community.

questions.question: Give the meaning of: social activities.
questions.answer: Social activities: Activities in which people come together and interact with one another.

questions.question: Give the meaning of: marriage.
questions.answer: Marriage: The union of a man and a woman as husband and wife.

questions.question: Give the meaning of: wedding.
questions.answer: Wedding: A ceremony held to celebrate a marriage.

questions.question: Give the meaning of: naming ceremony.
questions.answer: Naming ceremony: A ceremony held when a child is given a name.

questions.question: Give the meaning of: cultural festival.
questions.answer: Cultural festival: A special event where people celebrate and display their culture.

questions.question: Give the meaning of: community work.
questions.answer: Community work: Work done by people together to improve their community.

questions.question: Give the meaning of: discrimination.
questions.answer: Discrimination: Treating a person unfairly because of differences such as culture, tribe or religion.

questions.question: Give the meaning of: cultural diversity.
questions.answer: Cultural diversity: The existence of different cultures in one community or country.

questions.question: What is culture?
questions.answer: Culture is the way of life of a group of people.

questions.question: Mention six elements of culture.
questions.answer: Language, food, dressing, music, dance and religion.

questions.question: Give five examples of culture in Uganda.
questions.answer: Language, food, dressing, traditional dances and marriage customs.

questions.question: Why is culture important?
questions.answer: Culture gives people an identity, teaches people how to live, preserves traditions, promotes unity and helps people know their history.

questions.question: Why should children learn their culture?
questions.answer: Children should learn their culture to know their history, learn good cultural practices, respect elders, preserve culture and pass good traditions to future generations.

questions.question: Mention five languages spoken in Uganda.
questions.answer: Luganda, Lusoga, Luo, Runyankole-Rukiga and Ateso.

questions.question: Why is language important?
questions.answer: Language helps people communicate, share ideas, teach children and preserve culture.

questions.question: Mention five traditional foods eaten in Uganda.
questions.answer: Matooke, millet bread, sweet potatoes, cassava and beans.

questions.question: Mention five traditional forms of dressing.
questions.answer: Gomesi, kanzu, bark cloth, animal skins and traditional beads.

questions.question: What is traditional music?
questions.answer: Traditional music is music that belongs to a particular community and is passed from one generation to another.

questions.question: What is traditional dance?
questions.answer: Traditional dance is a dance performed according to the customs of a particular community.

questions.question: Mention four traditional dances in Uganda.
questions.answer: Bwola, Bakisimba, Ekitaguriro and Larakaraka.

questions.question: Why are traditional dances important?
questions.answer: Traditional dances entertain people, preserve culture, teach history and bring people together.

questions.question: What is a custom?
questions.answer: A custom is a way of behaving that has been followed by a particular community for a long time.

questions.question: What is a tradition?
questions.answer: A tradition is a belief or practice passed from one generation to another.

questions.question: Mention five good cultural values.
questions.answer: Respect, honesty, hard work, kindness and cooperation.

questions.question: What are social activities?
questions.answer: Social activities are activities in which people come together and interact with one another.

questions.question: Mention six social activities.
questions.answer: Weddings, introduction ceremonies, naming ceremonies, burial ceremonies, religious celebrations and sports.

questions.question: Why are social activities important?
questions.answer: They bring people together, promote unity, strengthen relationships, preserve culture and help people support one another.

questions.question: What is a wedding?
questions.answer: A wedding is a ceremony held to celebrate a marriage.

questions.question: What is a naming ceremony?
questions.answer: A naming ceremony is a ceremony held when a child is given a name.

questions.question: Why are naming ceremonies important?
questions.answer: They give a child a name, bring families together, introduce the child to the community and preserve cultural practices.

questions.question: Mention four religious activities.
questions.answer: Praying, worshipping, fasting and attending religious services.

questions.question: Why are religious activities important?
questions.answer: They bring believers together, teach good behaviour, strengthen faith and encourage people to help others.

questions.question: What is a cultural festival?
questions.answer: A cultural festival is a special event where people celebrate and display their culture.

questions.question: Mention five activities that take place during cultural festivals.
questions.answer: Traditional dancing, singing, storytelling, traditional food preparation and displaying traditional clothes.

questions.question: What is community work?
questions.answer: Community work is work done by people together to improve their community.

questions.question: Mention four examples of community work.
questions.answer: Cleaning roads, planting trees, cleaning water sources and repairing community facilities.

questions.question: Why is community work important?
questions.answer: It improves the community, promotes cooperation, keeps the environment clean and helps people solve problems.

questions.question: What are harmful cultural practices?
questions.answer: Harmful cultural practices are practices that can hurt people or prevent them from living healthy and peaceful lives.

questions.question: Mention four harmful cultural practices.
questions.answer: Child marriage, female genital mutilation, denying children education and discrimination.

questions.question: Why should harmful cultural practices be stopped?
questions.answer: They can hurt people, cause suffering, cause diseases and prevent community development.

questions.question: Mention five factors that cause cultural change.
questions.answer: Education, technology, religion, migration and trade.

questions.question: How does education change culture?
questions.answer: Education gives people new knowledge and ideas that may change some of their ways of living.

questions.question: How does migration change culture?
questions.answer: Migration brings people from different communities together, allowing them to share their languages, foods, dressing and other cultural practices.

questions.question: Why should we respect other people's cultures?
questions.answer: We should respect other cultures to promote peace, unity and good relationships.

questions.question: Give five ways of showing respect for other cultures.
questions.answer: Respecting their languages, customs, beliefs, traditions and ways of life.

questions.question: Why should we avoid discrimination?
questions.answer: We should avoid discrimination because it can cause hatred, conflicts and disunity.

questions.question: How can culture promote national unity?
questions.answer: Culture promotes national unity by bringing people together, encouraging respect and helping people appreciate different cultures.

A garden is 15 m long and 9 m wide. Find its perimeter and its area.
questions.answer: Perimeter = 2 × (15 + 9) = 48 m; Area = 15 × 9 = 135 m²

questions.question: What are parallel lines?
questions.answer: Lines that run in the same direction and never meet, however far they are drawn.

questions.question: Give one example of perpendicular lines in your classroom.

questions.question: Name the type of angle that measures 130°.

questions.question: Name the type of angle that measures exactly 90°.

A triangle has angles of 50° and 60°. Find the third angle.
Angles at a point are 120°, 150° and y. Find y.
Find the diameter of a circle whose radius is 3.5 cm.
Find the radius of a circle whose diameter is 10 cm.
Name the part of a circle that joins two points on the circle without passing through the centre.

How many lines of folding symmetry has a rectangle?
How many lines of folding symmetry has an equilateral triangle?
How many degrees are there in a quarter turn?
How many degrees are there in one complete revolution?
A learner facing north makes a quarter turn clockwise. Which direction is she facing?

Describe in two steps how you would construct a circle of radius 4 cm.

questions.question: Is zero positive, negative or neither?

questions.answer: 3 − 5 + 2 = 0, the ground floor

questions.answer: 4 + 7 = 11 degrees

items.subject: Science
subtopics: 3. POULTRY AND BEE FARMING AS A BUSINESS

questions.question: What is poultry? Name any five types.
questions.answer: Poultry are birds kept at home for meat, eggs and money. Any five of: chicken, turkeys, ducks, guinea fowls, geese, pigeons.

questions.question: Name any six external parts of a domestic fowl.
questions.answer: Any six of: comb, wattle, beak, eyes, feathers, wings, legs with scales, claws, tail, vent.

questions.question: Give three differences between a cock and a hen.
questions.answer: A cock has a big comb and wattles, bright feathers, long pointed tail feathers and spurs, and it crows; a hen has a smaller comb, a rounded body, lays eggs and broods.

questions.question: Name the four systems of keeping poultry and describe two.
questions.answer: Free range, deep litter, battery cage and fold. (Describe two, for example: in deep litter birds are kept in a house on a floor covered with coffee husks or wood shavings; in free range the birds move about freely and look for their own food.)

questions.question: Name any three breeds of chicken and what each is kept for.
questions.answer: Any three: White Leghorn — eggs; broilers — meat; Rhode Island Red — meat and eggs; local kienyeji — meat, eggs and hardiness.

questions.question: Give any six ways of caring for poultry.
questions.answer: Any six of: provide a clean, dry, well-ventilated house; give clean water always; feed a balanced ration; vaccinate; deworm and dust against parasites; isolate sick birds; remove wet litter; protect from predators and thieves; keep records.

questions.question: Name any four poultry diseases and any three poultry parasites.
questions.answer: Diseases: Newcastle, coccidiosis, fowl typhoid, fowl pox, gumboro (any four). Parasites: lice, mites, fleas, ticks, worms (any three).

questions.question: Name the three types of bees in a colony and the work of each.
questions.answer: Queen — the only fertile female, lays all the eggs; drones — males that mate with the queen; workers — sterile females that collect nectar, make honey, build combs, feed the young, guard and clean the hive.

questions.question: Give two traditional and two modern types of beehives.
questions.answer: Traditional: log hives and pot or basket hives. Modern: the Kenya Top Bar hive and the Langstroth hive.

questions.question: Give any four things to consider when siting an apiary.
questions.answer: Any four of: a quiet, shady place; near water and flowering plants; away from homes, paths and animals; safe from thieves; protected from ants by greasing the wires.

questions.question: Give the steps followed when harvesting honey.
questions.answer: Harvest in the evening or early morning → wear protective clothing → light the smoker and calm the bees → open the hive quietly → cut only combs with sealed honey, leaving some for the bees → put the combs in clean containers → close the hive → strain the honey and store it in a cool, dry place.

questions.question: Why is protective clothing and a smoker used during harvesting?
questions.answer: Because bees sting to defend the hive. Protective clothing keeps the stings off the body, and the smoke calms the bees so they do not attack the harvester.

questions.question: Name any five products got from bees.
questions.answer: Any five of: honey, beeswax, propolis, royal jelly, bee venom, and pollination services.

questions.question: Give any five reasons why poultry and bee keeping are good businesses.
questions.answer: Any five of: they need little land and little capital; they give food and income; they create employment; droppings give manure; bees pollinate crops; the products sell easily; they can be run beside other work.

questions.question: Give any four records a poultry farmer should keep.
questions.answer: Any four of: numbers of birds bought and sold; eggs collected each day; feeds used and their cost; vaccinations and treatments given; deaths; income and expenses.

questions.question: Give the difference between mass and weight.
questions.answer: Mass is the amount of matter in an object and never changes; weight is the pull of gravity on the object and changes from place to place.

questions.question: Name the instrument and the unit used for measuring: mass, weight, volume of a liquid.
questions.answer: Mass — beam balance, in kilogrammes; weight — spring balance, in newtons; volume of a liquid — measuring cylinder or jug, in litres or millilitres.

questions.question: Give the difference between capacity and volume.
questions.answer: Capacity is how much a container can hold; volume is the space a substance occupies.

questions.question: Change: 3 kg to grammes; 2.5 litres to millilitres; 4,000 cm³ to litres.
questions.answer: 3 kg = 3,000 g; 2.5 litres = 2,500 ml; 4,000 cm³ = 4 litres.

questions.question: Find the volume of a box 8 cm long, 5 cm wide and 4 cm high.
Why are standard measures better than the hand span or the calabash?
questions.answer: Because standard measures are the same everywhere and never change, while a hand span or calabash differs from person to person, so trade would be unfair and measurements could not be repeated.

questions.question: What makes an object float or sink?
questions.answer: An object floats if it is less dense than the liquid and sinks if it is more dense. Its shape also matters, because a shape that holds air pushes aside more water.

questions.question: Give three objects that float and three that sink in water.
questions.answer: Float: wood, cork, a plastic bottle with air (also ice, oil). Sink: a stone, a nail, a metal spoon (also sand, glass).

questions.question: Why does an iron sheet sink while a boat made of iron floats?
questions.answer: The flat sheet is denser than water so it sinks; the boat shape holds air and pushes aside much more water, so the boat as a whole is less dense than water and floats.

questions.question: Describe an experiment to show that an egg floats in salty water.
questions.answer: Put an egg in a glass of fresh water — it sinks. Add salt slowly, stirring, and keep watching. As more salt dissolves, the water becomes denser, and at some point the egg rises and floats. This shows that a liquid's density affects floating.

questions.question: Describe the displacement method for finding the volume of a stone.
questions.answer: Pour water into a measuring cylinder and read the level. Lower the stone gently on a string until it is fully covered. Read the new level. Subtract the first reading from the second — the difference is the volume of the stone.

questions.question: A stone raises the water level in a cylinder from 30 cm³ to 75 cm³. Find its volume.
Define density and give its formula and unit.
questions.answer: Density is the mass of a substance in a given volume. Density = mass ÷ volume, measured in g/cm³.

questions.question: An object of mass 240 g has a volume of 60 cm³. Find its density.
A block of density 2.5 g/cm³ has a volume of 40 cm³. Find its mass.
questions.answer: Mass = density × volume = 2.5 × 40 = 100 g

items.subject: Science
subtopics: 1. WHAT SOIL IS AND HOW IT IS FORMED
3. COMPONENTS OF SOIL AND HOW TO SHOW THEM

questions.question: What is soil? Give the two ways in which it is formed.
questions.answer: Soil is the loose top layer of the earth's surface in which plants grow. It is formed by the weathering of rocks and the decomposition of dead plant and animal matter.

questions.question: Name three kinds of weathering and give an example of each.
questions.answer: Physical — heat and cold cracking rocks; chemical — water and chemicals dissolving rocks; biological — plant roots and burrowing animals breaking rocks.

questions.question: Name the three types of soil and give two properties of each.
questions.answer: Sandy — large particles, drains very fast, poor at holding water; clay — very small particles, sticky when wet and hard when dry, holds too much water; loam — a mixture with plenty of humus, holds enough water and drains well.

questions.question: Which soil is best for farming, and why?
questions.answer: Loam, because it holds enough water but still drains well, contains air and plenty of humus, and is easy to work.

questions.question: Which soil is used for making pots and bricks, and why?
questions.answer: Clay, because its very fine particles stick together when wet and become hard when dried or fired.

questions.question: Name the layers of a soil profile from the top.
questions.answer: Top soil → sub soil → weathered rock → bedrock.

questions.question: Name the five components of soil.
questions.answer: Mineral (rock) particles, air, water, humus and living things.

questions.question: Describe an experiment to show that soil contains air.
questions.answer: Drop dry soil into a container of water. Bubbles rise to the surface, showing that air was trapped in the spaces between the soil particles.

questions.question: Describe an experiment to show that soil contains water.
questions.answer: Put soil in a dry test tube and heat it gently. Drops of water appear on the cooler upper part of the tube, showing that the soil contained water.

questions.question: Describe an experiment to show that soil contains humus.
questions.answer: Heat soil strongly in a tin or on a metal sheet. It gives off smoke and a burning smell and becomes lighter in colour, showing that the humus has burnt away.

questions.question: Give any six importances of soil.
questions.answer: Any six of: it anchors plants and supplies water and mineral salts; it is used for farming; it is a home for soil animals; it is used for building bricks and roads; it is used for pottery; it holds and filters water; some soils contain minerals.

questions.question: What is soil erosion? Name any four types.
questions.answer: Soil erosion is the carrying away of the top soil by water, wind or animals. Types: sheet, rill, gully, wind erosion and landslides (any four).

questions.question: Give any five causes of soil erosion.
questions.answer: Any five of: cutting down trees; bush burning; overgrazing; farming on steep slopes; over-cultivation; poor road drainage; heavy rain falling on bare soil.

questions.question: What is soil exhaustion, and what causes it?
questions.answer: Soil exhaustion is the loss of soil fertility. It is caused by growing the same crop again and again, over-cultivation, and failing to add manure or rest the land.

questions.question: Give any eight methods of soil conservation.
questions.answer: Any eight of: mulching; terracing; contour ploughing; strip cropping; crop rotation; applying manure and compost; planting cover crops and trees; controlled grazing; fallowing; digging trenches and check dams.

items.subject: Science
subtopics: 3. CARE OF VACCINES — THE COLD CHAIN
5. PROBLEMS THAT HINDER IMMUNISATION, AND SOLUTIONS

questions.question: What is immunity? Name its two types.
questions.answer: Immunity is the ability of the body to fight and resist disease. Its two types are natural and acquired (artificial) immunity.

questions.question: Give three examples of natural immunity.
questions.answer: Any three of: the skin, tears, saliva and stomach acid; white blood cells; antibodies a baby gets from the mother and from breast milk; immunity left after recovering from a disease.

questions.question: What is immunisation, and what is a vaccine?
questions.answer: Immunisation is giving a person a vaccine so that the body can make antibodies and resist a disease. A vaccine is a medicine, usually made from weakened or killed germs, given to protect the body.

questions.question: Name any six immunisable childhood diseases.
questions.answer: Any six of: tuberculosis, polio, diphtheria, whooping cough, tetanus, measles, hepatitis B, Haemophilus influenzae type b (also pneumonia and rotavirus today).

questions.question: Which vaccine protects against tuberculosis, and when is it given?
questions.answer: BCG, given at birth, on the right upper arm.

questions.question: Which five diseases are covered by the pentavalent vaccine?
questions.answer: Diphtheria, whooping cough, tetanus, hepatitis B and Haemophilus influenzae type b (Hib).

questions.question: At what ages are polio and pentavalent vaccines given?
questions.answer: Polio at birth, 6, 10 and 14 weeks; pentavalent at 6, 10 and 14 weeks.

questions.question: At what age is the measles vaccine given?
questions.answer: At 9 months (with a later second dose).

questions.question: What is the cold chain, and why is it necessary?
questions.answer: The cold chain is the system of keeping vaccines cold from the factory to the child. It is necessary because vaccines are spoilt by heat and strong light and would then fail to protect the child.

questions.question: Give any four ways of caring for vaccines.
questions.answer: Any four of: keep them in a refrigerator or cold box with ice packs; carry them in a vaccine carrier; check the temperature with a thermometer; keep them out of sunlight; never use them after the expiry date or when the vial monitor shows they are spoilt.

questions.question: What is an immunisation card, and why must it be kept safely?
questions.answer: It is the card that shows all the vaccines a child has received and the dates. It must be kept safely so that health workers know which doses are still due, and it is often needed when joining school.

questions.question: Give any five importances of immunisation.
questions.answer: Any five of: it prevents killer diseases and disabilities; it reduces child deaths; it is cheaper than treatment; it keeps children healthy and in school; it has wiped out smallpox; it protects the whole community.

questions.question: Which disease has been wiped out completely by immunisation?
questions.answer: Smallpox.

questions.question: Give any five problems that hinder immunisation in Uganda.
questions.answer: Any five of: ignorance and rumours; long distances and poor roads; power failure spoiling vaccines; parents forgetting or losing the card; insecurity in some areas; shortage of funds, staff or vaccines; religious or cultural objections.

questions.question: Suggest a solution to each of: rumours about vaccines, long distance to the clinic, power failure, forgetting the appointment.
questions.answer: Rumours — health education by radio, schools and village health teams; long distance — outreach and mobile clinics; power failure — solar fridges, cold boxes and ice packs; forgetting — reminders from village health teams and keeping the card where it is easily seen.

items.subject: Science
subtopics: 2. THE ALIMENTARY CANAL AND WHAT EACH PART DOES
4. DISEASES AND DISORDERS OF THE DIGESTIVE SYSTEM

questions.question: What is digestion? What is the digestive system?
questions.answer: Digestion is the breaking down of food into a form the body can absorb and use. The digestive system is the system of organs that breaks down food, absorbs it and removes the waste.

questions.question: Name the parts of the alimentary canal in order.
questions.answer: Mouth → oesophagus (gullet) → stomach → small intestine → large intestine → rectum → anus.

questions.question: Give the work of: the mouth, the stomach, the small intestine, the large intestine.
questions.answer: Mouth — chews the food and mixes it with saliva, which starts digesting starch; stomach — churns food with gastric juice and acid, which kill germs and start digesting protein; small intestine — completes digestion and absorbs the food into the blood; large intestine — absorbs water and mineral salts.

questions.question: What is peristalsis?
questions.answer: Peristalsis is the squeezing, wave-like movement of the walls of the alimentary canal that pushes food along.

questions.question: Name the four associated organs of the digestive system and the work of each.
questions.answer: Salivary glands — produce saliva; liver — produces bile, stores food and removes poisons; gall bladder — stores bile; pancreas — produces pancreatic juice.

questions.question: Which organ makes bile, where is it stored, and what does bile do?
questions.answer: The liver makes bile; it is stored in the gall bladder; bile breaks fats into small drops so they can be digested easily.

questions.question: Name the four types of teeth and the work of each.
questions.answer: Incisors — cutting and biting; canines — tearing; premolars — crushing and grinding; molars — chewing and grinding.

questions.question: How many teeth has an adult, and how many has a child?
questions.answer: An adult has 32; a child has 20 milk teeth.

questions.question: Into what is each of these digested: starch, protein, fats?
questions.answer: Starch → simple sugars (glucose); protein → amino acids; fats → fatty acids and glycerol.

questions.question: Where does most absorption take place, and through what?
questions.answer: In the small intestine, through tiny finger-like structures called villi.

questions.question: Name any six diseases or disorders of the digestive system and give the cause of each.
questions.answer: Any six, for example: diarrhoea — germs in dirty food and water; dysentery — bacteria or amoeba; cholera — bacteria in contaminated water; typhoid — bacteria in food and water; worms — worm eggs from dirt; constipation — little water and roughage; ulcers — too much acid and skipping meals; tooth decay — sugary foods and poor brushing.

questions.question: Give the signs of dysentery and of intestinal worms.
questions.answer: Dysentery: stool with blood and mucus, stomach pain and fever. Worms: stomach pain, pot belly, loss of weight, tiredness and anaemia.

questions.question: What is ORS, and how is a home mixture prepared?
questions.answer: ORS is oral rehydration salts, given to replace water and salts lost in diarrhoea. A home mixture: one litre of boiled, cooled water + eight level teaspoons of sugar + half a teaspoon of salt, stirred until dissolved.

questions.question: Give any eight ways of keeping the digestive system healthy.
questions.answer: Any eight of: eat a balanced diet with roughage; drink clean boiled water; wash hands with soap; wash fruits and cover food; chew well and eat at regular times; deworm every six months; brush teeth twice a day; use a clean latrine; avoid alcohol and self-medication; seek treatment early.

questions.question: Why should hands be washed with soap before eating?
questions.answer: Because germs and worm eggs from dirt, faeces and animals stay on the fingers. When we eat with dirty hands they enter the mouth and cause diarrhoea, dysentery, typhoid, cholera and worms. Soap removes them.

questions.question: What is matter? Give its three properties.
questions.answer: Matter is anything that has mass (weight) and occupies space. Properties: it has mass, it occupies space and it exerts pressure.

questions.question: Name the three states of matter and give two examples of each.
questions.answer: Solid — stone, ice; liquid — water, milk; gas — air, steam.

questions.question: Name the change of state in each: ice to water; water to steam; steam to water; water to ice.
questions.answer: Ice to water — melting; water to steam — evaporation (boiling); steam to water — condensation; water to ice — freezing.

questions.question: Define solute, solvent and solution, with an example of each.
questions.answer: Solute — the substance that dissolves, e.g. salt; solvent — the liquid it dissolves in, e.g. water; solution — the mixture formed, e.g. salty water.

questions.question: Give the difference between soluble and insoluble substances, with two examples of each.
questions.answer: Soluble substances dissolve, for example salt and sugar; insoluble ones do not, for example sand and stones.

questions.question: Name any six methods of separating mixtures and what each is used for.
questions.answer: Any six: hand picking — large pieces; winnowing — light from heavy; sieving — small from large; filtering — solids from liquids; decanting — settled solids from a liquid; evaporation — a dissolved solid; distillation — a pure liquid; magnetic separation — magnetic materials.

questions.question: How would you separate: salt from salty water; iron filings from sand; chaff from millet; mud from water?
questions.answer: Salt from salty water — evaporation; iron filings from sand — a magnet; chaff from millet — winnowing; mud from water — filtering (or decanting first).

questions.question: What is heat? Name any five sources of heat.
questions.answer: Heat is a form of energy that makes things hot. Sources: the sun, fire from firewood or charcoal, electricity, friction, chemical reactions (also geothermal heat and the body).

questions.question: Name the three ways in which heat travels and say where each mainly occurs.
questions.answer: Conduction — mainly in solids; convection — in liquids and gases; radiation — through empty space, needing no material.

questions.question: Describe an experiment to show conduction of heat.
questions.answer: Take a metal rod and stick pins along it with wax. Heat one end in a flame. The wax melts and the pins fall one after another from the hot end outwards, showing that heat travelled along the solid by conduction.

questions.question: Describe an experiment to show convection in water.
questions.answer: Heat water gently in a clear glass container and drop in a coloured crystal (or sawdust). The colour rises from the heated part, spreads at the top, sinks at the sides and circles, showing convection currents.

questions.question: Name any four good conductors and any four poor conductors of heat.
questions.answer: Good conductors: copper, aluminium, iron, silver. Poor conductors: wood, plastic, rubber, glass (also dry cloth, air, paper).

questions.question: Why are saucepans made of metal but their handles of wood or plastic?
questions.answer: The metal body conducts heat quickly to the food so it cooks fast, while the wooden or plastic handle is a poor conductor, so it stays cool and the cook is not burnt.

questions.question: Give any five effects of heat on matter.
questions.answer: Any five of: expansion when heated and contraction when cooled; change of state; burning; drying; killing germs; cooking food.

questions.question: Give any five uses and any four dangers of heat.
questions.answer: Uses (any five): cooking; boiling water to kill germs; warming the body and house; drying clothes and food; ironing; welding; generating electricity; making bricks and pots. Dangers (any four): burns and scalds; fires; smoke causing chest disease; suffocation from a charcoal stove in a closed room.

items.subject: Science
items.topic: Occupations in Our Community — Crop Growing
subtopics: 3. PESTS AND DISEASES OF TUBER CROPS

questions.question: What is a tuber? Give the two types with two examples of each.
questions.answer: A tuber is a swollen underground part of a plant in which food is stored. Root tubers — sweet potatoes and cassava; stem tubers — Irish potatoes and some yams.

questions.question: How can you tell a stem tuber from a root tuber?
questions.answer: A stem tuber has buds or "eyes" from which new shoots grow; a root tuber has no eyes and is grown from cuttings or the crown.

questions.question: What planting material is used for: sweet potatoes, cassava, Irish potatoes, carrots?
questions.answer: Sweet potatoes — vine cuttings; cassava — stem cuttings; Irish potatoes — seed tubers with eyes; carrots — seeds.

questions.question: Give the steps followed in growing a tuber crop.
questions.answer: Choose a suitable site → prepare the land into ridges or mounds → select clean planting materials → plant at the right spacing at the start of the rains → weed regularly → earth up → apply manure and rotate crops → control pests and diseases → harvest and store properly.

questions.question: Why are tuber crops planted on ridges or mounds?
questions.answer: Because ridges and mounds give loose, deep soil for the tubers to swell in, and they drain well so the tubers do not rot.

questions.question: What is earthing up, and why is it done?
questions.answer: Earthing up is heaping soil around the base of the plants. It covers the tubers so they do not become green or be attacked by weevils, supports the plant and controls weeds.

questions.question: Name any five pests of tuber crops and the damage each causes.
questions.answer: Any five: sweet potato weevil — bores into tubers, making them bitter; moles and rats — eat tubers underground; termites — eat stems and roots; aphids and whiteflies — suck sap and spread viruses; nematodes — cause galls and stunted plants.

questions.question: Name any four diseases of tuber crops and their signs.
questions.answer: Any four: cassava mosaic — yellow, twisted, small leaves; cassava brown streak — brown rot inside the tuber; potato blight — leaves turn black and the plant dies; bacterial wilt — sudden wilting and death.

questions.question: Which insect spreads cassava mosaic?
questions.answer: The whitefly.

questions.question: Give any six ways of controlling pests and diseases of tuber crops.
questions.answer: Any six of: plant clean, disease-free materials; use resistant varieties; practise crop rotation; earth up; weed and keep the garden clean; remove and burn diseased plants; harvest in time; trap rats and moles; use pesticides correctly; seek advice from the extension officer.

questions.question: Why should a farmer plant clean, disease-free cuttings?
questions.answer: Because diseases such as cassava mosaic and brown streak are carried in the cuttings themselves. Planting infected material spreads the disease to the whole garden, however well the farmer weeds or sprays.

questions.question: Give any four rules for harvesting tuber crops.
questions.answer: Any four of: dig carefully with a hoe or fork so the tubers are not cut or bruised; harvest when mature; harvest sweet potatoes piecemeal as needed; lift Irish potatoes when the leaves turn yellow; avoid harvesting in very wet conditions; keep damaged tubers separate.

questions.question: Give any five ways of storing tuber crops well.
questions.answer: Any five of: keep them in a cool, dry, dark, airy place; sort out damaged ones first; store Irish potatoes in crates or on racks, not heaps; dry cassava and make flour; slice and dry sweet potatoes; protect the store from rats and termites.

questions.question: Give any five uses of tuber crops.
questions.answer: Any five of: food rich in carbohydrates; income when sold; animal feed from peelings and vines; raw material for flour, starch and chips; planting material for the next season.

questions.question: Which tuber crop grows best in cool areas such as Kabale, and which one resists drought best?
questions.answer: Irish potatoes grow best in cool areas such as Kabale; cassava resists drought best.

items.subject: Science
subtopics: 3. PREVENTING AND CONTROLLING BACTERIAL AND FUNGAL DISEASES

questions.question: What are bacteria, and what instrument is used to see them?
questions.answer: Bacteria are very tiny living things (micro-organisms) that can only be seen with a microscope.

questions.question: Give any five characteristics of bacteria.
questions.answer: Any five of: they are very small; they are living and multiply very fast by splitting into two; they have different shapes — round, rod, spiral, comma; most need warmth, moisture, food and darkness; some form spores; some need air and others do not.

questions.question: Where are bacteria found, and where do they breed best?
questions.answer: They are found everywhere — in air, water, soil, food, on the skin and in the body. They breed best in warm, moist, dirty places such as rubbish heaps, stagnant water, uncovered food and dirty latrines.

questions.question: Give any five ways in which bacteria are useful.
questions.answer: Any five of: making yoghurt, sour milk and cheese; causing decay that returns nutrients to the soil; making manure and compost; fixing nitrogen in legume root nodules; helping digestion in the intestines; making vinegar, medicines and antibiotics; treating sewage; producing biogas.

questions.question: Name any six diseases caused by bacteria and how each is spread.
questions.answer: Any six: cholera — dirty water and food; typhoid — contaminated food and water; dysentery — dirty hands and flies; TB — coughing and sneezing; whooping cough and diphtheria — air; tetanus — dirt in wounds; pneumonia — droplets in air.

questions.question: What are fungi? Give any four examples.
questions.answer: Fungi are living things that have no chlorophyll, so they cannot make their own food, and feed on dead or living matter. Examples: mushrooms, yeast, moulds, the ringworm fungus.

questions.question: Give any four characteristics of fungi.
questions.answer: Any four of: they have no chlorophyll; they have no true roots, stems or leaves; they reproduce by spores; they grow in warm, damp, dark places; some are saprophytes and some parasites.

questions.question: Give the difference between a saprophyte and a parasite.
questions.answer: A saprophyte feeds on dead matter, for example the mould on bread; a parasite feeds on a living host, for example the ringworm fungus on human skin.

questions.question: Give any four ways in which fungi are useful.
questions.answer: Any four of: edible mushrooms as food; yeast for baking and brewing; penicillin and other medicines; causing decay that enriches the soil; flavouring cheese.

questions.question: Give any four ways in which fungi are harmful.
questions.answer: Any four of: they cause human diseases such as ringworm; they cause crop diseases such as blight; they spoil food, leather, clothes and books; some mushrooms are poisonous; moulds produce aflatoxins.

questions.question: Name two fungal diseases of human beings and two of crops.
questions.answer: Human: ringworm and athlete's foot (also thrush). Crops: potato blight and coffee leaf rust (also maize smut).

questions.question: What are aflatoxins, and how can they be prevented?
questions.answer: Aflatoxins are poisons produced by moulds growing on badly dried food such as groundnuts and maize. They are prevented by drying the produce properly, storing it in a dry, airy place, and throwing away mouldy or discoloured grain.

questions.question: Give any eight ways of preventing bacterial and fungal diseases.
questions.answer: Any eight of: bathe daily and wash hands with soap; wash, cover and cook food well; boil or treat drinking water; use latrines and dispose of rubbish properly; keep the body and clothes dry; do not share towels, combs or razor blades; sterilise instruments and use antiseptic on wounds; immunise children; take prescribed medicines correctly; dry and store food well.

questions.question: Why should a person finish the full course of antibiotics?
questions.answer: Because stopping early leaves some bacteria alive. They then multiply and become resistant, so the same medicine no longer works and the illness returns and is harder to treat.

questions.question: Why does ironing clothes and drying them in the sun help to prevent skin diseases?
questions.answer: Because the fungi and their spores, and parasites such as jiggers and lice, live in damp cloth. The sun's heat and the hot iron kill them, so the clothes are safe to wear.

items.subject: Science
items.topic: Types of Change — Biological, Physical and Chemical

questions.question: What is change? Name the three types.
questions.answer: Change is something becoming different from what it was. The three types are biological, physical and chemical.

questions.question: Name any five agents of change.
questions.answer: Any five of: heat and cold, water, air (oxygen and wind), living things such as bacteria, fungi, plants, animals and people, time, chemicals.

questions.question: What is a biological change? Give any four examples.
questions.answer: A biological change is a change that happens in living things as they grow and develop. Examples: germination of a seed; growth of a chick into a hen; a tadpole becoming a frog; decay of dead matter; healing of a wound (any four).

questions.question: Give the stages of growth in a human being.
questions.answer: Baby → child → adolescent → adult → old person.

questions.question: Give four physical changes that happen to girls and four that happen to boys at adolescence.
questions.answer: Girls: breasts develop; hips widen; menstruation begins; pubic and armpit hair grows. Boys: the voice deepens; shoulders broaden; wet dreams begin; pubic, armpit and facial hair grows.

questions.question: Give any six ways of caring for the body during these changes.
questions.answer: Any six of: bathe daily and wash the private parts with clean water; wear clean cotton underwear and change it daily; use and change clean sanitary materials; keep nails short and hair clean; eat well and rest; talk to a trusted adult about worries; choose good friends; abstain from sex.

questions.question: What should a child do if somebody tries to touch his or her private parts?
questions.answer: The child should say NO firmly, move away and tell a trusted adult at once — a parent, teacher, health worker, religious leader or the police. It must not be kept secret, and it is never the child's fault.

questions.question: What is a physical change? Give any five examples.
questions.answer: A physical change is one in which no new substance is formed and which can usually be reversed. Examples: melting ice; boiling water; dissolving salt; breaking a stick; bending a wire (any five).

questions.question: What is a chemical change? Give any five examples.
questions.answer: A chemical change is one in which a new substance is formed and which usually cannot be reversed. Examples: burning wood; rusting of iron; cooking food; souring of milk; rotting of fruit (any five).

questions.question: Give three differences between physical and chemical changes.
questions.answer: In a physical change no new substance is formed, it is usually reversible, and only shape, size or state changes; in a chemical change a new substance is formed, it is usually irreversible, and heat, light, gas or a smell is often produced.

questions.question: Classify each as physical or chemical: melting ice, burning wood, dissolving salt, rusting iron, breaking glass, souring milk.
questions.answer: Melting ice — physical; burning wood — chemical; dissolving salt — physical; rusting iron — chemical; breaking glass — physical; souring milk — chemical.

questions.question: What two things are needed for iron to rust?
questions.answer: Air (oxygen) and water (moisture).

questions.question: Give any four ways of preventing rusting.
questions.answer: Any four of: painting; oiling or greasing; galvanising (coating with zinc); coating with plastic; keeping the metal dry; using stainless steel or non-rusting metals.

questions.question: What is metamorphosis? Give the stages for a butterfly.
questions.answer: Metamorphosis is the change of form as an animal grows. For a butterfly: egg → larva (caterpillar) → pupa → adult butterfly.

questions.question: Why is cooking food said to be a chemical change?
questions.answer: Because cooking forms new substances — the food changes in colour, smell, taste and texture, and it cannot be turned back into the raw food it was.

questions.question: Name any six external parts of a goat.
questions.answer: Any six of: head, horns, beard, eyes, ears, nostrils, mouth, neck, back, udder or scrotum, legs, hooves, tail.

questions.question: Give four differences between a goat and a sheep.
questions.answer: A goat has a beard, a tail that points up, a coat of hair, and it browses on leaves; a sheep has no beard, a tail that hangs down, a woolly fleece, and it grazes on grass.

questions.question: Name two local and two exotic breeds of goats.
questions.answer: Local: Small East African and Mubende. Exotic: Toggenburg and Saanen (also Alpine, Boer).

questions.question: Name two local and two exotic breeds of sheep.
questions.answer: Local: East African Blackhead and Masai. Exotic: Merino and Dorper (also Corriedale).

questions.question: Give any five uses of goats and sheep.
questions.answer: Any five of: meat; milk; skins and hides; wool from sheep; manure; income and school fees; ceremonies; easy to keep on small land.

questions.question: Name any six external parts of a pig.
questions.answer: Any six of: snout, eyes, ears, bristles, back, hooves (cloven feet), curly tail, udder with teats, flank.

questions.question: Name any three exotic breeds of pigs.
questions.answer: Any three of: Large White, Landrace, Duroc, Hampshire.

questions.question: Give the meaning of: boar, sow, gilt, farrowing.
questions.answer: Boar — a male pig; sow — a female pig that has produced; gilt — a young female pig; farrowing — a pig giving birth.

questions.question: What is the gestation period of a pig?
questions.answer: About 114 days — three months, three weeks and three days.

questions.question: Give any six qualities of a good house for goats, sheep or pigs.
questions.answer: Any six of: raised and well-drained floor; well ventilated but not draughty; strong walls and a leak-proof roof; easy to clean with a slope and drainage; separate pens for the young and the sick; feeding troughs and drinkers; enough space; shade or a wallow for pigs.

questions.question: Why must a pig house have shade or a wallow?
questions.answer: Because pigs cannot sweat, so they cannot cool themselves in the usual way. Shade and a wallow keep them cool and also help control external parasites.

questions.question: Give any six ways of managing goats, sheep and pigs well.
questions.answer: Any six of: give clean water always; feed a balanced ration with mineral licks; deworm and vaccinate; spray or dip against parasites; clean the house daily; trim hooves; handle them gently; isolate sick animals; keep records; castrate males not needed for breeding.

questions.question: Name the products got from goats, from sheep and from pigs.
questions.answer: Goats: meat, milk, skins, manure, income. Sheep: meat, wool, skins, manure. Pigs: pork, bacon, ham, sausages, lard, bristles, manure.

questions.question: Name any four external and any three internal parasites of these animals.
questions.answer: External: ticks, lice, mites, fleas (also tsetse flies). Internal: round worms, tape worms, liver flukes (also lung worms).

questions.question: Name any five diseases, their signs and how each is prevented or controlled.
questions.answer: Any five, for example: pneumonia — coughing and fever, prevented by warm dry housing and treated early; foot and mouth — mouth and hoof sores, controlled by vaccination and quarantine; mange — itching and hair loss, controlled by spraying; worms — thin body and pot belly, controlled by deworming; African swine fever — high fever and sudden death, controlled only by hygiene and quarantine, as there is no cure.

items.subject: Science
subtopics: 4. FOOD VALUES AND A BALANCED DIET

questions.question: What is breastfeeding? For how long should a baby be breastfed exclusively?
questions.answer: Breastfeeding is feeding a baby on milk from the mother's breast. A baby should be breastfed exclusively for the first six months, then breastfed with other foods up to two years or beyond.

questions.question: Give any four advantages of breastfeeding to the baby and two to the mother.
questions.answer: To the baby (any four): breast milk is complete food; colostrum gives antibodies; it is clean, warm and ready; it is easy to digest; it builds love between mother and baby. To the mother: it costs nothing; it helps the womb return to normal (also delays another pregnancy).

questions.question: What is colostrum, and why is it important?
questions.answer: Colostrum is the first thick yellow milk produced after birth. It is important because it is rich in antibodies that protect the baby from disease, and in nutrients for a good start.

questions.question: What is bottle feeding? Give two advantages and four disadvantages.
questions.answer: Bottle feeding is feeding a baby milk from a bottle. Advantages: anybody can feed the baby; the amount can be measured. Disadvantages: bottles are easily contaminated and cause diarrhoea; formula and bottles are expensive; there are no antibodies; the bond with the mother is weaker; over-dilution causes malnutrition.

questions.question: If a mother must bottle feed, what four rules must she follow?
questions.answer: Sterilise the bottle and teat by boiling; use boiled water; mix exactly as instructed; feed the milk at once and never keep left-overs (using a cup and spoon is safer).

questions.question: Who are vulnerable people? Name any five groups.
questions.answer: Vulnerable people are those most easily harmed by poor feeding and disease. Any five of: babies and young children; expectant mothers; breastfeeding mothers; the sick, including people with HIV; the elderly; people with disabilities.

questions.question: What foods does an expectant mother especially need, and why?
questions.answer: She needs iron-rich foods (dodo, liver, beans), protein, fruits and vegetables and plenty of water, because she is feeding herself and the growing baby and is at risk of anaemia.

questions.question: Name the seven food values and give one example of each.
questions.answer: Carbohydrates — matooke; proteins — beans; fats and oils — cooking oil; vitamins — fruits; mineral salts — milk; water — clean drinking water; roughage — vegetables.

questions.question: What is a balanced diet? Give an example of a balanced meal from your home.
questions.answer: A balanced diet is a meal containing all the food values in the right amounts. Example: matooke with beans, greens, a fruit and water.

questions.question: Name any six deficiency diseases and the food value missing in each.
questions.answer: Any six: kwashiorkor — protein; marasmus — energy and protein; anaemia — iron; rickets — vitamin D and calcium; night blindness — vitamin A; scurvy — vitamin C; goitre — iodine; beriberi — vitamin B1.

questions.question: Give the signs of kwashiorkor and of marasmus.
questions.answer: Kwashiorkor: swollen legs and face, thin light hair, pot belly, misery and loss of appetite. Marasmus: very thin body, "old man's face", loose skin, ribs showing.

questions.question: How can anaemia be prevented?
questions.answer: By eating iron-rich foods such as dodo, nakati, liver, beans and meat, together with vitamin C fruits to absorb the iron; by deworming regularly; by sleeping under a treated mosquito net to avoid malaria; and by treating bleeding early.

questions.question: Give any six rules of food hygiene.
questions.answer: Any six of: wash hands with soap before handling food and eating; wash fruits and vegetables; use clean water and utensils; cover food against flies; keep animals out of the kitchen; do not let a person with diarrhoea or a wound cook for others; wash the cooking place daily.

questions.question: Give any four ways of preparing food so that the food value is not lost.
questions.answer: Any four of: do not overcook vegetables; steam rather than boil; use the cooking water in the sauce; cut vegetables just before cooking; cook with the lid on; avoid too much oil and salt.

questions.question: Give any five ways of storing food well, and say why mouldy groundnuts must never be eaten.
questions.answer: Any five of: dry grains and legumes well; store in clean, dry, airy places; use sacks on pallets or granaries; protect from rats, weevils and moulds; keep milk, meat and cooked food covered and cool and reheat well. Mouldy groundnuts must never be eaten because the moulds produce aflatoxins, poisons that damage the liver and can cause cancer.

items.subject: Science
items.topic: Primary Health Care and Family Care
subtopics: 4. PHC ACTIVITIES THAT PROMOTE COMMUNITY HYGIENE

questions.question: What is Primary Health Care?
questions.answer: Primary Health Care is essential health care made available to all people in the community at a cost they can afford, with their full participation, aimed at preventing disease and promoting health.

questions.question: Name any six elements of PHC.
questions.answer: Any six of: health education; proper nutrition; safe water and basic sanitation; maternal and child health including family planning; immunisation; prevention and control of local endemic diseases; treatment of common diseases and injuries; provision of essential drugs; control of HIV/AIDS; care of the disabled and elderly.

questions.question: Name any four principles of PHC and explain two.
questions.answer: Any four of: community participation, equitable distribution, appropriate technology, intersectoral collaboration, focus on prevention, affordability. (Explain two, for example: community participation means the people themselves plan and run their health services; appropriate technology means using simple, cheap methods such as pit latrines and ORS that the community can manage.)

questions.question: Why is prevention said to be better than cure?
questions.answer: Because preventing a disease costs far less than treating it, saves lives and suffering, keeps children in school and adults at work, and stops the disease from spreading to others.

questions.question: Give any six PHC activities that promote community hygiene.
questions.answer: Any six of: digging rubbish pits and using latrines; protecting water sources; draining stagnant water and clearing bushes; building drying racks, bath shelters and hand-washing facilities; health education; immunisation days; kitchen gardens; school health clubs and clean-up days.

questions.question: Give any five responsibilities of an individual in keeping healthy.
questions.answer: Any five of: keep the body clean; eat a balanced diet; use the latrine and wash hands with soap; sleep under a treated net; seek treatment early; avoid alcohol, smoking and drug abuse; keep the surroundings clean.

questions.question: Give any five responsibilities of a family in keeping its members healthy.
questions.answer: Any five of: build and maintain a latrine, bath shelter, rubbish pit and drying rack; boil or treat drinking water; feed the family well; take children for immunisation; care for the sick, elderly and disabled; keep the home and compound clean.

questions.question: Give any four responsibilities of the community and four of the government.
questions.answer: Community: protect water sources; hold clean-up days; support village health teams; build and maintain health centres (also report outbreaks). Government: train and pay health workers; supply drugs and vaccines; build health centres; make and enforce public health laws (also run health campaigns).

questions.question: What is a family? Name the four types.
questions.answer: A family is a group of people related by blood, marriage or adoption who live together and care for one another. Types: nuclear, extended, single-parent and child-headed.

questions.question: Give any five duties of parents and five duties of children.
questions.answer: Parents: provide food, shelter, clothing, medical care and education; give love, guidance and discipline; protect the children. Children: obey and respect parents; help with chores; go to school and work hard; care for younger ones and the elderly; keep clean; report anything that frightens or hurts them.

questions.question: How should the family care for a sick person?
questions.answer: Give clean bedding and a quiet, airy room; provide soft, tasty food and plenty of fluids; give the medicine on time and complete the dose; keep the person clean and comfortable; watch for danger signs and take them to a health worker quickly.

questions.question: How should the family care for the elderly and for people with disabilities?
questions.answer: The elderly need soft food, warmth, company, help with washing and moving, and respect. People with disabilities need support without pity, help to attend school and work, assistive aids where possible, and full inclusion in family activities.

questions.question: Name any six things found in a healthy home.
questions.answer: Any six of: a clean compound; a latrine; a rubbish pit; a drying rack; a bath shelter; a kitchen with a raised fireplace; clean covered water storage; mosquito nets on the beds; a kitchen garden.

questions.question: Who are village health teams, and what do they do?
questions.answer: Village health teams are trained community volunteers. They teach families about health, encourage immunisation and use of latrines and nets, treat or refer simple illnesses, follow up sick people and report outbreaks.

questions.question: Give any four ways in which a school can practise PHC.
questions.answer: Any four of: keeping the compound and latrines clean; running hand-washing points with soap; a school health club with drama, posters and talks; growing vegetables in a school garden; inspecting pupils' hygiene; inviting health workers; deworming and immunisation days.

items.subject: Social Studies
items.topic: Location of Uganda on the Map of East Africa
subtopics: 5. THE SIZE AND POSITION OF UGANDA

questions.question: Name the five countries that neighbour Uganda and give the direction of each.
questions.answer: Kenya — east; South Sudan — north; D.R. Congo — west; Rwanda — south-west; Tanzania — south.

questions.question: What is a compass used for? Name the four cardinal and four semi-cardinal points.
questions.answer: A compass is used to find direction. Cardinal: North, East, South, West. Semi-cardinal: North-East, South-East, South-West, North-West.

questions.question: Define lines of latitude and lines of longitude.
