questions.answer: Lines of latitude are imaginary lines running from west to east, showing distance north or south of the Equator. Lines of longitude run from the North Pole to the South Pole, showing distance east or west of the Prime Meridian.

questions.question: Which line of latitude passes through Uganda, and what does it do to the country?
questions.answer: The Equator. It divides Uganda so that part of the country lies in the Northern Hemisphere and part in the Southern Hemisphere.

questions.question: Between which lines of latitude and longitude does Uganda lie?
questions.answer: Between about 4°N and 1°S, and between about 29°E and 35°E.

questions.question: Why is Uganda called a landlocked country, and which two ports does it use?
questions.answer: Because it has no coastline of its own. It uses the ports of Mombasa in Kenya and Dar es Salaam in Tanzania.

questions.question: Name the five elements of a map.
questions.answer: Title, key, scale, compass (direction) and frame.

questions.question: Give the use of a key and of a scale on a map.
questions.answer: The key explains the symbols used on the map; the scale shows how distance on the map compares with distance on the ground.

questions.question: On a map of scale 1 : 50,000, two towns are 8 cm apart. Find the real distance.
How is a grid reference read?
questions.answer: Read the eastings (the lines going across) first, then the northings (the lines going up).

questions.question: What is the capital city of Uganda, and where is the international airport?
questions.answer: The capital is Kampala; the international airport is at Entebbe.

questions.question: About how big is Uganda, and about how much of it is water and swamp?
questions.answer: About 241,000 km², and about one fifth of it is open water and swamp.

questions.question: Name the four regions of Uganda.
questions.answer: Central, Eastern, Northern and Western.

questions.question: Give one reason why the number of districts in Uganda keeps changing.
questions.answer: Because government creates new districts by splitting the old ones, to bring services nearer to the people.

questions.question: Draw the map of Uganda showing the Equator, Kampala and the neighbouring countries.
questions.answer: Learner's map. It should show Uganda with the Equator crossing the south, Kampala marked near Lake Victoria, and the five neighbours named in their correct positions.

items.subject: Social Studies
subtopics: 3. THE RIFT VALLEY, PLATEAUX AND PLAINS
5. HOW PHYSICAL FEATURES AFFECT PEOPLE'S LIVES

questions.question: What are physical features? Name any six found in Uganda.
questions.answer: Physical features are the natural land forms found on the earth's surface. Any six of: mountains, hills, plateaux, plains, rift valleys, lakes, rivers, waterfalls, swamps, islands.

questions.question: Name the highest mountain in Uganda, its highest peak and its height.
questions.answer: Mt Rwenzori; its highest peak is Margherita, about 5,109 metres high.

questions.question: Name any three volcanic mountains in Uganda and say where each is.
questions.answer: Any three: Mt Elgon — Mbale in the east; Muhavura — Kisoro in the south-west; Moroto — Karamoja in the north-east (also Kadam, Napak).

questions.question: Give the difference between a block mountain and a volcanic mountain, with one Ugandan example of each.
questions.answer: A block mountain is formed when land between two faults is pushed up or the sides sink, for example Rwenzori; a volcanic mountain is formed when molten rock comes out of the earth, cools and piles up, for example Elgon.

questions.question: What is a rift valley? Name three lakes found in Uganda's rift valley.
questions.answer: A rift valley is a deep, wide valley formed when the land between two faults sinks. Lakes: Albert, Edward and George.

questions.question: Name any five lakes in Uganda and say how each type was formed.
questions.answer: Any five, for example: Victoria and Kyoga — down-warping; Albert, Edward and George — faulting; Katwe — volcanic (crater); a lake behind a dam — man-made.

questions.question: What is a crater lake? Give one example in Uganda.
questions.answer: A crater lake is a lake formed in the mouth of an old volcano. Example: Lake Katwe (also Nyamunuka).

questions.question: Trace the course of the River Nile through Uganda, naming its two parts.
questions.answer: The Nile leaves Lake Victoria at Jinja as the Victoria Nile, flows through Lake Kyoga, over Murchison Falls into Lake Albert, and then flows north as the Albert Nile into South Sudan.

questions.question: Name any four waterfalls in Uganda and the rivers on which they are found.
questions.answer: Any four: Murchison (Kabalega) Falls and Karuma Falls — the Victoria Nile; Bujagali and Owen Falls — the Nile near Jinja; Sipi Falls — the River Sipi on Mt Elgon.

questions.question: Name any three islands of Uganda.
questions.answer: Any three of: the Ssese Islands, Buvuma, Koome (all in Lake Victoria).

questions.question: Give any five ways in which physical features help the people of Uganda.
questions.answer: Any five of: mountains give relief rainfall and fertile soils; lakes and rivers give water, fish and transport; rivers give hydro-electric power; features attract tourists; swamps give papyrus, clay and water; they form natural boundaries.

questions.question: Give any four problems caused by physical features.
questions.answer: Any four of: mountains make road building hard; steep slopes cause soil erosion and landslides; rivers and lakes flood; swamps breed mosquitoes and bilharzia snails; some areas are cut off in the rains.

questions.question: Why do landslides happen at Bududa, and how can they be prevented?
questions.answer: Because people have cleared the trees and farm on very steep slopes on Mt Elgon, so heavy rain loosens the bare soil and it slides. Prevention: plant trees and grass on the slopes, dig terraces and contour trenches, avoid cultivating very steep land, and resettle people from dangerous slopes.

questions.question: Give any five ways of caring for physical features.
questions.answer: Any five of: plant trees on hills and river banks; dig terraces and contour trenches; do not build or farm in swamps; do not pour waste into lakes and rivers; avoid bush burning; restore quarried land; obey environmental laws.

questions.question: Draw the map of Uganda and mark on it Mt Rwenzori, Lake Victoria and Murchison Falls.
questions.answer: Learner's map. Rwenzori in the west, Lake Victoria in the south, and Murchison Falls on the Victoria Nile in the north-west.

items.subject: Social Studies
subtopics: 3. FACTORS THAT INFLUENCE THE CLIMATE OF UGANDA
5. PROBLEMS ASSOCIATED WITH CLIMATE, AND SOLUTIONS

questions.question: Give the difference between weather and climate.
questions.answer: Weather is the condition of the atmosphere at a particular time, while climate is the average weather of a place over a long period, usually 30 years or more.

questions.question: Name any five elements of weather and the instrument used to measure each.
questions.answer: Any five: rainfall — rain gauge; temperature — thermometer; wind direction — wind vane; wind speed — anemometer; humidity — hygrometer; air pressure — barometer; sunshine — sunshine recorder.

questions.question: What is a Stevenson screen, and why is it painted white?
questions.answer: A Stevenson screen is the white wooden box in which weather instruments are kept at a weather station. It is painted white to reflect heat, so the readings are not affected by the sun.

questions.question: Name the climatic regions of Uganda and describe any two.
questions.answer: Equatorial (wet), tropical (savannah), semi-arid and montane. (Describe any two, for example: the equatorial region has rain almost all year, over 1,200 mm, and is warm and humid; the semi-arid region has under 750 mm of unreliable rain, long dry spells and very high temperatures.)

questions.question: Which part of Uganda is the wettest, and which is the driest?
questions.answer: The wettest is the Lake Victoria basin and the south-west; the driest is Karamoja.

questions.question: Give any five factors that influence the climate of Uganda.
questions.answer: Any five of: altitude, nearness to water bodies, relief, vegetation, winds, latitude, human activities.

questions.question: Why is it cold in Kabale and on the Rwenzori Mountains?
questions.answer: Because they lie at a high altitude, and temperature falls by about 1 °C for every 150 metres you climb.

questions.question: Explain how Lake Victoria influences the climate of the areas near it.
questions.answer: Water evaporates from the lake and forms clouds, so the areas near it receive more rainfall; the lake also cools the air by day and warms it at night, giving a moderate temperature.

questions.question: What is relief rainfall, and what is a rain shadow?
questions.answer: Relief rainfall is rain formed when moist air is forced to rise over a mountain, cools and condenses. A rain shadow is the dry leeward side of the mountain, which receives little rain.

questions.question: Give three activities favoured by the wet equatorial region.
questions.answer: Any three of: growing coffee, bananas, sugar cane, tea or vanilla; fishing; lumbering.

questions.question: Give two activities carried out in the semi-arid region of Karamoja and say why.
questions.answer: Nomadic pastoralism, because the pasture and water are scattered and seasonal, so herders move to find them; and growing drought-resistant crops such as sorghum and millet, because the rainfall is too little for crops that need much water.

questions.question: Give any five problems associated with climate in Uganda.
questions.answer: Any five of: drought and famine, floods, landslides, hailstorms and lightning, soil erosion, unreliable rainfall, crop pests and diseases.

questions.question: Give a solution to each of: drought, floods, landslides, soil erosion.
questions.answer: Drought — irrigation and water harvesting; floods — drainage channels and not building in wetlands; landslides — terracing, planting trees and avoiding steep slopes; soil erosion — contour ploughing, mulching and cover crops.

questions.question: Give any four human activities that are changing the climate of Uganda.
questions.answer: Any four of: cutting down forests; draining swamps; bush burning; smoke from factories and vehicles; overgrazing; quarrying and mining.

questions.question: Suggest any four ways of protecting the climate of Uganda.
questions.answer: Any four of: plant trees (afforestation and reafforestation); protect wetlands and forest reserves; use energy-saving stoves, biogas and solar; stop bush burning; teach people about the environment; enforce environmental laws.

items.subject: Social Studies
subtopics: 2. TYPES OF NATURAL VEGETATION IN UGANDA

questions.question: What is vegetation? Give the two main types with two examples of each.
questions.answer: Vegetation is the general plant cover of an area. Natural vegetation grows on its own — forests and swamps; planted vegetation is planted by people — plantations and woodlots.

questions.question: Name any four types of natural vegetation found in Uganda and where each is found.
questions.answer: Any four: tropical rain forest — Mabira, Budongo, Bwindi; savannah — central and northern Uganda; semi-desert — Karamoja; montane — Rwenzori and Elgon slopes; swamp vegetation — around Lakes Kyoga and Victoria.

questions.question: Name any four natural forests in Uganda and the districts where they are.
questions.answer: Any four: Mabira — Buikwe; Budongo — Masindi; Bwindi — Kanungu; Kibale — Kabarole; Mpanga — Mpigi.

questions.question: Describe how vegetation changes as you climb Mt Rwenzori.
questions.answer: It changes in bands: forest at the bottom, then bamboo, then heath, then moorland, and finally bare rock, ice and snow at the top, because it becomes colder as you climb.

questions.question: Give any five factors that influence the distribution of vegetation in Uganda.
questions.answer: Any five of: rainfall, temperature, soil type, relief and altitude, drainage, human activities.

questions.question: Why does thick forest grow around Lake Victoria but not in Karamoja?
questions.answer: Because the area around Lake Victoria receives heavy, reliable rainfall and has deep fertile soils, which support tall trees, while Karamoja is semi-arid, with under 750 mm of unreliable rain, so only short grass and thorn bushes can survive.

questions.question: Give any six importances of vegetation.
questions.answer: Any six of: timber, poles, firewood and charcoal; herbal medicine and wild foods; pasture; attracting rainfall; preventing soil erosion; a home for wild animals; attracting tourists; raw materials for industry; filtering water in wetlands; shade and beauty.

questions.question: Give three uses of papyrus from the swamps.
questions.answer: Making mats, baskets and hats; thatching and fencing; and making crafts for sale (papyrus also filters water and provides mulch).

questions.question: Which vegetation zones are densely populated, and why?
questions.answer: The savannah, the Lake Victoria crescent and the lower mountain slopes, because they have good rainfall, fertile soils and land that is easy to clear and farm.

questions.question: Which vegetation zones are sparsely populated, and why?
questions.answer: Thick forests (hard to clear, poor leached soils, pests), semi-desert Karamoja (too dry) and swamps (waterlogged, mosquitoes, hard to build on).

questions.question: Give any five effects of a growing population on vegetation.
questions.answer: Any five of: deforestation for farmland and firewood; swamp reclamation; overgrazing; bush burning; soil erosion and loss of fertility; loss of wildlife habitats; disappearance of some plant species.

questions.question: Give the difference between afforestation and reafforestation.
questions.answer: Afforestation is planting trees in an area where there were none before; reafforestation is replanting trees where they were cut down.

questions.question: Give any six ways of conserving vegetation.
questions.answer: Any six of: afforestation and reafforestation; agroforestry; energy-saving stoves, biogas and solar; gazetting forest reserves and parks; protecting wetlands and river banks; controlled grazing and burning; public education; enforcing laws.

questions.question: Name the two bodies that protect Uganda's forests and environment.
questions.answer: The National Forestry Authority (NFA) and the National Environment Management Authority (NEMA).

questions.question: Draw the map of Uganda and shade Mabira Forest, the Karamoja dry area and Bwindi Forest.
questions.answer: Learner's map. Mabira in the centre near Jinja, Karamoja in the north-east, and Bwindi in the far south-west.

items.subject: Social Studies
subtopics: 2. MINERALS AND WHERE THEY ARE FOUND
3. USES OF NATURAL RESOURCES AND THEIR ECONOMIC VALUE
4. PROBLEMS FACED IN DEVELOPING NATURAL RESOURCES
5. BAD PRACTICES THAT DESTROY NATURAL RESOURCES

questions.question: What are natural resources? Name any six found in Uganda.
questions.answer: Natural resources are useful things provided by nature which people use to satisfy their needs. Any six of: land and soil, water, minerals, forests and vegetation, wildlife, climate, people.

questions.question: Name the mineral mined at each of: Kilembe, Hima, Katwe, Busia.
questions.answer: Kilembe — copper; Hima — limestone; Katwe — salt; Busia — gold.

questions.question: Where was oil discovered in Uganda, and give one use of it.
questions.answer: In the Albertine Graben (around Hoima and Buliisa). It is used to make fuel such as petrol, diesel and paraffin, and it earns the country money.

questions.question: Give the difference between open cast and shaft mining, with a Ugandan example of each.
questions.answer: Open cast mining removes the soil above the mineral and scoops it out, for example limestone at Hima; shaft mining sinks deep shafts and tunnels underground, for example copper at Kilembe.

questions.question: Give any five uses of water as a natural resource.
questions.answer: Any five of: drinking and domestic use; irrigation; fishing; transport; hydro-electric power; tourism; watering animals; industry.

questions.question: Name any four hydro-electric power stations in Uganda.
questions.answer: Any four of: Nalubaale, Kiira, Bujagali, Isimba, Karuma.

questions.question: Give any five ways in which natural resources help the economy of Uganda.
questions.answer: Any five of: they earn foreign exchange; they create employment; they give government taxes and royalties; they supply raw materials for industries; they lead to building of roads and towns; they raise people's incomes.

questions.question: Why are people also called a natural resource?
questions.answer: Because the people supply the labour and skills needed to use every other resource, they pay taxes, and they form the market that buys the goods produced.

questions.question: Give any six problems faced in developing Uganda's natural resources.
questions.answer: Any six of: shortage of capital; low technology and few skilled people; poor transport; small scattered deposits; unstable world prices; pollution; land disputes; corruption and smuggling; pests, diseases and drought; over-exploitation.

questions.question: Give any six bad practices that destroy natural resources.
questions.answer: Any six of: deforestation; bush burning; swamp draining; over-fishing and use of poison or wrong nets; poaching; overgrazing; over-cultivation; mining without restoring land; pouring waste into water; careless use of chemicals.

questions.question: Give any five ways of caring for the soil.
questions.answer: Any five of: crop rotation, mulching, terracing, contour ploughing, applying manure, planting cover crops, fallowing, controlled grazing.

questions.question: Give any four ways of protecting fish in Uganda's lakes.
questions.answer: Any four of: using the recommended net sizes; observing closed seasons; banning poison and explosives; encouraging fish farming; patrolling the lakes; removing water hyacinth.

questions.question: Name the three government bodies that protect the environment, forests and wildlife.
questions.answer: NEMA (environment), the National Forestry Authority (NFA) and the Uganda Wildlife Authority (UWA).

questions.question: Why is it better to process minerals in Uganda than to export them raw?
questions.answer: Because processing adds value, so the goods sell at a much higher price; it also creates jobs at home, supplies local industries, and saves the country from depending on unstable raw-material prices.

questions.question: Draw the map of Uganda and mark Kilembe, Tororo and Lake Katwe.
questions.answer: Learner's map. Kilembe in the west near the Rwenzori, Tororo in the east, and Lake Katwe in the western rift valley.

items.subject: Social Studies
subtopics: 1. THE MAJOR ETHNIC GROUPS OF UGANDA

questions.question: What is an ethnic group? Name the four major ethnic groups of Uganda.
questions.answer: An ethnic group is a large group of people who share the same origin, language family and customs. The four are the Bantu, the Luo (River–Lake Nilotes), the Nilo-Hamites (Plain Nilotes) and the Hamites (Cushites).

questions.question: Give the cradle land of each of the four groups.
questions.answer: Bantu — Central and West Africa; Luo — Bahr-el-Ghazal, South Sudan; Nilo-Hamites — Ethiopia; Hamites — North-East Africa.

questions.question: Name any three tribes in each of the Bantu and Luo groups.
questions.answer: Bantu: Baganda, Banyankole, Bagisu (also Banyoro, Batooro, Bakiga, Basoga). Luo: Acholi, Langi, Alur (also Japadhola).

questions.question: Give any five reasons why the ethnic groups migrated into Uganda.
questions.answer: Any five of: search for fertile land and pasture; population pressure; wars and conflicts; drought and famine; diseases and pests; the wish to expand; following their cattle.

questions.question: Give any four problems they met during their migration.
questions.answer: Any four of: resistance from people already there; wild animals; diseases; thick forests, rivers and swamps; shortage of food and water; long distances; language barriers.

questions.question: Give any four effects of the migrations on Uganda.
questions.answer: Any four of: population increased; new skills such as iron working and farming spread; intermarriage created new communities; kingdoms and chiefdoms were formed; wars broke out over land; some peoples lost their land and culture.

questions.question: What is a clan, and what is a totem?
questions.answer: A clan is a group of related families with a common ancestor. A totem is an animal or plant respected by a clan, which members never eat or kill.

questions.question: Give any five features of the social organisation of pre-colonial Uganda.
questions.answer: Any five of: people lived in clans with totems; the extended family lived and worked together; marriage was arranged between clans with bride price; they believed in a supreme god, spirits and ancestors; they held ceremonies such as naming, initiation and burial rites; education was informal, through work, folk tales and proverbs.

questions.question: Give the difference between a centralised and a decentralised society, with two examples of each.
questions.answer: A centralised society is ruled by one leader such as a king, for example Buganda and Bunyoro; a decentralised society has no single ruler and is led by clan elders, for example the Acholi and the Karimojong.

questions.question: Name the traditional titles of the rulers of Buganda, Bunyoro, Ankole and Busoga.
questions.answer: Buganda — Kabaka; Bunyoro — Omukama; Ankole — Omugabe; Busoga — Kyabazinga.

questions.question: Describe how the kingdom of Buganda was governed.
questions.answer: The Kabaka was the head. He was helped by the Katikkiro (prime minister) and the Lukiiko (council). Below them were county (Ssaza), sub-county (Ggombolola) and parish (Muluka) chiefs, who collected tribute, kept order, settled cases and raised the army.

questions.question: How were decisions made in a decentralised society?
questions.answer: By discussion and agreement among the clan elders, who settled disputes, shared out land, led ceremonies and organised defence; there was no single king to decide for everyone.

questions.question: Give any six economic activities of pre-colonial Uganda.
questions.answer: Any six of: crop growing; cattle keeping; iron working; bark cloth making; pottery and basketry; salt making; fishing; hunting; barter trade.

questions.question: What is barter trade, and what was used as money before coins?
questions.answer: Barter trade is exchanging goods for goods without using money. Before coins, people used cowrie shells as money.

questions.question: Draw the map of Uganda and shade the areas settled by the Bantu and the Luo.
questions.answer: Learner's map. The Bantu areas should cover the south, west and parts of the east; the Luo areas the north and north-west.

items.subject: Social Studies
subtopics: 1. THE FOREIGNERS WHO CAME TO UGANDA

questions.question: Name any four groups of foreigners who came to Uganda and say where each came from.
questions.answer: Any four: Arab traders — from Arabia in Asia; Indian traders — from India; European explorers — from Europe; missionaries — from Europe; colonial administrators — from Britain.

questions.question: Who was the first Arab to reach Buganda, when, and during whose reign?
questions.answer: Ahmed bin Ibrahim, in about 1844, during the reign of Kabaka Suna II.

questions.question: What did the Arabs bring, and what did they take away?
questions.answer: They brought guns, gunpowder, cloth, carpets, cowrie shells, beads and mirrors, and they took away ivory, slaves, gold, salt and animal skins.

questions.question: Give two positive and two negative effects of the Arab traders.
questions.answer: Positive: trade grew and cowrie shells became money; Islam was introduced. Negative: the slave trade took away many people; guns spread and increased wars.

questions.question: Which two explorers reached the source of the Nile, and in which year?
questions.answer: John Hanning Speke and James Grant, in 1862.

questions.question: What did Sir Samuel Baker reach in 1864?
questions.answer: Lake Albert and Murchison Falls.

questions.question: Who wrote the letter that invited missionaries to Buganda, and in which year?
questions.answer: Henry Morton Stanley, in 1875.

questions.question: Name the two missionary groups, the years they came, and one leader of each.
questions.answer: The CMS (Protestants) came in 1877 — Rev. Shergold Smith (or Rev. C. T. Wilson); the White Fathers (Catholics) came in 1879 — Fr. Simeon Lourdel, called Mapeera (or Bro. Amans).

questions.question: Give any four things the missionaries did in Uganda.
questions.answer: Any four of: built churches; started schools; built hospitals; translated the Bible and wrote down local languages; introduced new crops and skills; fought the slave trade; trained teachers and nurses.

questions.question: Who are the Uganda Martyrs, and when are they remembered?
questions.answer: They are the young Christian converts killed at Namugongo in 1885–1887 during the reign of Kabaka Mwanga. They are remembered every 3rd June, when pilgrims go to Namugongo.

questions.question: Give any four reasons why the explorers came to Uganda.
questions.answer: Any four of: to find the source of the Nile; to map the interior; to look for raw materials and markets; for adventure and fame; to see how the slave trade could be stopped.

questions.question: Give any five problems the explorers faced.
questions.answer: Any five of: tropical diseases; hostile people; wild animals; thick forests, swamps and rivers; language barriers; shortage of food and clean water; desertion by porters; long distances.

questions.question: In which year did Uganda become a British Protectorate, and what was the 1900 Buganda Agreement?
questions.answer: The 1900 Buganda Agreement was signed between Sir Harry Johnston and the Buganda regents; it divided land into mailo and Crown land, fixed taxes, and set out how Buganda would be governed under British protection.

questions.question: Give any six positive effects of foreign influence in Uganda.
questions.answer: Any six of: Christianity and Islam were introduced; schools and hospitals were built; roads and the railway were built; new cash crops were introduced; the slave trade was stopped; trade and money replaced barter; local languages were written down; the peoples were joined into one country.

questions.question: Give any six negative effects of foreign influence in Uganda.
questions.answer: Any six of: Uganda lost its independence; forced labour and heavy taxes; land was taken; traditional rulers lost power; African culture and religion were despised; religious wars broke out; new diseases came; raw materials were exploited.

questions.question: Where did the name "Uganda" come from?
questions.answer: From the Kiswahili form of the word Buganda, used by the Arab and Swahili traders and later adopted by the British for the whole Protectorate.

questions.question: What did the letters IBEACo stand for, and what was its work?
questions.answer: The Imperial British East Africa Company. It was given a royal charter in 1888 to trade in and administer the area on behalf of Britain.

questions.question: Who was Captain Lugard, and what did he do in 1890?
questions.answer: He was the British officer sent by the IBEACo. In 1890 he arrived in Buganda and signed a treaty with Kabaka Mwanga, placing Buganda under the Company's protection.

questions.question: In which year did Uganda become a British Protectorate?
Name the four agreements signed in colonial Uganda and the years.
questions.answer: The Buganda Agreement (1900), the Toro Agreement (1900), the Ankole Agreement (1901) and the Bunyoro Agreement (1933).

questions.question: Who signed the 1900 Buganda Agreement on each side?
questions.answer: Sir Harry Johnston for Britain, and the regents of the young Kabaka Daudi Chwa for Buganda.

questions.question: Give any four things contained in the 1900 Buganda Agreement.
questions.answer: Any four of: Buganda accepted British protection; land was divided into mailo and Crown land; hut tax and gun tax were introduced; the Lukiiko was recognised and the Kabaka ruled under British advice; Buganda's boundaries were fixed, taking some counties from Bunyoro.

questions.question: What is mailo land?
questions.answer: Mailo land is land that was given out in square miles to the Kabaka, chiefs and notables under the 1900 Buganda Agreement.

questions.question: What were the "lost counties", and why did they cause a quarrel?
questions.answer: They were counties taken from Bunyoro and given to Buganda under the 1900 Agreement as a reward for helping the British. Bunyoro felt robbed, and the quarrel lasted until a referendum returned two of them to Bunyoro in 1964.

questions.question: Who was Semei Kakungulu, and what did he do?
questions.answer: He was a Muganda chief used by the British to bring Bukedi, Bugisu, Teso and Lango under colonial rule. He set up chiefs there on the Buganda model and founded the town of Mbale.

questions.question: Which Omukama resisted the British, and what happened to him in 1899?
questions.answer: Omukama Kabalega of Bunyoro. He was captured in 1899 and sent into exile, together with Kabaka Mwanga.

questions.question: Draw the ladder of colonial administration from the Governor down to the village chief.
questions.answer: Governor → Provincial Commissioner → District Commissioner → County (Ssaza) chief → Sub-county (Ggombolola) chief → Parish (Muluka) chief → Village chief.

questions.question: What was LEGCO, when was it formed, and when did Africans first join it?
questions.answer: LEGCO was the Legislative Council, which made the laws of the Protectorate. It was formed in 1921, and the first Africans joined it in 1945.

questions.question: Give any five duties of the colonial chiefs.
questions.answer: Any five of: collecting taxes; keeping law and order; settling minor cases; organising forced labour on roads; making people grow cash crops; carrying out the District Commissioner's orders.

questions.question: Give any five positive and five negative effects of Uganda becoming one nation.
questions.answer: Positive: the peoples were joined into one country; peace was enforced; roads, railway, schools and hospitals were built; cash crops and trade spread; a common administration and written law came in. Negative: Uganda lost its independence; kingdoms lost power and rulers were exiled; land was given away and Bunyoro lost counties; forced labour and heavy taxes; tribal and religious divisions deepened.

questions.question: Give any six reasons why Ugandans wanted independence.
questions.answer: Any six of: to rule themselves; to stop forced labour and heavy taxes; to end racial discrimination; to control their own resources; to get better prices for their crops; to restore African dignity; to get better services; the example of India and Ghana; the return of ex-soldiers; the growth of education.

questions.question: Give any six methods used in the struggle for independence.
questions.answer: Any six of: forming political parties; forming cooperative societies; trade unions and strikes; boycotts; newspapers; petitions and delegations; demonstrations; constitutional conferences; taking part in elections.

questions.question: Name the first political party in Uganda, the year it was formed and its founder.
questions.answer: The Uganda National Congress (UNC), formed in 1952 by Ignatius Kangave Musaazi.

questions.question: Name any three other political parties, their years and their leaders.
questions.answer: DP — 1954, led by Benedicto Kiwanuka; UPC — 1960, founded by Milton Obote; KY — 1961, supporters of the Kabaka.

questions.question: What did the letters KY stand for, and what did the party want?
questions.answer: Kabaka Yekka, meaning "the Kabaka only". It wanted to protect the position of the Kabaka and of Buganda in an independent Uganda.

questions.question: Who was Benedicto Kiwanuka, and what two positions did he hold?
questions.answer: He was the leader of the DP. He became the first Chief Minister in 1961 and the first Prime Minister in March 1962.

questions.question: Who was Milton Obote, and what position did he hold at independence?
questions.answer: He was the founder of the UPC. At independence in October 1962 he became the Prime Minister of Uganda.

questions.question: What happened to Kabaka Muteesa II in 1953, and why?
questions.answer: He was deported (exiled) to Britain by Governor Sir Andrew Cohen because he demanded a timetable for independence and opposed the plan for an East African federation.

questions.question: How did the Kabaka's deportation affect the struggle for independence?
questions.answer: It made Ugandans very angry and united them against colonial rule; when he returned in 1955 he was a national hero, and the demand for independence became much stronger.

questions.question: What was the trade boycott of 1959–60, and who led it?
questions.answer: It was a refusal to buy from Asian and European shops or to use their buses, organised to force better trading chances for Africans. It was led by Augustine Kamya and the Uganda National Movement.

questions.question: Give the dates of internal self-government and of independence.
questions.answer: Internal self-government — 1 March 1962; independence — 9 October 1962.

questions.question: Where was the independence ceremony held, and what happened there?
questions.answer: At Kololo in Kampala. The Union Jack was lowered and the Uganda flag was raised at midnight, and the Duke of Kent handed over the instruments of power.

questions.question: Who became the first President of Uganda, and in which year?
questions.answer: Sir Edward Muteesa II, in 1963, when Uganda became a republic within the Commonwealth.

questions.question: Give any six problems faced by the nationalists.
questions.answer: Any six of: arrest, imprisonment and detention; deportation of leaders; banning of parties and newspapers; lack of funds and transport; disunity along religious and tribal lines; illiteracy; harsh colonial laws; fear among the people; the Buganda question.

questions.question: Draw a timeline showing any six important events on Uganda's road to independence.
questions.answer: Learner's timeline. Any six correct events with their years, in order — for example 1921 LEGCO, 1945 Africans in LEGCO, 1952 UNC, 1955 Kabaka returns, 1962 independence, 1963 republic.

questions.question: Name any five national symbols of Uganda.
questions.answer: Any five of: the national flag, the crested crane, the coat of arms, the national anthem, the national motto, the Constitution, the Mace.

questions.question: Describe the flag of Uganda and say what each colour stands for.
questions.answer: It has six stripes — black, yellow, red, black, yellow, red — with the crested crane in a white circle. Black stands for the African people, yellow for the sunshine, and red for the blood that unites all people.

questions.question: What is the national bird of Uganda, and what does it stand for?
questions.answer: The crested crane. It stands on one leg, showing that Uganda is always moving forward, and it is a gentle, peaceful bird.

questions.question: Name any six things shown on Uganda's coat of arms and what each represents.
questions.answer: Any six: the shield and spears — defence of the country; the lion — courage; the crested crane — the nation; the waves — the lakes and rivers; the sun — sunshine; the drum — culture and tradition; coffee and cotton — agriculture.

questions.question: Who composed the national anthem, and what is the national motto?
questions.answer: George Wilberforce Kakoma; the motto is "For God and My Country".

questions.question: In which year did Uganda become a republic, and who became the first President?
questions.answer: In 1963; Sir Edward Muteesa II became the first President.

questions.question: What happened to the kingdoms in 1967 and in 1993?
questions.answer: In 1967 a new Constitution abolished the kingdoms; in 1993 they were restored as cultural institutions, without political power.

questions.question: Name any five leaders Uganda has had since independence.
questions.answer: Any five of: Sir Edward Muteesa II, Milton Obote, Idi Amin, Yusuf Lule, Godfrey Binaisa, Paulo Muwanga, Tito Okello Lutwa, Yoweri Museveni.

questions.question: In which year did the NRM take over, and on what date is it remembered?
questions.answer: In 1986, remembered on 26 January as Liberation Day.

questions.question: When was the present Constitution promulgated?
questions.answer: On 8 October 1995.

questions.question: Give any six achievements of independent Uganda.
questions.answer: Any six of: a written Constitution and regular elections; UPE and USE; more schools, hospitals and universities; better roads, electricity and water; peace and security in most areas; growth of industry, trade and tourism; restoration of cultural institutions; membership of the EAC, AU, Commonwealth and UN; progress against HIV/AIDS.

questions.question: Give any six challenges facing Uganda today.
questions.answer: Any six of: poverty and unemployment; rapid population growth; corruption; poor roads and few industries; diseases such as malaria and HIV/AIDS; tribalism and political conflict; insecurity and cattle rustling; environmental destruction; illiteracy; dependence on foreign aid.

questions.question: Suggest a solution to each of: poverty, corruption, malaria, environmental destruction.
questions.answer: Poverty — skills training and support for small businesses; corruption — strong laws, accountability and punishing offenders; malaria — mosquito nets, draining stagnant water and early treatment; environmental destruction — planting trees, protecting wetlands and enforcing NEMA laws.

questions.question: Name any five national days of Uganda and what each remembers.
questions.answer: Any five: Independence Day 9 October — independence in 1962; Liberation Day 26 January — the NRM takeover; Martyrs' Day 3 June — the Uganda Martyrs; Heroes' Day 9 June — those who served the nation; Labour Day 1 May — workers; Women's Day 8 March — women.

questions.question: Why is 9th October important to every Ugandan?
questions.answer: Because it is the day Uganda stopped being ruled by the British and began to govern itself. It reminds every Ugandan of those who struggled for freedom and of the duty to keep the country united, peaceful and developing.

questions.question: What is government? Give any four reasons why a country needs one.
questions.answer: Government is the group of people who make laws, carry them out and settle disputes in a country. Reasons: to make and enforce laws; to keep peace and security; to provide services; to collect and spend revenue; to protect people's rights; to represent the country abroad (any four).

questions.question: Name the three arms of government and the work of each.
questions.answer: Legislature (Parliament) — makes the laws; Executive — carries out the laws and runs the country; Judiciary — interprets the laws and settles disputes.

questions.question: Who heads each of the three arms?
questions.answer: Legislature — the Speaker; Executive — the President; Judiciary — the Chief Justice.

questions.question: Give any four duties of the President of Uganda.
questions.answer: Any four of: Head of State; Head of Government; Commander-in-Chief of the armed forces; appoints ministers, judges and ambassadors; signs Bills into law; opens Parliament; represents Uganda abroad.

questions.question: Describe how a Bill becomes law.
questions.answer: A Bill is drafted and tabled in Parliament → it is read and debated, and studied by a committee → Parliament passes it → the President signs it → it is published and becomes an Act of Parliament.

questions.question: What is decentralisation?
questions.answer: Decentralisation is the transfer of powers, responsibilities and services from the central government to local governments such as districts and sub-counties.

questions.question: Name the five levels of local council and the leader of each.
questions.answer: LC I — village, Chairperson LC I; LC II — parish; LC III — sub-county; LC IV — county; LC V — district, the District Chairperson.

questions.question: Give any five duties of a local government.
questions.answer: Any five of: keeping law and order; settling small disputes; running primary schools and health centres; maintaining feeder roads and water sources; collecting local revenue; planning development projects; mobilising people for immunisation and clean-ups.

questions.question: What is an election, and which body organises elections in Uganda?
questions.answer: An election is the process of choosing leaders by voting. It is organised by the Electoral Commission.

questions.question: Outline the steps of the electoral process.
questions.answer: Registration of voters → nomination of candidates → campaigning → polling day with a secret ballot → counting the votes → declaring the results → swearing in the winners.

questions.question: Give the qualifications of a voter in Uganda.
questions.answer: A voter must be a citizen of Uganda, 18 years or above, registered as a voter, and of sound mind.

questions.question: Give any four challenges of elections and two solutions.
questions.answer: Challenges: rigging; bribery; violence and intimidation; illiteracy; late delivery of materials; low turnout (any four). Solutions: an independent Electoral Commission with a clean register and voter education; observers, agents and police at polling stations, with offenders punished and disputes settled in court.

questions.question: Give the four ways of becoming a citizen of Uganda.
questions.answer: By birth, by descent, by registration and by naturalisation.

questions.question: Give any five rights and five responsibilities of a citizen.
questions.answer: Rights (any five): life; education; property; freedom of speech, worship and association; health care; a fair trial; voting; movement. Responsibilities (any five): obeying the law; paying taxes; protecting public property and the environment; voting; respecting others' rights; keeping peace; reporting crime.

questions.question: Give any five sources of government revenue and any five ways the money is used.
questions.answer: Sources (any five): taxes; licences and permits; fees for services; court fines; rent from government property; loans and grants; earnings from exports. Uses (any five): paying civil servants; building schools and hospitals; making roads and water systems; defence and security; paying debts; running Parliament and the courts; emergency relief.

questions.question: Define population, population growth, population distribution and population density.
questions.answer: Population — the number of people living in a place at a particular time; population growth — the increase in that number over time; population distribution — the way people are spread over an area; population density — the number of people per square kilometre.

questions.question: Write the formula for population density. A district has 720,000 people and covers 9,000 km². Find its density.
questions.answer: Density = total population ÷ total area. 720,000 ÷ 9,000 = 80 people per km².

questions.question: What is a census? Which body carries it out in Uganda, and how often?
questions.answer: A census is the official counting of all the people in a country. It is carried out by the Uganda Bureau of Statistics (UBOS), about every ten years.

questions.question: Give the population of Uganda according to the 2024 census.
questions.answer: About 45.9 million people.

questions.question: Give any five reasons why a census is important.
questions.answer: Any five of: to know the number of people and the growth rate; to plan schools, hospitals, water and roads; to plan food production and jobs; to share government services and money fairly; to plan immunisation and health services; to help investors and researchers.

questions.question: Give any six factors that influence population distribution.
questions.answer: Any six of: relief, climate, soils, vegetation, water supply, pests and diseases, transport, social services, employment and industries, security, government policy.

questions.question: Name any three densely populated areas of Uganda and give a reason for each.
questions.answer: Any three, for example: the Lake Victoria crescent — fertile soils, rainfall and jobs; Kigezi — fertile volcanic soils and a cool climate; the Elgon slopes — volcanic soils and reliable relief rainfall.

questions.question: Name any three sparsely populated areas of Uganda and give a reason for each.
questions.answer: Any three, for example: Karamoja — semi-arid with little water and insecurity; national parks — people are not allowed to settle there; swamps and thick forests — waterlogged or hard to clear, with pests.

questions.question: Give any five causes of rapid population growth in Uganda.
questions.answer: Any five of: high birth rate; early marriages; polygamy; low use of family planning; better health services lowering the death rate; improved food supply; cultural and religious beliefs; immigration and refugees.

questions.question: Give any six problems caused by rapid population growth.
questions.answer: Any six of: land shortage and conflicts; unemployment and poverty; pressure on schools, hospitals and water; food shortage; overcrowding and slums; poor sanitation and disease; destruction of forests and wetlands; traffic congestion; crime.

questions.question: Give any four advantages of a large population.
questions.answer: Any four of: a large labour force; a bigger market for goods; more taxes for government; more ideas and skills; cheaper labour that attracts investment; development of new areas.

questions.question: Suggest any six solutions to the problems of rapid population growth.
questions.answer: Any six of: family planning education and services; educating girls and discouraging early marriage; creating jobs; improving farming methods; resettling people; building more social services; developing rural areas; proper town planning.

questions.question: What is rural–urban migration, and give two reasons why young people move to towns?
questions.answer: Rural–urban migration is the movement of people from villages to towns. Young people move to look for jobs and better pay, and for better schools, hospitals, electricity and town life.

questions.question: Give any four effects of HIV/AIDS on the population of Uganda.
questions.answer: Any four of: it raised the death rate, especially among young working adults; it left many orphans and child-headed families; it reduced the labour force; it increased costs for families and government; it lowered the population growth rate for a time.

questions.question: Draw the map of Uganda and shade one densely and one sparsely populated area, giving a reason for each.
questions.answer: Learner's map. For example, the Lake Victoria crescent shaded as densely populated because of fertile soils and jobs, and Karamoja shaded as sparsely populated because it is semi-arid.

questions.question: Define road safety.
questions.answer: Road safety is the practice of using roads in ways that prevent accidents and protect road users.

questions.question: Mention six road users.
questions.answer: Pedestrians, drivers, passengers, cyclists, motorcyclists and animal handlers.

questions.question: Mention three types of traffic signs.
questions.answer: Warning signs, regulatory signs and information signs.

questions.question: State five causes of road accidents.
questions.answer: Over-speeding, drunk driving, reckless driving, careless crossing and using mobile phones while driving.

questions.question: State five effects of road accidents.
questions.answer: Death, injuries, disability, damage to property and loss of income.

questions.question: Give five road safety rules for pedestrians.
questions.answer: Use footpaths, cross at safe places, obey traffic signals, avoid playing on roads and remain alert.

questions.question: Give five road safety rules for drivers.
questions.answer: Obey traffic rules, avoid over-speeding, wear seat belts, avoid drunk driving and maintain vehicles properly.

questions.question: Give four road safety rules for passengers.
questions.answer: Wear seat belts, sit properly, do not distract the driver and keep body parts inside the vehicle.

questions.question: Give four safety rules for cyclists.
questions.answer: Wear a helmet, obey traffic rules, maintain the bicycle and use lights or reflectors when necessary.

questions.question: Give four safety rules for motorcyclists.
questions.answer: Wear a helmet, obey traffic rules, avoid speeding and maintain the motorcycle.

questions.question: What does a red traffic light mean?
questions.answer: It means stop.

questions.question: What does a green traffic light mean?
questions.answer: It means proceed when the way is clear and safe.

questions.question: What is a zebra crossing?
questions.answer: It is a marked place on a road where pedestrians can cross.

questions.question: What is a helmet?
questions.answer: A helmet is protective headgear worn to protect the head.

questions.question: What is a seat belt?
questions.answer: A seat belt is a safety device used to secure a person in a vehicle.

questions.question: Why should children not play on roads?
questions.answer: Because they may be hit by vehicles and seriously injured or killed.

questions.question: Why should drivers not use mobile phones while driving?
questions.answer: Because mobile phones distract drivers and reduce their concentration on the road.

questions.question: Why should motorcyclists wear helmets?
questions.answer: To protect their heads and reduce the severity of head injuries during crashes.

questions.question: Why should passengers wear seat belts?
questions.answer: Seat belts help protect passengers during sudden stops or collisions.

questions.question: Mention five ways of preventing road accidents.
questions.answer: Obey traffic rules, avoid speeding, avoid drunk driving, use safe crossing points and maintain vehicles properly.

questions.question: What is the responsibility of every road user?
questions.answer: Every road user should use the road responsibly, obey traffic rules and protect the safety of other road users.

questions.question: What is debating?
questions.answer: Debating is the formal discussion of a motion in which people give arguments for or against it.

questions.question: Who supports a motion?
questions.answer: The proposer supports the motion.

questions.question: Who opposes a motion?
questions.answer: The opposer opposes the motion.

questions.question: Who controls a debate?
questions.answer: The chairperson controls the debate.

questions.question: Who keeps records during a debate?
questions.answer: The secretary keeps records.

questions.question: Who keeps track of time?
questions.answer: The timekeeper keeps track of time.

questions.question: Who listens to the debate?
questions.answer: The audience listens to the debate.

questions.question: What is a motion?
questions.answer: A motion is a statement or topic presented for debate.

questions.question: What is an argument?
questions.answer: An argument is a reason given to support or oppose an idea.

questions.question: What is an opinion?
questions.answer: An opinion is a person's belief or view about something.

questions.question: What is a point of order?
questions.answer: It is a formal interruption concerning the rules or procedure of a debate.

questions.question: What is a point of information?
questions.answer: It is a brief request for or provision of relevant information during a debate.

questions.question: What is a point of inquiry?
questions.answer: It is a request for clarification or further information.

questions.question: What does "previous" mean?
questions.answer: It means something that happened before.

questions.question: What does "current" mean?
questions.answer: It means something happening or existing now.

questions.question: What does "conclude" mean?
questions.answer: It means to bring something to an end.

questions.question: What is direct speech?
questions.answer: Direct speech gives the exact words spoken by a person.

questions.question: What is indirect speech?
questions.answer: Indirect speech reports what someone said without giving the exact words.

questions.question: What does "even though" express?
questions.answer: It expresses contrast.

questions.question: What does "although" express?
questions.answer: It expresses contrast.

questions.question: What does "if" express?
questions.answer: It introduces a condition.

questions.question: What does "whereas" express?
questions.answer: It expresses contrast between two ideas, people or things.

questions.question: Why should speakers listen to one another?
questions.answer: They listen so that they can understand and respond appropriately to different arguments.

questions.question: Why should speakers respect one another?
questions.answer: Respect makes the debate peaceful, fair and productive.

questions.question: What makes a good debater?
questions.answer: A good debater understands the motion, researches the topic, prepares strong points, speaks clearly, listens carefully, responds appropriately, respects other people's opinions, remains confident and keeps within the time limit.

questions.question: What is a family?
questions.answer: A family is a group of people related by birth, marriage or adoption.

questions.question: What is a relative?
questions.answer: A relative is a person related to another person.

questions.question: Who is a grandparent?
questions.answer: A grandparent is a grandfather or grandmother.

questions.question: Who is an auntie?
questions.answer: An auntie is the sister of one's parent or a woman related through marriage.

questions.question: Who is an uncle?
questions.answer: An uncle is the brother of one's parent or a man related through marriage.

questions.question: Who is a cousin?
questions.answer: A cousin is the child of one's uncle or aunt.

questions.question: Who is a nephew?
questions.answer: A nephew is the son of one's brother or sister.

questions.question: Who is a niece?
questions.answer: A niece is the daughter of one's brother or sister.

questions.question: Who is a stepmother?
questions.answer: A stepmother is a woman married to one's father who is not one's biological mother.

questions.question: Who is a stepfather?
questions.answer: A stepfather is a man married to one's mother who is not one's biological father.

questions.question: Who is a half-brother?
questions.answer: A half-brother shares one biological parent with another person.

questions.question: Who is a half-sister?
questions.answer: A half-sister shares one biological parent with another person.

questions.question: Who are twins?
questions.answer: Twins are two children born at the same birth.

questions.question: Who are triplets?
questions.answer: Triplets are three children born at the same birth.

questions.question: Who are quadruplets?
questions.answer: Quadruplets are four children born at the same birth.

questions.question: What does "elder" mean?
questions.answer: Elder means older than another person.

questions.question: What does "eldest" mean?
questions.answer: Eldest means the oldest among a group.

questions.question: What does "scarcely populated" mean?
questions.answer: It means having very few people living in an area.

questions.question: What does "densely populated" mean?
questions.answer: It means having many people living closely together in an area.

questions.question: What does "marry" mean?
questions.answer: It means to enter into marriage.

questions.question: What does "give birth to" mean?
questions.answer: It means to produce a baby through childbirth.

questions.question: What is a family tree?
questions.answer: A family tree is a diagram showing family relationships.

questions.question: Why is a family tree important?
questions.answer: It helps us understand how family members are related.

questions.question: What is a good family relationship based on?
questions.answer: It is based on love, care, respect, trust, forgiveness, cooperation and communication.

questions.question: What is a preposition?
questions.answer: A preposition is a word that shows a relationship between words in a sentence.

questions.question: What does "just" mean when used as an adverb?
questions.answer: It can show that something happened very recently.

questions.question: What does "already" mean?
questions.answer: It shows that something has happened before the present time.

questions.question: What does "rather...than" show?
questions.answer: It shows preference.

questions.question: What does "too...to" show?
questions.answer: It shows that something is beyond the suitable or possible degree for an action.

questions.question: What does "such...that" show?
questions.answer: It shows a strong degree of something and its resulting effect.

questions.question: What does "but" show in a sentence?
questions.answer: "But" shows contrast.

questions.question: What are the four main sub-topics under Occupations?
questions.answer: Carpentry, Tailoring, Baking and Keeping Animals.

questions.question: Who makes wooden furniture?
questions.answer: A carpenter.

questions.question: Who makes clothes?
questions.answer: A tailor or seamstress.

questions.question: Who makes bread and cakes?
questions.answer: A baker.

questions.question: What is a saw used for?
questions.answer: It is used for cutting wood.

questions.question: What is a plane used for?
questions.answer: It is used for smoothing wood.

questions.question: What is sandpaper used for?
questions.answer: It is used for smoothing surfaces.

questions.question: What is wood glue used for?
questions.answer: It is used for joining pieces of wood.

questions.question: What is a tape measure used for?
questions.answer: It is used for taking measurements.

questions.question: What is a needle used for?
questions.answer: It is used for sewing.

questions.question: What are scissors used for?
questions.answer: They are used for cutting cloth and other materials.

questions.question: What is a thimble used for?
questions.answer: It protects the finger during hand sewing.

questions.question: What is an oven used for?
questions.answer: It is used for baking and cooking.

questions.question: What is a recipe?
questions.answer: A recipe is a set of instructions for preparing food.

questions.question: What is dough?
questions.answer: Dough is a mixture prepared for making baked products.

questions.question: What does kneading mean?
questions.answer: It means pressing and folding dough repeatedly.

questions.question: What is animal welfare?
questions.answer: It is the proper care and well-being of animals.

questions.question: What is animal husbandry?
questions.answer: It is the care, breeding and management of domestic animals.

questions.question: Why should animals be given shelter?
questions.answer: To protect them from weather, predators and other dangers.

questions.question: Why should animals receive veterinary care?
questions.answer: To prevent and treat diseases and injuries.

questions.question: What is rearing?
questions.answer: It is raising and caring for animals or birds.

questions.question: What is livelihood?
questions.answer: It is the way a person earns a living.

questions.question: What is earning?
questions.answer: It is receiving money for work or services.

questions.question: What is farming?
questions.answer: It is growing crops and/or keeping animals.

questions.question: What is an adverb of manner?
questions.answer: It tells us how an action is performed.

questions.question: What is an adverb of time?
questions.answer: It tells us when an action happens.

questions.question: What is an adverb of place?
questions.answer: It tells us where an action happens.

questions.question: What is an adverb of emphasis?
questions.answer: It adds emphasis or force to a statement.

questions.question: What is an adverb of quality?
questions.answer: It describes the quality or manner of an action or situation.

questions.question: What is a hotel?
questions.answer: A hotel is a building or establishment where people pay to stay, eat and receive other services while away from home.

questions.question: Who is a hotel guest?
questions.answer: A hotel guest is a person who stays in a hotel.

questions.question: Why do people stay in hotels?
questions.answer: People stay in hotels to get accommodation, food, drinks and other services when they are away from home.

questions.question: Mention five services offered by hotels.
questions.answer: Any five: accommodation, food and drinks, laundry services, room cleaning, internet services.

questions.question: What is accommodation?
questions.answer: Accommodation is a place where people stay or live temporarily.

questions.question: Who is a hotel manager?
questions.answer: A hotel manager is a person who supervises the activities of a hotel.

questions.question: Who is a receptionist?
questions.answer: A receptionist is a hotel worker who welcomes guests, records their details and helps them with accommodation.

questions.question: What is the work of a chef?
questions.answer: A chef prepares food for hotel guests.

questions.question: What is the work of a waiter or waitress?
questions.answer: A waiter or waitress serves food and drinks to guests.

questions.question: What is the work of a housekeeper?
questions.answer: A housekeeper keeps hotel rooms and other areas clean and tidy.

questions.question: What is the work of a security guard in a hotel?
questions.answer: A security guard protects the hotel, workers and guests from danger.

questions.question: What is the work of a gardener in a hotel?
questions.answer: A gardener maintains flowers, lawns, trees and other plants around the hotel.

questions.question: Mention five people who work in a hotel.
questions.answer: Any five: hotel manager, receptionist, chef, waiter or waitress, housekeeper, security guard, gardener.

questions.question: Mention four types of hotels.
questions.answer: Budget hotels, luxury hotels, resort hotels and business hotels.

questions.question: Why are hotels important?
questions.answer: Because they provide accommodation, food and other services to travellers.

questions.question: How do hotels provide employment?
questions.answer: Hotels employ people such as managers, receptionists, chefs, waiters, housekeepers and security guards.

questions.question: How do hotels promote tourism?
questions.answer: Hotels provide accommodation and other services to tourists, making it easier for them to visit and stay in different places.

questions.question: How do hotels contribute to the development of a country?
questions.answer: Hotels create employment, generate income, pay taxes and support other businesses.

questions.question: Mention five rules that hotel guests should follow.
questions.answer: Keep hotel rooms clean; respect hotel workers and other guests; avoid damaging hotel property; pay for services received; follow hotel rules.

questions.question: What can happen if hotel guests damage hotel property?
questions.answer: They may be required to pay for the damaged property and may face other action according to hotel rules.

questions.question: What is a dictionary?
questions.answer: A dictionary is a reference book that gives information about words, including their meanings, spellings and pronunciations.

questions.question: Mention five uses of a dictionary.
questions.answer: A dictionary is used to find meanings, check spelling, check pronunciation, learn new words and understand how words are used.

questions.question: What are guide words?
questions.answer: Guide words are words printed at the top of dictionary pages that help users locate words quickly.

questions.question: What is a thesaurus?
questions.answer: A thesaurus is a reference book used mainly to find words with similar or related meanings and opposites.

questions.question: What is an abbreviation?
questions.answer: An abbreviation is a shortened form of a word or group of words.

questions.question: What is an acronym?
questions.answer: An acronym is a word formed from the initial letters of other words.

questions.question: What is alphabetical order?
questions.answer: Alphabetical order is the arrangement of words according to the order of letters in the alphabet.

questions.question: Why should we learn to use a dictionary?
questions.answer: We should learn to use a dictionary so that we can find information about words independently and improve our English.

questions.question: What should you do whenever you find a difficult word?
questions.answer: Whenever I find a difficult word, I should refer to the dictionary to find its meaning and other information about it.

questions.question: How does a dictionary help us to pronounce words correctly?
questions.answer: It provides pronunciation information that shows how words should be spoken.

questions.question: How does a dictionary help us to spell words correctly?
questions.answer: It provides the standard spelling of words, allowing us to check and correct our spelling.

questions.question: How does dictionary work help us become independent learners?
questions.answer: It teaches us how to find information about unfamiliar words without always depending on another person.

questions.question: Give the difference between equal sets and equivalent sets, with an example of each.
questions.answer: Equal sets have exactly the same members, e.g. {1, 2, 3} and {3, 1, 2}. Equivalent sets have the same number of members but not the same members, e.g. {1, 2, 3} and {a, b, c}.

questions.question: Define the universal set and the complement of a set.
questions.answer: The universal set contains all the members under discussion. The complement of a set contains all members of the universal set that are not in that set.

questions.question: Given A = {1, 2, 3, 4} and B = {3, 4, 5}, find A ∪ B, A ∩ B, A − B and B − A.
How many subsets has a set with 5 members?
questions.answer: 2⁵ = 32 subsets

questions.question: How many proper subsets has a set with 3 members?
questions.answer: 2³ − 1 = 7 proper subsets

questions.question: List all the subsets of {m, n}.
Given n(A) = 15, n(B) = 12 and n(A ∩ B) = 4, find n(A ∪ B).
In a class of 40 pupils, 22 like tea, 25 like milk and 10 like both. How many like neither?
questions.answer: At least one = 22 + 25 − 10 = 37. Neither = 40 − 37 = 3 pupils

questions.question: In a group of 60 farmers, 35 grow maize, 30 grow beans and 5 grow neither. How many grow both?
questions.answer: At least one = 60 − 5 = 55. Both = 35 + 30 − 55 = 10 farmers

questions.question: A bag has 4 blue and 6 green pens. Find the probability of picking a blue pen.
questions.answer: Total = 10. P(blue) = 4/10 = 2/5

questions.question: A die is thrown once. Find the probability of getting an odd number.
questions.answer: Odd numbers 1, 3, 5 → 3 out of 6. P = 1/2

questions.question: Given ε = {a, b, c, d, e} and P = {a, e}, find P′ and n(P′).
If a set has 64 subsets, how many members has it?
questions.answer: 2ⁿ = 64 and 2⁶ = 64, so the set has 6 members.

questions.question: In a class of 30 pupils, 18 study French only, 5 study both French and German, and 3 study neither. How many study German altogether?
questions.answer: At least one language = 30 − 3 = 27. German altogether = 27 − 18 = 9 pupils

questions.question: List all the prime numbers between 10 and 30.
Which of these is divisible by 3: 5,124 or 5,125? Show your working.
questions.answer: 5+1+2+4 = 12 → divisible by 3; 5+1+2+5 = 13 → not divisible. So 5,124.

questions.question: Is 6,570 divisible by 2, 3 and 5? Give a reason for each.
questions.answer: Yes to all three: it ends in 0, so it is divisible by 2 and by 5; the digits add to 6+5+7+0 = 18, which is divisible by 3.

questions.answer: Total = 15. P(blue) = 6/15 = 2/5

questions.question: A number is picked at random from 1 to 20. Find the probability that it is a multiple of 4.
questions.answer: Multiples of 4 from 1 to 20: 4, 8, 12, 16, 20 → 5 out of 20. P = 1/4

questions.question: What is a currency? Give the currency used in Rwanda, Ghana and Japan.
questions.answer: A currency is the money used in a particular country. Rwanda — the franc; Ghana — the cedi; Japan — the yen.

questions.question: Name the currency of each: Kenya, Burundi, South Africa, the United Kingdom.
questions.answer: Kenya — Kenya shilling; Burundi — Burundian franc; South Africa — rand; the United Kingdom — pound sterling.

questions.question: What is an exchange rate?
questions.answer: An exchange rate is the value of one country's money in terms of another country's money.

questions.question: Give any three reasons why people change money from one currency to another.
questions.answer: Any three of: travelling abroad; importing or exporting goods; paying fees abroad; sending or receiving money from relatives working outside; tourism; paying for services in another currency.

questions.question: Change 54 km/hr to metres per second.
Change 25 m/s to kilometres per hour.
A train left at 7:00 a.m. and arrived at 11:00 a.m., having covered 320 km. Find its average speed.
questions.answer: Time = 4 hours → 320 ÷ 4 = 80 km/hr

questions.question: A driver covered 150 km in 3 hours, rested for 1 hour and then covered 200 km in 4 hours. Find the average speed for the whole journey.
questions.answer: Total distance = 350 km; total time = 8 hours → 350 ÷ 8 = 43.75 km/hr

questions.question: A journey of 240 km took 4 hours including a 30-minute stop. Find the speed while the vehicle was moving.
questions.answer: Moving time = 3½ hours → 240 ÷ 3.5 = about 68.6 km/hr

questions.question: On a distance–time graph, what does a flat line mean?
questions.answer: It means the traveller is resting — the distance is not changing.

questions.question: On a distance–time graph, what does a steeper line mean?
questions.answer: It means the traveller is moving faster.

questions.question: A traveller covered 80 km between 9:00 a.m. and 10:00 a.m., rested for half an hour, then covered 60 km in the next hour. Find the total distance, the total time and the average speed.
questions.answer: Total distance = 80 + 60 = 140 km; total time = 1 + ½ + 1 = 2½ hours; average speed = 140 ÷ 2.5 = 56 km/hr

questions.question: A lorry travels 45 km in 30 minutes. What is its speed in km/hr?
questions.answer: 30 minutes = ½ hour → 45 ÷ 0.5 = 90 km/hr

questions.question: Change 3.6 km to metres and 4,250 g to kilogrammes.
Change 2.4 litres to millilitres and 5,000 cm³ to litres.
questions.answer: 2.4 litres = 2,400 ml; 5,000 cm³ = 5 litres

questions.question: Find the perimeter of a rectangle 18 m by 11 m.
Find the circumference of a circle of radius 14 cm.
Find the circumference of a circle of diameter 42 cm.
The circumference of a circle is 88 cm. Find its radius.
Find the area of a rectangle 25 m by 16 m.
Find the area of a triangle with base 20 cm and height 13 cm.
Find the area of a circle of radius 21 cm.
Find the area of a circle of diameter 14 cm.
Find the volume of a cuboid 15 cm by 10 cm by 6 cm.
Find the volume of a cube of side 9 cm.
Find the volume of a cylinder of radius 14 cm and height 10 cm.
Find the capacity in litres of a tank 100 cm by 60 cm by 50 cm.
questions.answer: Volume = 300,000 cm³ → 300 litres

questions.question: A rectangular garden 40 m by 25 m has a path 2 m wide all round it outside. Find the area of the path.
questions.answer: Outer = 44 × 29 = 1,276 m²; garden = 1,000 m²; path = 276 m²

questions.question: Give the difference between parallel and perpendicular lines, and write the symbol for each.
questions.answer: Parallel lines never meet and stay the same distance apart (symbol ∥); perpendicular lines meet at 90° (symbol ⊥).

questions.question: Name the five types of angles according to size.
questions.answer: Acute, right, obtuse, straight and reflex.

questions.question: What is the complement of 35°? What is the supplement of 35°?
questions.answer: Complement = 90 − 35 = 55°; supplement = 180 − 35 = 145°.

questions.question: Two parallel lines are cut by a transversal. One angle is 65°. Find the co-interior and the alternate angle.
questions.answer: Alternate angle = 65°; co-interior angle = 180 − 65 = 115°.

questions.question: Describe briefly how to construct an angle of 60°.
questions.answer: Draw a straight line. Place the compass point at one end and draw an arc cutting the line. Without changing the radius, place the point where the arc cuts the line and draw another arc crossing the first. Join the end of the line to the crossing point.

questions.question: How do you construct an angle of 45°?
questions.answer: First construct 90°, then bisect it.

questions.question: Describe how to construct a regular hexagon using a pair of compasses.
questions.answer: Draw a circle of any radius. Keeping the compasses at the same radius, step round the circumference making six marks, then join the six points in order.

questions.question: State Pythagoras' theorem.
questions.answer: In a right-angled triangle, the square of the hypotenuse is equal to the sum of the squares of the other two sides: a² + b² = c².

questions.question: The two shorter sides of a right-angled triangle are 6 cm and 8 cm. Find the hypotenuse.
The hypotenuse is 17 cm and one side is 8 cm. Find the other side.
A ladder 13 m long has its foot 5 m from a wall. How far up the wall does it reach?
State any three properties of a rhombus.
questions.answer: Any three of: all four sides are equal; opposite angles are equal; opposite sides are parallel; the diagonals cross at 90°.

questions.question: Give the difference between a trapezium and a parallelogram.
questions.answer: A trapezium has only one pair of parallel sides, while a parallelogram has two pairs of parallel sides with opposite sides equal.

questions.question: Find the sum of the interior angles of a hexagon, and each angle if it is regular.
questions.answer: (6 − 2) × 180 = 720°; each angle of a regular hexagon = 720 ÷ 6 = 120°

questions.question: How many faces, edges and vertices has a triangular prism?
questions.answer: 5 faces, 9 edges and 6 vertices.

items.subject: Mathematics
subtopics: 5. APPLICATION OF INTEGERS IN DAILY LIFE

questions.question: What is an integer? Give two examples of each kind.
questions.answer: An integer is any whole number that is positive, negative or zero. Positive: +3, +10; negative: −3, −10; and zero itself.

questions.question: Which of these are not integers: −4, 0, ½, 7, 0.3?
questions.answer: ½ and 0.3 are not integers.

questions.question: Arrange in ascending order: 5, −3, 0, −8, 2, −1.
Arrange in descending order: −6, 4, −2, 7, 0.
Give the additive inverse of: +9, −15, 0.
Find the absolute value of −13 and of +4.
Work out (+7) + (+6).
Work out (−8) + (−5).
Using a number line, work out (−4) + 6.
questions.answer: Start at −4 and move 6 steps right → +2

questions.question: The temperature was −6 °C in the morning and rose by 14 degrees. Find the new temperature.
A trader had a debt of 40,000 shillings and earned 95,000. Find his position.
A team scored 22 goals and conceded 30. Find its goal difference.
A lift on the 3rd floor went down 7 floors. Where did it stop?
questions.answer: 3 − 7 = −4, that is 4 floors below the ground

questions.question: Give any four real-life situations where integers are used.
questions.answer: Any four of: temperature above and below freezing; money saved and money owed; height above and below sea level; goals scored and conceded; floors above and below the ground; forward and backward movement.

questions.question: Which is bigger, −15 or −9? Give a reason.
questions.answer: −9 is bigger, because it is nearer to zero on the number line; the further left a number is, the smaller it is.

questions.question: Give the difference between an expression and an equation.
questions.answer: An expression is a group of terms with no equals sign, such as 3x + 5; an equation has an equals sign, such as 3x + 5 = 20.

questions.question: Explain the terms like terms and coefficient.
questions.answer: Like terms are terms with exactly the same letter, such as 4x and 7x. A coefficient is the number in front of a letter — in 8y it is 8.

questions.question: Simplify 8a + 6a − 5a.
questions.answer: 9a

questions.question: Simplify 9x + 4y − 3x + 6y.
Simplify 10m + 7 − 4m − 2.
Remove the brackets and simplify: 5(x + 4).
Remove the brackets and simplify: 4(2a + 1) + 3(a − 2).
If p = 6 and q = 4, find the value of 3p + 2q.
If a = 7 and b = 2, find the value of a² − 4b.
If x = 8, y = 3 and z = 2, find (x + y) ÷ z.
Solve x + 12 = 30.
Solve 6n = 54.
Solve 2y + 7 = 23.
Solve 5k − 9 = 26.
Solve 3(m + 4) = 27.
Solve 8x = 5x + 21.
A number less 8 gives 19. Find the number.
Four times a number, plus 6, gives 38. Find the number.
Sarah is 5 years older than Peter. Together they are 29 years old. Find their ages.
questions.answer: Let Peter be x: x + (x + 5) = 29 → 2x = 24 → x = 12. Peter is 12 and Sarah is 17.

questions.question: The perimeter of a rectangle is 36 m and its length is twice its width. Find the length and the width.
questions.answer: 2(w + 2w) = 36 → 6w = 36 → w = 6. Width 6 m, length 12 m.

items.subject: Science
subtopics: 4. CARE FOR AND PROTECTION OF ANIMALS

questions.question: What is classification, and give two reasons why animals are classified?
questions.answer: Classification is the grouping of living things according to their similarities and differences. Reasons: it makes study easier and it helps us identify animals and know how to care for them.

questions.question: Give the difference between vertebrates and invertebrates.
questions.answer: Vertebrates have a backbone; invertebrates do not.

questions.question: Name the five classes of vertebrates and one example of each.
questions.answer: Mammals — cow; birds — hen; reptiles — lizard; fish — tilapia; amphibians — frog.

questions.question: Which two classes of vertebrates are warm-blooded?
questions.answer: Mammals and birds.

questions.question: Give any four characteristics of mammals.
questions.answer: Any four of: body covered with hair or fur; have mammary glands and feed young on milk; give birth to live young; breathe using lungs; are warm-blooded; have external ears.

questions.question: Give any four characteristics of birds.
questions.answer: Any four of: body covered with feathers; have a beak; have two wings and two legs; lay eggs with hard shells; are warm-blooded; have light hollow bones.

questions.question: Give three differences between reptiles and amphibians.
questions.answer: Reptiles: dry scaly skin, live on land (or water) and breathe with lungs all their life, lay leathery eggs on land. Amphibians: moist smooth skin, live both in water and on land, young breathe with gills and adults with lungs and skin, lay eggs in water. (Any three pairs.)

questions.question: How do fish breathe, and how do they move in water?
