questions.answer: Fish breathe using gills, and they move using fins and a tail.

questions.question: Name the three main groups of invertebrates.
questions.answer: Arthropods, molluscs and worms.

questions.question: Name the four groups of arthropods and give one example of each.
questions.answer: Insects — housefly; arachnids — spider; myriapods — millipede; crustaceans — crab.

questions.question: Give three differences between insects and arachnids.
questions.answer: Insects have 6 legs, arachnids have 8; insects have 3 body parts, arachnids 2; most insects have wings and antennae, arachnids have neither.

questions.question: Give the difference between a millipede and a centipede.
questions.answer: A millipede has two pairs of legs on each body segment and rolls up when touched; a centipede has one pair per segment and is a fast-moving hunter with poison claws.

questions.question: Why is a bat classified as a mammal and not a bird?
questions.answer: Because it has hair on its body, mammary glands and gives birth to live young which it feeds on milk — even though it flies, it has no feathers or beak.

questions.question: Give any five ways of caring for animals.
questions.answer: Any five of: give clean food and water; provide clean dry shelter; treat and vaccinate them; handle them gently; protect them from thieves and wild animals; do not poach; protect their habitats.

questions.question: Give any five uses of animals to human beings.
questions.answer: Any five of: food such as meat, milk, eggs and honey; hides and skins; manure; transport and work; money and employment; tourism; pest control; pollination; company from pets.

items.subject: Science
subtopics: 4. HOW SOUND IS PRODUCED, STORED AND REPRODUCED

questions.question: What is sound, and how is it produced?
questions.answer: Sound is a form of energy produced when objects vibrate.

questions.question: Give any three natural and three artificial sources of sound.
questions.answer: Natural: thunder, wind, animal calls (also flowing water, the human voice). Artificial: a drum, a radio, a bell (also vehicles and machines).

questions.question: Give the difference between pitch and volume.
questions.answer: Pitch is how high or low a sound is and depends on frequency; volume is how loud or soft a sound is and depends on the size of the vibration.

questions.question: What is frequency, and how does it affect pitch?
questions.answer: Frequency is the number of vibrations in one second. The higher the frequency, the higher the pitch.

questions.question: In which medium does sound travel fastest, and why?
questions.answer: In a solid, because its particles are packed closely together and pass the vibrations on quickly.

questions.question: Why can sound not travel through a vacuum?
questions.answer: Because a vacuum has no particles (no medium) to carry the vibrations.

questions.question: Describe one experiment that shows sound travels through solids.
questions.answer: Place your ear flat on a desk while a friend scratches or taps the far end of the desk. The sound heard through the wood is louder and clearer than through the air, showing that solids carry sound well.

questions.question: What is an echo, and where can it be heard?
questions.answer: An echo is a sound heard again after bouncing off a hard surface. It can be heard in valleys, near cliffs, in empty halls and near high walls.

questions.question: Name the three main parts of the human ear.
questions.answer: The outer ear, middle ear and inner ear.

questions.question: Name the three small bones of the middle ear.
questions.answer: The hammer, anvil and stirrup.

questions.question: State the work of: the pinna, the ear drum, the cochlea, the auditory nerve.
questions.answer: Pinna — collects sound and directs it into the ear canal; ear drum — vibrates when sound hits it; cochlea — changes vibrations into nerve messages; auditory nerve — carries the messages to the brain.

questions.question: Which part of the ear keeps the body in balance?
questions.answer: The semi-circular canals.

questions.question: Name any four diseases or disorders of the ear.
questions.answer: Any four of: deafness, otitis media (ear infection), a perforated ear drum, ear wax blockage, foreign bodies in the ear, boils in the ear canal.

questions.question: Give any five ways of caring for the ear.
questions.answer: Any five of: never put sharp objects in the ear; clean only the outer ear with a damp cloth; avoid very loud noise and loud earphones; treat infections early; do not slap anyone on the ear; protect ears from cold; go for check-ups.

questions.question: Name the three types of musical instruments and give one example of each.
questions.answer: String — guitar or adungu; wind — flute or whistle; percussion — drum or xylophone.

items.subject: Science
subtopics: 5. DISEASES AND DISORDERS OF THE SYSTEM

questions.question: Name the three parts of the circulatory system.
questions.answer: The heart, the blood vessels and the blood.

questions.question: Where is the heart found, and what protects it?
questions.answer: In the chest, slightly to the left, protected by the ribs (and the breastbone).

questions.question: Name the four chambers of the heart and state the work of each.
questions.answer: Right atrium — receives blood without oxygen from the body; right ventricle — pumps it to the lungs; left atrium — receives blood with oxygen from the lungs; left ventricle — pumps it to the whole body.

questions.question: Why does the left ventricle have the thickest wall?
questions.answer: Because it pumps blood to the whole body, which needs much greater force than pumping to the lungs.

questions.question: What is the work of the valves in the heart?
questions.answer: They stop blood from flowing backwards.

questions.question: Name the three types of blood vessels and give one difference between arteries and veins.
questions.answer: Arteries, veins and capillaries. Arteries carry blood away from the heart with thick elastic walls at high pressure, while veins carry blood back to the heart, have thinner walls and contain valves.

questions.question: Which artery carries blood without oxygen, and which vein carries blood with oxygen?
questions.answer: The pulmonary artery carries blood without oxygen; the pulmonary vein carries blood with oxygen.

questions.question: Name the four parts of blood and give the work of each.
questions.answer: Plasma — carries food, water, salts and waste; red blood cells — carry oxygen; white blood cells — fight germs; platelets — help the blood to clot.

questions.question: Name the four blood groups.
questions.answer: A, B, AB and O.

questions.question: Give any four functions of blood.
questions.answer: Any four of: transporting oxygen; transporting food and water; carrying waste to the excretory organs; fighting germs; clotting to stop bleeding; spreading heat round the body.

questions.question: Name any four diseases or disorders of the circulatory system.
questions.answer: Any four of: anaemia, sickle cell disease, leukaemia, high blood pressure, heart attack, haemophilia, varicose veins.

questions.question: Give three ways in which HIV can be spread through blood, and three ways of preventing this.
questions.answer: Spread: transfusion of untested blood; sharing needles or syringes; sharing razor blades or other skin-cutting instruments (also mother to child). Prevention: use only screened blood; use sterile single-use needles; never share razor blades or sharp instruments (and mothers who are HIV positive should follow medical advice).

questions.question: Give any five ways of increasing the volume of blood in the body.
questions.answer: Any five of: eat iron-rich foods such as dodo, nakati, liver, beans and meat; eat fruits rich in vitamin C; deworm regularly; sleep under a mosquito net; treat wounds and bleeding quickly; exercise; rest well; have a transfusion of screened blood in serious cases.

questions.question: Why should blood for transfusion be tested first?
questions.answer: To make sure it is the right blood group for the patient and that it is free from germs and infections such as HIV, hepatitis and syphilis, so that the transfusion helps instead of harming.

questions.question: Trace the path of blood from the body back to the body, naming the chambers and the lungs.
questions.answer: Body → right atrium → right ventricle → lungs (to get oxygen) → left atrium → left ventricle → back to the body.

items.subject: Science
items.topic: Alcohol, Smoking and Drugs in Society
subtopics: 4. WHY PEOPLE FALL INTO THESE HABITS
5. LIFE SKILLS THAT PROTECT A YOUNG PERSON

questions.question: What is alcoholism? Who is an alcoholic?
questions.answer: Alcoholism is the condition of being unable to stop taking alcohol — addiction to alcohol. An alcoholic is a person who is addicted to alcohol.

questions.question: Give any four effects of alcoholism on the individual.
questions.answer: Any four of: damage to the liver, stomach and brain; loss of memory and poor judgement; accidents and injuries; loss of job and poverty; poor health, malnutrition and early death.

questions.question: Give any three effects of alcoholism on the family and three on the community.
questions.answer: Family: money wasted instead of buying food and paying fees; quarrels and violence; children dropping out of school; neglect of the family. Community: crime and insecurity; road accidents; loss of a productive workforce; extra burden on hospitals and police. (Any three each.)

questions.question: Name any three harmful substances found in tobacco smoke and what each does.
questions.answer: Nicotine — causes addiction; tar — causes cancer; carbon monoxide — reduces the oxygen carried by the blood.

questions.question: Give the difference between active and passive smoking.
questions.answer: Active smoking is smoking a cigarette yourself; passive smoking is breathing in the smoke of somebody else who is smoking.

questions.question: Why is passive smoking dangerous, especially for children and pregnant mothers?
questions.answer: Because passive smokers breathe the same harmful substances and suffer the same diseases, and children's lungs and unborn babies are still developing, so the harm is greater — it can cause coughs, chest infections, poor growth and low birth weight.

questions.question: Give any four effects of smoking on a person's health.
questions.answer: Any four of: lung cancer; chronic cough and bronchitis; tuberculosis; heart disease; stained teeth and bad breath; poor appetite; addiction.

questions.question: What are essential drugs? Give any four examples.
questions.answer: Essential drugs are the medicines a community most needs and which should always be available at a health centre. Examples: ORS, paracetamol, anti-malarial tablets, antibiotics, deworming tablets, vaccines (any four).

questions.question: Give any four characteristics of good drugs.
questions.answer: Any four of: within the expiry date; properly sealed and labelled; from a licensed health centre or pharmacy; with the correct name, dose and instructions; not discoloured, crushed or damp.

questions.question: Give any five rules for storing drugs safely in a home.
questions.answer: Any five of: keep them in a cool, dry, dark place; keep them in the original labelled container; close them tightly; keep them out of reach of children, preferably locked; do not store them with food or paraffin; check the expiry date; destroy or return expired drugs safely.

questions.question: Give the difference between drug abuse and drug misuse, with one example of each.
questions.answer: Drug abuse is using a drug for a purpose it was not meant for, for example sniffing petrol. Drug misuse is using a proper medicine wrongly, for example taking the wrong dose or using somebody else's prescription.

questions.question: What is drug dependence?
questions.answer: Drug dependence is when the body or the mind can no longer do without the drug, so the person suffers when he or she stops taking it.

questions.question: Name any four commonly abused substances.
questions.answer: Any four of: alcohol, tobacco, marijuana (njaga), khat (mairungi), petrol or glue fumes, cocaine, heroin, wrongly used sleeping tablets.

questions.question: Give any five factors that lead young people into alcoholism, smoking or drug abuse.
questions.answer: Any five of: peer pressure; curiosity; idleness and too much free time; copying parents or film and music stars; advertising; frustration and family problems; easy availability; lack of guidance.

questions.question: Name any five life skills that help a young person to refuse drugs, and explain one of them.
questions.answer: Any five of: assertiveness, peer pressure resistance, decision-making, critical thinking, self-esteem, coping with stress, effective communication, using free time well. Assertiveness, for example, is the ability to say NO firmly and to repeat it without fear or apology, and to walk away from the situation.

questions.question: Give the difference between flowering and non-flowering plants, with two examples of each.
questions.answer: Flowering plants produce flowers and seeds, for example maize and mango; non-flowering plants do not produce flowers, for example ferns and pine.

questions.question: Name the three groups of non-flowering plants and give one example of each.
questions.answer: Spore-bearing plants — fern; conifers — pine; algae — spirogyra (or seaweed).

questions.question: Give three differences between legumes and cereals.
questions.answer: Legumes: seeds in pods, two seed leaves, root nodules that add nitrogen, rich in protein. Cereals: grasses grown for grain, one seed leaf, fibrous roots, rich in carbohydrates. (Any three pairs.)

questions.question: Why is planting legumes good for the soil?
questions.answer: Because their root nodules contain bacteria that add nitrogen to the soil, making it fertile again for the next crop.

questions.question: Name the male and the female parts of a flower and state the work of each.
questions.answer: The stamen (anther and filament) is the male part and makes pollen; the pistil (stigma, style and ovary) is the female part and receives pollen and holds the ovules.

questions.question: What is pollination, and what happens to the ovary after fertilisation?
questions.answer: Pollination is the transfer of pollen from the anther to the stigma. After fertilisation the ovary becomes the fruit and the ovules become seeds.

questions.question: What is seed dispersal, and give any four reasons why it is necessary?
questions.answer: Seed dispersal is the scattering of seeds away from the parent plant. Reasons: to avoid overcrowding; to reduce competition for water, light and food; to spread the plant to new areas; to reduce the spread of pests and diseases (any four).

questions.question: Name the five agents of seed dispersal.
questions.answer: Wind, water, animals (and birds), explosive mechanism, and people.

questions.question: Give the features of a seed dispersed by wind and one dispersed by animals.
questions.answer: Wind: the seed is light and has wings, hairs or a parachute. Animals: the fruit is sweet and fleshy so it is eaten, or the seed has hooks that stick to fur and clothes.

questions.question: What is plant propagation? Name its two types.
questions.answer: Plant propagation is the way new plants are produced from old ones. Its two types are sexual (by seeds) and vegetative (asexual).

questions.question: Name any six methods of vegetative propagation, with one example of each.
questions.answer: Any six: cuttings — cassava; suckers — banana; tubers — Irish potato; bulbs — onion; rhizomes — ginger; runners — grass; grafting — mango; layering — guava.

questions.question: Give two advantages and two disadvantages of vegetative propagation.
questions.answer: Advantages: the new plant is exactly like the parent and it matures faster. Disadvantages: diseases are passed on easily and there is no variety among the plants.

questions.question: Give any six economic values of plants.
questions.answer: Any six of: food; cash crops and employment; timber and poles; firewood and charcoal; medicine; raw materials for industries; fodder for animals; shade and windbreaks; protection of the environment and supply of oxygen; tourism.

questions.question: Why do farmers plant beans in a garden where maize was grown the season before?
questions.answer: Because the beans are a legume whose root nodules add nitrogen to the soil, restoring the fertility that the maize used up. This is crop rotation.

questions.question: Give one plant grown from each of: cuttings, suckers, bulbs, rhizomes, tubers.
questions.answer: Cuttings — cassava; suckers — banana; bulbs — onion; rhizomes — ginger; tubers — Irish potato (or sweet potato).

items.subject: Science
subtopics: 3. EXTERNAL FEATURES OF A COW AND A BULL

questions.question: Name the four types of cattle and what each is kept for.
questions.answer: Dairy — milk; beef — meat; dual-purpose — both milk and meat; work (draught) — ploughing and pulling carts.

questions.question: Give the difference between indigenous and exotic breeds, with two examples of each.
questions.answer: Indigenous breeds have always been in the country, for example Ankole long-horned and Zebu; exotic breeds were brought from other countries, for example Friesian and Jersey.

questions.question: Give two advantages of indigenous breeds and two of exotic breeds.
questions.answer: Indigenous: resist diseases and heat, and can walk long distances for pasture and water. Exotic: give much more milk or meat, and mature faster.

questions.question: Name any six external features of a cow.
questions.answer: Any six of: horns, eyes, ears, muzzle, dewlap, hump, udder with teats, tail, hooves, hide, back, flank.

questions.question: Give three differences between a cow and a bull.
questions.answer: A cow has an udder with four teats while a bull has none; a bull has a larger head and thicker neck and shoulders; a bull is usually stronger and fiercer, while the cow is gentler and produces milk.

questions.question: Define: heifer, steer, calf.
questions.answer: Heifer — a young female that has not yet calved; steer (ox) — a castrated male; calf — the young one of cattle.

questions.question: Name any four methods of grazing cattle.
questions.answer: Any four of: free range, paddocking, tethering, zero grazing, strip grazing.

questions.question: Give three advantages of zero grazing.
questions.answer: Any three of: it suits a small piece of land; the milk and the animal stay clean; manure is easily collected; the animal uses less energy so it gives more milk; it is easy to control diseases and feeding.

questions.question: Name any five feeds given to cattle.
questions.answer: Any five of: pasture grasses, fodder such as elephant grass, legumes such as calliandra, crop residues, concentrates such as dairy meal, mineral salt licks, and clean water.

questions.question: Give any five qualities of a good cattle shed.
questions.answer: Any five of: spacious, dry, well ventilated, easy to clean, with a concrete or sloping floor, a good roof, feeding and watering places, a calf pen, a milking area and a crush.

questions.question: What is the gestation period of a cow? What is calving?
questions.answer: The gestation period is about nine months (280 days). Calving is the act of giving birth to a calf.

questions.question: What is colostrum, and why must the calf get it?
questions.answer: Colostrum is the first thick yellow milk produced after calving. The calf must get it because it is rich in antibodies that protect it from disease, and in nutrients for a good start.

questions.question: Give any three advantages of artificial insemination.
questions.answer: Any three of: a farmer can use a very good bull without keeping one; it prevents diseases spread by mating; one bull can serve very many cows; it improves the breed quickly; it is cheaper than keeping a bull.

questions.question: Give any six rules of clean milking.
questions.answer: Any six of: milk at the same time daily; wash hands and the udder with clean warm water and dry them; use clean dry metal containers; use the full-hand method; milk quickly and completely; keep the shed clean; sieve and cool the milk at once; a sick person or sick cow must not supply milk.

questions.question: Name any five milk products.
questions.answer: Any five of: ghee, butter, yoghurt, cheese, sour milk, cream, powdered milk, ice cream.

questions.question: Name any four cattle pests and the harm each causes.
questions.answer: Any four: ticks — suck blood and spread East Coast fever; tsetse flies — spread nagana; worms — cause anaemia and poor growth; lice and mites — cause irritation and wounds.

questions.question: Name any four cattle diseases and one way of controlling each.
questions.answer: Any four, for example: foot and mouth disease — vaccination and quarantine; East Coast fever — spraying or dipping against ticks; nagana — control tsetse flies and clear bush; mastitis — clean milking and treatment; anthrax — vaccination and never opening the carcass.

questions.question: Give any five practices that harm cattle.
questions.answer: Any five of: beating and overworking; rough or over-milking; tethering with no shade or water; overstocking and overgrazing; using dirty instruments for dehorning or castration; burning pasture; using wrong or expired drugs.

questions.question: Give any six steps in starting a livestock farm.
questions.answer: Any six of: choose a suitable site; decide the type of cattle and the system; get capital and plan; prepare land, pasture and fencing; build the shed and crush; buy healthy stock; arrange feeds and water; register with the veterinary officer; keep records; find a market.

questions.question: Why should a farmer keep records on a cattle farm?
questions.answer: Because records show which cows produce most milk, when each was served and is due to calve, what treatment was given, and how much money came in and went out — so the farmer can plan, breed better animals and know whether the farm is making a profit.

items.subject: Science
subtopics: 3. HOW PEOPLE USE THE RESOURCES AVAILABLE

questions.question: What is a resource? Give three living and three non-living resources.
questions.answer: A resource is anything in the environment that people use to satisfy their needs. Living: plants, animals, fish (also birds, insects, people). Non-living: soil, water, air (also minerals, sunlight, rocks).

questions.question: Why are human beings called a resource?
questions.answer: Because people provide labour, skills, ideas and leadership that are needed to use all the other resources and to develop the country.

questions.question: What is harvesting? Give the way each of these is harvested: fish, timber, salt, minerals.
questions.answer: Harvesting is collecting a resource from the environment for use. Fish — nets, hooks and traps; timber — felling trees and sawing; salt — evaporating water from salt lakes such as Katwe; minerals — mining, quarrying, drilling or panning.

questions.question: Give any five good harvesting practices.
questions.answer: Any five of: take only what is needed; use the right tools and methods; leave young plants, fish and animals to grow; avoid poison, explosives and undersized nets; replant after cutting trees; avoid harvesting in the breeding season; store the harvest well.

questions.question: Give any four uses of water and four uses of soil.
questions.answer: Water: drinking, cooking and washing, irrigation, fishing, transport, hydro-electric power (any four). Soil: growing crops, making bricks, making pots, building, holding plant roots (any four).

questions.question: Give the difference between renewable and non-renewable resources.
questions.answer: Renewable resources can be replaced or never run out, such as sunlight and wind; non-renewable resources get used up and cannot be replaced, such as gold and petroleum.

questions.question: Classify these as renewable or non-renewable: sunlight, copper, wind, petroleum, forests.
questions.answer: Renewable: sunlight, wind, forests. Non-renewable: copper, petroleum.

questions.question: Why are plants and animals renewable only under certain conditions?
questions.answer: Because they can only replace themselves if they are given time and conditions to reproduce. If people cut trees or catch fish faster than they can reproduce, they are used up completely and may become extinct.

questions.question: What is meant by depletion of a resource? Give one example.
questions.answer: Depletion is using up a resource until very little is left, for example over-fishing on a lake until the fish stocks nearly disappear (or over-cutting of forests).

questions.question: What does it mean when an animal species is said to be extinct?
questions.answer: It means the species no longer exists anywhere — every member of it has died and it can never be brought back.

questions.question: What is conservation?
questions.answer: Conservation is protecting and using resources carefully so that they are not destroyed or used up.

questions.question: Give any five ways of conserving soil.
questions.answer: Any five of: mulching, terracing, contour ploughing, crop rotation, applying manure, planting cover crops, controlled grazing, planting trees.

questions.question: Give any four ways of conserving water.
questions.answer: Any four of: harvesting rain water, protecting springs and wetlands, avoiding pollution, closing taps, careful irrigation, repairing leaking pipes.

questions.question: Give any four ways of conserving forests and four ways of protecting wild animals and fish.
questions.answer: Forests: afforestation, reafforestation, agroforestry, energy-saving stoves, forest reserves (any four). Animals and fish: game parks and sanctuaries, laws against poaching, closed fishing seasons, correct net sizes, fish farming (any four).

questions.question: Give any five reasons why resources must be conserved.
questions.answer: Any five of: so that resources last for future generations; to keep the environment healthy; to keep soil fertile and rainfall reliable; to protect wildlife and tourism; to avoid famine and poverty; to prevent conflicts over scarce resources.

items.subject: Science
subtopics: 4. DISEASES AND DISORDERS OF THE SYSTEM

questions.question: Give the difference between breathing and respiration.
questions.answer: Breathing is simply taking in and giving out air, while respiration is the process by which the body breaks down food to release energy inside the cells.

questions.question: Name any six organs of the respiratory system.
questions.answer: Any six of: nose, pharynx, epiglottis, larynx, trachea, bronchi, bronchioles, alveoli, lungs, diaphragm.

questions.question: State the work of: the nose, the epiglottis, the trachea, the alveoli, the diaphragm.
questions.answer: Nose — takes in air and filters, warms and moistens it; epiglottis — closes the windpipe when swallowing; trachea — carries air to the lungs; alveoli — where oxygen enters the blood and carbon dioxide leaves; diaphragm — the muscle that flattens and relaxes to help breathing.

questions.question: Trace the path taken by air from outside the body to the blood.
questions.answer: Nose → pharynx → larynx → trachea → bronchi → bronchioles → alveoli → blood.

questions.question: Why is it better to breathe through the nose than through the mouth?
questions.answer: Because the nose has hairs and mucus that trap dust and germs, and it warms and moistens the air before it reaches the lungs; the mouth does none of these.

questions.question: Describe what happens to the diaphragm and the ribs when a person breathes in.
questions.answer: The diaphragm flattens and moves downwards, the ribs move upwards and outwards, the chest cavity increases in size and air rushes into the lungs.

questions.question: Give three differences between inhaled and exhaled air.
questions.answer: Any three of: inhaled air has more oxygen (21% against 16%); exhaled air has much more carbon dioxide (about 4% against 0.03%); exhaled air has more water vapour; exhaled air is warmer.

questions.question: Describe one experiment that shows exhaled air contains carbon dioxide.
questions.answer: Breathe out through a straw into lime water. The lime water turns milky, showing that carbon dioxide is present. (Comparing with air blown in by a pump shows the difference.)

questions.question: Describe one experiment that shows exhaled air contains water vapour.
questions.answer: Breathe onto a cold mirror or glass. Tiny drops of water form on it, showing that exhaled air contains water vapour.

questions.question: Write the word equation for respiration.
questions.answer: Food (glucose) + oxygen → energy + carbon dioxide + water

questions.question: Give any four uses of the energy released during respiration.
questions.answer: Any four of: movement and work; growth and repair of the body; keeping the body warm; the beating of the heart and the working of other organs; thinking; digestion.

questions.question: Name any five diseases of the respiratory system.
questions.answer: Any five of: tuberculosis, pneumonia, bronchitis, asthma, the common cold and flu, whooping cough, lung cancer, diphtheria.

questions.question: Give the cause and two signs of tuberculosis.
questions.answer: Tuberculosis is caused by bacteria spread through coughing and sneezing by an infected person. Signs: a cough lasting more than two weeks, chest pain, weight loss, night sweats, fever (any two).

questions.question: Give any six ways of keeping the respiratory system healthy.
questions.answer: Any six of: do not smoke and avoid other people's smoke; keep rooms well ventilated; avoid dust and cooking smoke; cover the mouth when coughing; immunise children; eat a balanced diet; exercise regularly; breathe through the nose; avoid overcrowded rooms; treat coughs and colds early; plant trees.

questions.question: How does the circulatory system help the respiratory system?
questions.answer: The blood, especially the red blood cells, carries oxygen from the alveoli to every cell of the body, and carries the waste carbon dioxide back to the lungs to be breathed out. Without the circulatory system, the oxygen would never reach the cells.

items.subject: Science
items.topic: Science at Home and in Our Community
subtopics: 2. METHODS OF MAKING WATER CLEAN AND SAFE

questions.question: Give the difference between clean water and safe water.
questions.answer: Clean water has no dirt that you can see, while safe water is free from germs and harmful substances and can be drunk without causing disease. Water can look clean and still be unsafe.

questions.question: Name any five impurities found in water and where each comes from.
questions.answer: Any five, for example: human wastes — from poor latrines and open defecation; animal wastes — from animals at the water source; fertilisers and pesticides — from gardens; oils and chemicals — from factories and garages; silt and leaves — washed in by rain; rubbish and polythene — from homes.

questions.question: Name any four diseases caused by drinking unsafe water.
questions.answer: Any four of: cholera, typhoid, dysentery, diarrhoea, bilharzia, worms, hepatitis.

questions.question: Name five methods of making water safe for drinking.
questions.answer: Boiling, filtering, treating with chemicals, distilling and decanting (also solar disinfection).

questions.question: Describe how water is made safe by decanting.
questions.answer: The dirty water is left to stand undisturbed in a container until the heavy particles settle at the bottom. The clear water on top is then poured off carefully into another clean container, leaving the sediment behind.

questions.question: Why is boiling the commonest method used in homes?
questions.answer: Because it is cheap and easy — every home has a fire — and it kills the germs that cause disease, needing no special chemicals or equipment.

questions.question: Which method gives the purest water, and why?
questions.answer: Distillation, because boiling turns the water into steam, leaving germs, salts and other dissolved substances behind; the steam is then cooled back into very pure water.

questions.question: Give the correct order of treating very dirty water and say why that order is used.
questions.answer: First decant or filter to remove the dirt you can see, then boil or treat to kill the germs, then store in a clean covered container. Filtering first is important because dirt and solid matter can protect germs from the treatment and make chemicals less effective.

questions.question: Give any four rules for storing drinking water safely.
questions.answer: Any four of: use a clean covered container; use a tap or long-handled cup so hands do not enter; never mix treated with untreated water; clean the container regularly; keep it away from animals and small children.

questions.question: Give any five ways of protecting a water source.
questions.answer: Any five of: fence the source; build a drainage channel; keep latrines at least 30 m away and downhill; do not wash clothes or bathe at the source; do not water animals there; do not dig or farm next to it; plant grass around it.

questions.question: Name any four plant materials used to make salt.
questions.answer: Any four of: dry banana peelings, banana stems, bean stalks, millet stalks, papyrus reeds, water-lily plants.

questions.question: Describe, in steps, how salt is made from plant materials.
questions.answer: Dry the plant material → burn it into ash → put the ash in a container or funnel-shaped basket lined with grass → pour clean water slowly through the ash (leaching) → collect the filtrate → boil it until all the water evaporates → the solid salt is left behind.

questions.question: Which three science processes are shown when making salt from plants?
questions.answer: Dissolving, filtering and evaporation.

questions.question: Give any six steps followed when washing clothes at home.
questions.answer: Any six of: sort the clothes; empty the pockets and shake off dust; soak them in soapy water; wash by rubbing or brushing the dirty parts; rinse two or three times; hang them in the sun to dry; iron them; fold and store them cleanly.

questions.question: Give any four reasons why clothes should be washed and ironed.
questions.answer: Any four of: to remove dirt, sweat and bad smell; to kill germs and prevent skin diseases; to kill jiggers and lice by ironing; to make the clothes last longer; to look smart and keep self-respect.

questions.question: What is first aid, and who is a first aider?
questions.answer: First aid is the immediate help given to an injured or suddenly sick person before a health worker arrives or before the person reaches hospital. A first aider is the person who gives it.

questions.question: Give any four aims of first aid.
questions.answer: Any four of: to save life; to prevent the injury from getting worse; to relieve pain; to promote recovery; to get the person quickly to proper medical care.

questions.question: Give any five qualities of a good first aider.
questions.answer: Any five of: calm and confident; quick but careful; clean; kind and comforting; observant; knows his or her limits; sends for help early.

questions.question: Name any eight items found in a first-aid kit.
questions.answer: Any eight of: cotton wool, bandages, gauze, plaster, scissors, antiseptic, gloves, a thermometer, safety pins, clean water, a torch, ORS, a splint, a notebook and pen.

questions.question: Give the difference between a burn and a scald, with one cause of each.
questions.answer: A burn is caused by dry heat, for example fire or a hot iron; a scald is caused by moist heat, for example hot water or steam.

questions.question: Give the steps of first aid for a burn.
questions.answer: Remove the person from the source of heat (switching off electricity if needed) → cool the part with clean cool water for 10–20 minutes → remove tight clothing near the burn before swelling → cover with a clean dry non-fluffy cloth → give fluids if the person is fully awake → take them to a health centre if the burn is large, deep or on the face or hands.

questions.question: Name any four things that should never be put on a burn.
questions.answer: Any four of: cow dung, engine oil, paraffin, mud, butter, toothpaste, ash, ice.

questions.question: Give any four ways of preventing burns and scalds at home.
questions.answer: Any four of: keep children away from the fireplace and kitchen; turn saucepan handles inwards; put out fires properly; lock away paraffin, petrol and matches; do not overload sockets; put out candles before sleeping; keep hot drinks away from table edges.

questions.question: What is fever, and what is the normal body temperature?
questions.answer: Fever is a body temperature higher than normal. The normal body temperature is about 37 °C.

questions.question: Give the first aid for a child with a high fever.
questions.answer: Move the child to a cool airy place → remove heavy clothing → sponge with lukewarm water → give plenty of fluids → give the correct dose of fever medicine if available → take the child for a malaria test and treatment quickly.

questions.question: What are convulsions? Give three causes.
questions.answer: Convulsions are sudden uncontrollable jerking of the body. Causes: very high fever in a child, epilepsy, cerebral malaria or meningitis (any three).

questions.question: Give any five steps of first aid for a person having convulsions, and two things you must not do.
questions.answer: Do: stay calm and call for help; lay the person on the floor on their side away from fire, water and sharp objects; loosen tight clothing; put something soft under the head; after the fit, keep them on their side and take them to a health centre. Do not: put anything in the mouth; hold the person down or pour cold water on them.

questions.question: Give the first aid for a person who has nearly drowned, and say why a weak swimmer should not jump in.
questions.answer: Reach out to the person with a stick, rope or floating object; once out, lay them on their side so water drains; check breathing; keep them warm; if they are not breathing, give rescue breathing if trained and keep calling for help; take them to hospital. A weak swimmer should not jump in because the drowning person panics and clings, and both can drown.

questions.question: Give any five ways of preventing drowning.
questions.answer: Any five of: learn to swim; never swim alone or in flooded rivers; do not overload boats and wear life jackets; never play near wells or tanks; cover wells and tanks; watch small children near any water; do not swim after a heavy meal or in a storm.

questions.question: What is fainting? Give three causes and the first aid given.
questions.answer: Fainting is a short loss of consciousness caused by too little blood reaching the brain. Causes: standing too long in the sun, hunger, tiredness, shock or fear (any three). First aid: lay the person flat in a cool airy place, raise the legs, loosen tight clothing, allow fresh air, sponge the face, and give water when they wake.

questions.question: Why is a person who has fainted made to lie down with the legs raised?
questions.answer: Because raising the legs helps blood flow back to the brain, which is what was lacking, so the person recovers quickly.

questions.question: What is a foreign body? Give the first aid for an insect in the ear and for dust in the eye.
questions.answer: A foreign body is anything that enters the body where it does not belong. Insect in the ear: pour a little clean cooking oil or warm water to float it out, then see a health worker if it remains. Dust in the eye: do not rub; wash it out with clean water, or lift the upper eyelid over the lower one.

questions.question: What should be done for a child who has swallowed paraffin, and what must never be done?
questions.answer: The child should be taken to hospital immediately, carrying the container if possible, and kept calm and on their side. Never make the child vomit, because paraffin coming back up can enter the lungs and cause serious damage.

questions.question: Give the first aid for a person choking on food.
questions.answer: Encourage the person to cough; bend a child forward and give firm back blows between the shoulder blades; keep checking the mouth and remove anything you can see easily; call for help at once if the object does not come out.

questions.question: Why should a person who has nearly drowned be taken to hospital even if they look well?
questions.answer: Because water that entered the lungs can cause breathing problems and infection several hours later, so the person must be checked by a health worker even if they seem to have recovered.

items.subject: Science
subtopics: 3. IMPORTANCE OF USING A TOILET OR LATRINE

questions.question: What is sanitation?
questions.answer: Sanitation is keeping the surroundings clean and disposing of human waste and rubbish safely so that people stay healthy.

questions.question: Name any five diseases caused by poor sanitation.
questions.answer: Any five of: cholera, typhoid, dysentery, diarrhoea, worms, bilharzia, hepatitis, jiggers.

questions.question: Give the full meaning of VIP latrine.
questions.answer: Ventilated Improved Pit latrine.

questions.question: Name three special features of a VIP latrine and explain how it removes smell.
questions.answer: Features: a vent pipe from the pit to above the roof, a fly screen at the top of the pipe, and a dark interior with an uncovered squat hole. The sun heats the vent pipe so the air inside rises and carries the smell out, while fresh air enters through the door.

questions.question: How does a VIP latrine control flies?
questions.answer: Flies in the dark pit fly towards the light at the top of the vent pipe and are trapped by the fly screen, where they die.

questions.question: Give one advantage and one disadvantage of an ordinary pit latrine.
questions.answer: Advantage: it is cheap and easy to build with local materials and needs no water. Disadvantage: it smells and attracts flies (it also fills up and must be replaced).

questions.question: What is an Ecosan toilet, and what is added after each use?
questions.answer: An Ecosan (ecological sanitation) toilet is one that separates urine from faeces and turns the waste into manure. Ash or dry soil is added after each use.

questions.question: Give any three advantages of an Ecosan toilet.
questions.answer: Any three of: it provides manure; it suits rocky, sandy, waterlogged or crowded areas; it does not pollute ground water; there is no smell when ash is used; no deep pit has to be dug.

questions.question: In what kind of areas is an Ecosan toilet especially useful, and why?
questions.answer: In rocky, sandy, waterlogged or very crowded areas, because a deep pit cannot be dug safely there and a pit would collapse or pollute the ground water.

questions.question: What is a potty, and how should it be used and cleaned?
questions.answer: A potty is a small portable container used by babies and small children who cannot use the latrine. It must be emptied into the latrine immediately, washed with clean water and soap, and dried in the sun — never emptied in the compound.

questions.question: What is a water closet? Give two advantages and two disadvantages.
questions.answer: A water closet is a flush toilet with a cistern and a water seal that carries waste to a septic tank or sewer. Advantages: it is clean and has no smell; it is comfortable and free from flies. Disadvantages: it needs plenty of piped water; it is expensive and blocks easily.

questions.question: Give any six importances of using a toilet or latrine.
questions.answer: Any six of: it prevents diseases such as cholera and worms; it keeps the compound and gardens free of human waste; it controls flies and bad smells; it protects water sources; it gives privacy and dignity; it keeps the home clean; it is required by public health law.

questions.question: Explain how disease travels from faeces to the mouth, and how using a latrine breaks the path.
questions.answer: Faeces left in the open are carried to food and the mouth by flies, fingers, food, fluids and fields — the "five Fs". Using a latrine keeps the faeces sealed in a pit so flies and feet cannot carry them, and washing hands with soap removes what is on the fingers, so the path is broken.

questions.question: Give any six rules for the proper use of a latrine.
questions.answer: Any six of: use the latrine every time; aim into the hole and keep the slab clean; cover the hole after use in an ordinary latrine; put used paper in the pit; add ash in an Ecosan toilet; flush a water closet; wash hands with soap afterwards; teach children to use the potty properly.

questions.question: Give any six ways of maintaining a latrine.
questions.answer: Any six of: sweep and scrub the floor and slab daily; use water or disinfectant; keep soap and water at the door; repair cracks, doors and roofs; keep the vent screen in good order; keep the door closed; do not throw rubbish into the pit; plant grass around it; dig a new pit when it is nearly full.

questions.question: Why should rubbish and polythene never be thrown into a pit latrine?
questions.answer: Because they do not rot, so they fill the pit quickly and shorten its life, and in a flush toilet they cause blockages.

questions.question: Where should a latrine be sited in relation to a water source and the house?
questions.answer: At least 30 metres from a water source and downhill from it, and about 6 metres from the house, downwind, on firm well-drained ground.

questions.question: Give the difference between a VIP latrine and an ordinary pit latrine in the way the squat hole is treated.
questions.answer: In a VIP latrine the squat hole is left uncovered so that air can flow through the pit and up the vent pipe; in an ordinary pit latrine the hole is covered after use to keep out flies and reduce the smell.

questions.question: Why should hands be washed with soap after using a latrine?
questions.answer: Because germs from faeces remain on the fingers, and hands touch food, water and other people. Washing with soap removes those germs and prevents diseases such as diarrhoea, cholera and worms.

questions.question: What should be done when a pit latrine is nearly full?
questions.answer: It should be closed and covered with soil and a new pit dug elsewhere; the slab can be moved to the new pit, and the old site should be marked and, in time, planted with trees.

items.subject: Science
subtopics: 6. CARE FOR THE REPRODUCTIVE ORGANS AND COMMON DISORDERS

questions.question: Give the difference between growth and development.
questions.answer: Growth is an increase in the size and weight of the body, while development is the change that makes the body able to do more, such as walking, talking and reproducing.

questions.question: What is puberty, and at about what age does it begin in girls and in boys?
questions.answer: Puberty is the stage at which the reproductive organs become mature and a young person becomes able to produce children. It begins at about 10–14 years in girls and 12–16 years in boys.

questions.question: What is adolescence?
questions.answer: Adolescence is the period of change between childhood and adulthood, affecting the body, the mind and the feelings.

questions.question: Give any four physical changes at puberty in girls and four in boys.
questions.answer: Girls: breasts develop; hips widen; menstruation begins; pubic and armpit hair grows (also oily skin, rapid growth). Boys: the voice deepens; the chest and shoulders broaden; wet dreams begin; facial, pubic and armpit hair grows.

questions.question: Give any four social and emotional changes during adolescence.
questions.answer: Any four of: wanting independence; strong peer influence; quick changes of mood; shyness; interest in the opposite sex; wanting privacy; new interest in appearance.

questions.question: Give the difference between primary and secondary sex characteristics, with two examples of each.
questions.answer: Primary characteristics are the reproductive organs present at birth, for example the testes and the ovaries. Secondary characteristics appear at puberty, for example breasts in girls and a deep voice in boys.

questions.question: Name any four parts of the male reproductive system and the work of each.
questions.answer: Any four: testes — produce sperm cells; scrotum — holds the testes and keeps them cool; sperm duct — carries sperms; urethra — passes semen and urine out; penis — the organ through which semen and urine leave the body.

questions.question: Name any four parts of the female reproductive system and the work of each.
questions.answer: Any four: ovaries — produce egg cells; fallopian tubes — carry the egg and are where fertilisation happens; uterus — where the baby develops; cervix — the neck of the uterus; vagina — the passage to the outside.

questions.question: Where are sperm cells produced, and where are egg cells produced?
questions.answer: Sperm cells are produced in the testes; egg cells are produced in the ovaries.

questions.question: What is menstruation, and about how long is the menstrual cycle?
questions.answer: Menstruation is the monthly flow of blood and the lining of the uterus through the vagina when the egg has not been fertilised. The cycle is about 28 days.

questions.question: What is fertilisation, and where does it take place?
questions.answer: Fertilisation is the joining of a sperm cell and an egg cell. It takes place in the fallopian tube (oviduct).

questions.question: Give the meaning of conception, zygote and gestation.
questions.answer: Conception — the fertilised egg attaching to the wall of the uterus and beginning to grow; zygote — the single cell formed at fertilisation; gestation — the period the baby develops in the womb.

questions.question: How long does pregnancy last, and what is the work of the placenta?
questions.answer: Pregnancy lasts about nine months (40 weeks). The placenta supplies the baby with food and oxygen from the mother and carries away its waste.

questions.question: Give any four signs of pregnancy.
questions.answer: Any four of: the monthly periods stop; morning sickness; the breasts enlarge; the abdomen grows; tiredness; changes in appetite.

questions.question: Give any six ways of caring for a pregnant mother.
questions.answer: Any six of: attend antenatal clinic early and regularly; eat a balanced diet rich in iron; take the supplements given; sleep under a treated mosquito net; rest and avoid heavy work; avoid alcohol, smoking and self-medication; keep clean; deliver at a health centre with a trained health worker.

questions.question: Give any four problems that can occur during pregnancy.
questions.answer: Any four of: anaemia, malaria, high blood pressure, miscarriage, bleeding, excessive vomiting, obstructed labour, malnutrition, infections including HIV.

questions.question: Give any five effects of teenage pregnancy and four ways of preventing it.
questions.answer: Effects (any five): danger to the health and life of the girl and baby; obstructed labour and fistula; low birth weight; dropping out of school; poverty; stigma and rejection; unsafe abortion. Prevention (any four): stay in school; abstain from sex; avoid bad company, alcohol and drugs; refuse gifts and lifts from older people; report abuse to a trusted adult; get correct information from parents and health workers.

questions.question: Give any six ways of caring for the reproductive organs.
questions.answer: Any six of: bathe daily and wash the private parts with clean water; wear clean cotton underwear and change it daily; wipe from front to back; use and change clean sanitary materials; never insert anything into the private parts; avoid harmful traditional practices; treat itching or discharge early; abstain from sex; report anybody who touches you wrongly.

questions.question: What is family planning? Give any five reasons why it is important.
questions.answer: Family planning is deciding how many children to have and when to have them, using acceptable methods. Importance (any five): it protects the mother's health; it gives each child better care and education; it reduces infant and maternal deaths; it helps the family plan its money; it slows very rapid population growth; it allows parents to work and rest.

questions.question: Name three natural and three artificial methods of family planning, and correct any two myths about family planning.
questions.answer: Natural: abstinence, the calendar (rhythm) method, breastfeeding in the early months. Artificial: condoms, pills, injections (also implants, the loop). Myths corrected: "family planning makes a woman permanently barren" — most methods are reversible and fertility returns when they are stopped; "it is only for women" — it is the responsibility of both partners.

items.subject: Social Studies
items.topic: The Road to Independence in East Africa
subtopics: 2. THE STRUGGLE FOR INDEPENDENCE, COUNTRY BY COUNTRY
4. DEMOCRATIC RULE IN EAST AFRICAN COUNTRIES

questions.question: Who is an explorer? Name any four explorers who came to East Africa.
questions.answer: An explorer is a person who travels to an unknown place in order to find out about it. Any four of: Speke, Grant, Burton, Baker, Livingstone, Stanley, Krapf, Rebmann.

questions.question: Which two explorers reached the source of the Nile, and in which year?
questions.answer: John Hanning Speke and James Grant, in 1862.

questions.question: Give any four reasons why the explorers came to East Africa.
questions.answer: Any four of: to find the source of the Nile; to map the interior; to look for raw materials and markets; to spread Christianity; to help stop the slave trade; for adventure and fame.

questions.question: Give any four challenges the explorers faced.
questions.answer: Any four of: tropical diseases; hostile people; wild animals; thick forests, swamps and mountains; language barriers; shortage of food and clean water; desertion by porters.

questions.question: Name the colonial master of each: Uganda, Kenya, Tanganyika (after 1919), Rwanda and Burundi.
questions.answer: Uganda — Britain; Kenya — Britain; Tanganyika after 1919 — Britain (Germany before); Rwanda and Burundi — Belgium (Germany before).

questions.question: Give the difference between a colony and a protectorate.
questions.answer: A colony is ruled directly by the foreign power, whose officers govern it; a protectorate is protected and controlled by the foreign power but is governed largely through its own traditional rulers.

questions.question: What is indirect rule, and which colonial power used it?
questions.answer: Indirect rule is governing a colony through the existing African chiefs and traditional systems. It was used by Britain.

questions.question: Give any four positive and four negative effects of colonial rule in East Africa.
questions.answer: Positive: roads and railways were built; schools and hospitals were started; new cash crops were introduced; the slave trade was stopped (any four). Negative: Africans lost independence and land; forced labour and heavy taxes; African culture was weakened; traditional rulers lost power; raw materials were exploited (any four).

questions.question: What was the Mau Mau, and in which country did it take place?
questions.answer: The Mau Mau was an armed struggle (1952–1960) for land and freedom. It took place in Kenya.

questions.question: Give the date of independence of Uganda, Kenya, Tanganyika, Rwanda and Burundi.
questions.answer: Uganda — 9 October 1962; Kenya — 12 December 1963; Tanganyika — 9 December 1961; Rwanda — 1 July 1962; Burundi — 1 July 1962.

questions.question: Name the first leader of each East African country at independence.
questions.answer: Uganda — Milton Obote (Prime Minister), with Sir Edward Mutesa II as first President; Kenya — Jomo Kenyatta; Tanganyika — Julius Nyerere; Rwanda — Grégoire Kayibanda; Burundi — Mwami Mwambutsa IV.

questions.question: How was Tanzania formed?
questions.answer: Tanzania was formed on 26 April 1964 by the union of Tanganyika and Zanzibar.

questions.question: Give any four methods used by East Africans in the struggle for independence.
questions.answer: Any four of: forming political parties; forming trade unions; strikes and boycotts; petitions and delegations; newspapers and rallies; armed struggle; taking part in elections.

questions.question: Give any five challenges faced by East African countries after independence.
questions.answer: Any five of: military coups; dictatorship and abuse of human rights; civil wars; the 1994 genocide against the Tutsi in Rwanda; tribalism and nepotism; corruption; poverty and unemployment; refugees; heavy foreign debts.

questions.question: Define democracy and give any four features of a democratic country.
questions.answer: Democracy is government of the people, by the people and for the people. Features: free and fair elections; freedom of speech and the press; respect for human rights; the rule of law; accountable leaders (any four).

questions.question: Give four ways in which a person can become a citizen.
questions.answer: By birth, by descent, by registration and by naturalisation.

questions.question: Give any five rights and five responsibilities of a citizen.
questions.answer: Rights: life, education, property, freedom of speech and worship, health care, a fair trial, voting, movement (any five). Responsibilities: obeying the law, paying taxes, protecting public property and the environment, voting, respecting others' rights, keeping peace, reporting crime (any five).

questions.question: Outline the steps of the electoral process.
questions.answer: Voter registration → nomination of candidates → campaigning → polling day with a secret ballot → counting the votes → declaring the results → swearing in of the winner (with complaints going to the courts).

questions.question: Give any five challenges of the electoral process and three solutions.
questions.answer: Challenges: rigging; bribery of voters; violence and intimidation; illiteracy; late delivery of materials; low turnout; errors in the register (any five). Solutions: an independent Electoral Commission with a clean register; civic and voter education; observers, agents and police at polling stations, with rigging and bribery punished (any three).

questions.question: Draw the map of East Africa and write in each country its year of independence.
questions.answer: Learner's map. Tanganyika 1961, Uganda 1962, Rwanda 1962, Burundi 1962, Kenya 1963.

items.subject: Social Studies
items.topic: Responsible Living in the East African Environment
subtopics: 5. CONSEQUENCES OF IRRESPONSIBLE LIVING IN THE EAST AFRICAN ENVIRONMENT

questions.question: Define the environment and environmental conservation.
questions.answer: The environment is everything that surrounds us — land, water, air, plants, animals and people. Conservation is protecting and looking after natural resources so that they are not used up or destroyed.

questions.question: Give the difference between afforestation and reafforestation.
questions.answer: Afforestation is planting trees where there were none before, while reafforestation is replanting trees in an area where trees were cut down.

questions.question: Name any five proper methods of farming that protect the soil.
questions.answer: Any five of: crop rotation, mulching, terracing, contour ploughing, strip cropping, applying manure, controlled grazing, fallowing, planting cover crops.

questions.question: Give any four alternative sources of energy that save trees.
questions.answer: Any four of: solar energy, biogas, hydro-electric power, wind energy, energy-saving stoves, briquettes.

questions.question: What is waste management?
questions.answer: Waste management is the collecting, sorting, treating and disposing of rubbish and other waste in a safe way.

questions.question: Give the difference between biodegradable and non-biodegradable waste, with two examples of each.
questions.answer: Biodegradable waste rots naturally, for example food remains and leaves. Non-biodegradable waste does not rot, for example polythene bags and glass.

questions.question: Explain the three Rs of waste management.
questions.answer: Reduce — use less of what becomes rubbish; Reuse — use items such as bottles and sacks again; Recycle — make waste into new useful things such as plastic basins from old plastic.

questions.question: Give any four dangers of poor waste disposal.
questions.answer: Any four of: blocked drainage and flooding; diseases such as cholera and malaria; pollution of soil, water and air; bad smells; injuries from broken glass; death of animals that swallow polythene; ugly surroundings.

questions.question: What does NEMA stand for, and in which year did it start work?
questions.answer: National Environment Management Authority; it started work in 1995.

questions.question: State any five functions of NEMA.
questions.answer: Any five of: coordinating environmental activities; making and enforcing standards; carrying out environmental impact assessments; monitoring pollution; protecting wetlands and forests; educating the public; advising government; punishing offenders.

questions.question: Define climate change and give any four of its causes.
questions.answer: Climate change is a long-term change in the normal climate of an area. Causes: deforestation, bush burning, swamp reclamation, smoke from factories and vehicles, overgrazing (any four).

questions.question: Give any four effects of climate change in East Africa.
questions.answer: Any four of: unreliable rainfall; longer droughts; heavier storms and floods; melting of ice on Kilimanjaro and Rwenzori; drying lakes and rivers; famine; more crop pests.

questions.question: Give any five consequences of irresponsible living in the environment.
questions.answer: Any five of: floods, landslides, desertification, pollution of land, water and air, diseases, resource depletion, pressure from a very fast-growing population, loss of wildlife, soil erosion, silting of lakes.

questions.question: Why is it dangerous to build houses in a wetland?
questions.answer: Because a wetland holds water like a sponge. When it is filled in and built on, the water has nowhere to go, so the area floods; the houses stand on weak, waterlogged ground; the wetland can no longer filter water or provide fish, papyrus and water for the community.

questions.question: Give any two causes of landslides and two ways of preventing them.
questions.answer: Causes: cutting trees and farming on steep slopes; heavy prolonged rain on loose soil (also digging and building on steep ground). Prevention: plant trees and grass on steep slopes; make terraces and dig contour trenches; avoid cultivating and settling on very steep land; resettle people from dangerous slopes.

questions.question: What is desertification, and which parts of East Africa are most affected?
questions.answer: Desertification is the spread of desert conditions into land that was not desert before. It affects Karamoja in Uganda and northern Kenya most (also parts of central Tanzania).

questions.question: Give any six solutions to the environmental problems of East Africa.
questions.answer: Any six of: afforestation and reafforestation; energy-saving stoves, biogas and solar; proper farming methods; protecting wetlands and river banks; proper waste management; treating sewage and factory waste; enforcing laws through NEMA; environmental education; family planning education; resettling people from dangerous areas; joint EAC action.

questions.question: Give any four things a P.6 learner can do to protect the environment.
questions.answer: Any four of: plant and water a tree; use both sides of paper; pick up and sort rubbish; never burn polythene; use a latrine; save water and switch off lights; join the school environment club; teach others.

questions.question: Why should the East African countries work together on environmental issues?
questions.answer: Because the environment is shared — Lake Victoria, the River Nile, the air and the migrating wildlife cross borders. Pollution or deforestation in one country affects the others, so laws, research and clean-up efforts work best when the countries act together through the EAC.

questions.question: Draw a poster message of not more than ten words encouraging people to protect the environment.
questions.answer: Learner's poster. For example: "Plant a tree today, save your tomorrow."

questions.question: What are the two sub-topics under School Holidays in Primary Seven?
questions.answer: Holiday Plans and Holiday Activities.

questions.question: What is the main purpose of the School Holidays topic?
questions.answer: It equips learners with language skills and values that help them interact effectively with others during holiday situations.

questions.question: What is a holiday plan?
questions.answer: An arrangement of activities a learner intends to carry out during a holiday.

questions.question: Mention five things that can be included in a holiday plan.
questions.answer: Study, visiting relatives, travelling, household chores and recreation.

questions.question: What is a programme?
questions.answer: A planned list of activities and their times.

questions.question: What is a remedial class?
questions.answer: An additional lesson designed to help learners improve areas where they have difficulties.

questions.question: What is the difference between urban and rural?
questions.answer: Urban refers to towns and cities, while rural refers to countryside areas.

questions.question: What does "commence" mean?
questions.answer: To begin.

questions.question: What does "board" mean?
questions.answer: To get onto a means of transport.

questions.question: What is a holiday activity?
questions.answer: Something a learner does during a school holiday.

questions.question: Mention six holiday activities.
questions.answer: Studying, visiting relatives, farming, travelling, cooking and playing games.

questions.question: What are chores?
questions.answer: Regular small jobs that need to be done.

questions.question: Why should learners help with chores?
questions.answer: To develop responsibility, cooperation and useful life skills.

questions.question: What is a routine?
questions.answer: A regular pattern of activities.

questions.question: What is a tour?
questions.answer: A journey made to visit different places.

questions.question: What is a concert?
questions.answer: A public performance of music.

questions.question: What is a bash?
questions.answer: An informal party or celebration.

questions.question: What is fare?
questions.answer: Money paid for travelling.

questions.question: What is the structure used to talk about planned future actions?
questions.answer: am/is/are going to + verb.

questions.question: Make a sentence using "going to".
questions.answer: I am going to visit my aunt next holiday.

questions.question: What is a question tag?
questions.answer: A short question added to the end of a statement.

questions.question: Add the correct question tag: You will travel tomorrow, ?
questions.answer: won't you?

questions.question: What is reported speech?
questions.answer: It is used to report what someone said without giving the exact words.

questions.question: Change into reported speech: John said, "I am going to visit my uncle."
questions.answer: John said that he was going to visit his uncle.

questions.question: What is a present participle?
questions.answer: A verb form usually ending in -ing.

questions.question: Give two present participles.
questions.answer: Travelling and studying.

questions.question: What is active voice?
questions.answer: A sentence structure in which the subject performs the action.

questions.question: Give an example of active voice.
questions.answer: Mary cleaned the house.

questions.question: What is the third conditional used for?
questions.answer: It is used to talk about unreal or imagined past situations and their possible results.

questions.question: Give the structure of the third conditional.
questions.answer: If + past perfect, would have + past participle.

questions.question: Complete: If I had seen him, he have helped me.
questions.answer: would.

questions.question: What is an adjective?
questions.answer: A word that describes a noun.

questions.question: Give three adjectives that can describe a holiday.
questions.answer: Interesting, exciting and enjoyable.

questions.question: What is cooperation?
questions.answer: Working together to achieve a common goal.

questions.question: Mention the values emphasised in the School Holidays topic.
questions.answer: Responsibility, cooperation, sharing, care, respect and love.

questions.question: Mention the life skills developed through the topic.
questions.answer: Effective communication, creative thinking, critical thinking, interpersonal relationships and friendship formation.

questions.question: What communication skills should learners develop?
questions.answer: Fluency, confidence, accuracy and logical presentation of ideas.

questions.question: What critical-thinking skills are developed?
questions.answer: Responding appropriately to questions, giving reasons for actions, making good use of available information and analysing statements.

questions.question: What friendship skills are developed?
questions.answer: Sharing, playing with others and working in groups.

questions.question: What is letter writing?
questions.answer: It is communicating a message to another person or organisation in written form.

questions.question: What are the two main types of letters studied in P.7?
questions.answer: Informal letters and formal letters.

questions.question: What is an informal letter?
questions.answer: A personal letter written to someone we know well.

questions.question: What is a formal letter?
questions.answer: An official letter written for a particular formal purpose.

questions.question: Mention five components of an informal letter.
questions.answer: Address, date, salutation, body and complimentary close.

questions.question: Mention five components of a formal letter.
questions.answer: Writer's address, date, receiver's address, salutation and body.

questions.question: Who can receive informal letters?
questions.answer: Friends, relatives and classmates.

questions.question: Who can receive formal letters?
questions.answer: Officials, employers, organisations and institutions.

questions.question: Mention four reasons for writing informal letters.
questions.answer: To give information, maintain friendship, ask questions and thank someone.

questions.question: Mention four reasons for writing formal letters.
questions.answer: To apply for a job, make a request, make a complaint and give official information.

questions.question: What is a salutation?
questions.answer: A greeting at the beginning of a letter.

questions.question: Give two informal salutations.
questions.answer: Dear John and Dear Mary.

questions.question: Give two formal salutations.
questions.answer: Dear Sir and Dear Madam.

questions.question: What is a complimentary close?
questions.answer: A polite expression used at the end of a letter before the writer's name.

questions.question: What is normally used after "Dear Sir/Madam"?
questions.answer: Yours faithfully.

questions.question: What can be used when the person's name is known?
questions.answer: Yours sincerely.

questions.question: What does "hardly" mean?
questions.answer: Almost not or almost never.

questions.question: Make a sentence using "hardly".
questions.answer: I hardly receive letters from my old friend.

questions.question: What does "is likely to" mean?
questions.answer: It means something will probably happen.

questions.question: Make a sentence using "is likely to".
questions.answer: Mary is likely to visit us tomorrow.

questions.question: What grammar areas are taught under informal letters?
questions.answer: Present continuous tense and adjectives.

questions.question: What language structure is taught under formal letters?
questions.answer: "Barely..." and "... barely ..."

questions.question: What grammar areas are taught under formal letters?
questions.answer: Abbreviations and formation of adverbs.

questions.question: What does "c.c." mean?
questions.answer: Carbon copy.

questions.question: What does "Re:" mean?
questions.answer: Reference.

questions.question: What does "Dr" mean?
questions.answer: Doctor.

questions.question: What does "Rev." mean?
questions.answer: Reverend.

questions.question: What is a vacancy?
questions.answer: An available job or position.

questions.question: What is an application?
questions.answer: A formal request for something.

questions.question: What is a referee?
questions.answer: A person who provides information about an applicant's character, ability or suitability.

questions.question: What is a draft?
questions.answer: The first version of a piece of writing.

questions.question: What does "edit" mean?
questions.answer: To check and improve writing.

questions.question: What is a signature?
questions.answer: A person's written name or personal mark.

questions.question: What is an official form?
questions.answer: A document with spaces provided for required information.

questions.question: Why should official forms be filled carefully?
questions.answer: To ensure that the information provided is correct.

questions.question: What is an application letter?
questions.answer: A formal letter written to apply for a job or position.

questions.question: What is a job advertisement?
questions.answer: A notice giving information about an available job.

questions.question: What is an apology?
questions.answer: An expression of regret for something wrong that one has done.

questions.question: What does regret mean?
questions.answer: Feeling sorry about something that happened or something one did.

questions.question: What are the main skills developed through letter writing?
questions.answer: Effective communication, creative thinking, critical thinking and self-expression.

questions.question: What values are emphasised?
questions.answer: Appreciation and respect.

questions.question: Give one word for: a person sitting an examination.
questions.answer: A candidate.

questions.question: Give one word for: the person who watches over candidates in the examination room.
questions.answer: An invigilator.

questions.question: Give the meaning of aggregate and malpractice.
questions.answer: Aggregate — the total of the grades scored in the subjects. Malpractice — cheating or any dishonest act in an examination.

questions.question: What is leakage in an examination, and give one of its effects?
questions.answer: Leakage is examination questions getting out before the examination. One effect: the examination may be cancelled and the candidates disqualified (it also makes the results unfair and spoils the name of the school).

questions.question: Complete: You must revise your work you will fail. (two words)
questions.answer: or else

questions.question: Complete: We look forward to (write) our examinations in November.
questions.answer: writing

questions.question: Rewrite using Despite: Although she was sick, she came for the examination.
questions.answer: Despite being sick, she came for the examination. (Also: Despite her sickness, she came for the examination.)

questions.question: Rewrite using In spite of: Although it rained heavily, the paper started on time.
questions.answer: In spite of the heavy rain, the paper started on time.

questions.question: Join using Whereas: Many candidates passed. Okello failed.
questions.answer: Whereas many candidates passed, Okello failed.

questions.question: Complete: Cheating lead to the closure of an examination centre. (could / can hardly)
questions.answer: could

questions.question: Fill in: The paper was difficult, so many candidates complained. (quite / rather)
questions.answer: rather

questions.question: Fill in with the correct possessive: This pen is (I) and that one is (they).
questions.answer: This pen is mine and that one is theirs.

questions.question: Fill in: The school lost trophy because raining heavily. (its / it's)
questions.answer: The school lost its trophy because it's raining heavily.

questions.question: Give any five rules a candidate must follow in the examination room.
questions.answer: Any five of: arrive early; carry your examination card and instruments; leave books, notes and phones outside; listen to the invigilator; write your name and index number on every sheet; read all instructions first; use ink; work silently and alone; never copy or exchange work; check your work before handing in.

questions.question: Give any five ways of preparing well for an examination.
questions.answer: Any five of: make and follow a revision timetable; revise a little every day; do past papers under time; ask the teacher what you do not understand; join a serious discussion group; keep your card and instruments safely; eat well and get enough sleep.

questions.question: Say exactly what each instruction asks you to do: underline, tick, arrange, state, explain.
questions.answer: Underline — draw a line under the word; tick — put a ✓ against the right answer; arrange — put the items in the correct order; state — give a short answer without explaining; explain — give a fuller answer in sentences.

questions.question: What three things should a candidate check on the examination card?
questions.answer: His or her names, the index number, and the examination centre (and the subjects entered).

questions.question: Give two effects of examination malpractice on a candidate.
questions.answer: The candidate's results are cancelled (disqualification), and he or she may be barred from sitting the examination for some years; it also brings shame to the candidate, the family and the school.

questions.question: Use the word invigilator in a sentence of your own.
questions.answer: Learner's sentence, for example: The invigilator told us to stop writing when the time was over.

questions.question: Write a short paragraph (about six sentences) advising a P.6 pupil on how to prepare for examinations.
questions.answer: Learner's paragraph. It should be one paragraph, in the present or future tense, with clear advice such as making a revision timetable, revising daily, doing past papers, asking teachers, resting well and avoiding cheating.

questions.question: What is electronic media? Give any four examples.
questions.answer: Electronic media are means of communication that use electricity or electronic devices. Examples: radio, television, the internet, DVD and CD players (any four).

questions.question: Give the meaning of: presenter, studio, aerial, eject.
questions.answer: Presenter — the person who introduces and runs a programme; studio — the room from which programmes are made or broadcast; aerial — the rod or wire that receives the signal; eject — to push out, for example a disc from a player.

questions.question: Give the full meaning of CD, DVD and CD-ROM.
questions.answer: CD — compact disc; DVD — digital versatile disc; CD-ROM — compact disc read-only memory.
