questions.answer: Positive: population increased; new skills and crops such as iron working and farming spread; intermarriages took place and new communities formed; trade developed; kingdoms were formed; languages spread. Negative: the indigenous people lost land; wars and conflicts broke out; cultures were changed or lost; diseases spread; lives and property were lost. (Any three and any two.)

questions.question: Why did most migrating groups avoid thick forests and deserts?
questions.answer: Because thick forests and deserts were difficult to travel through, had little food or pasture, and carried dangers such as wild animals, pests and shortage of water. Grasslands and river valleys offered water, pasture and easy movement.

questions.question: Many young people today leave the village for Kampala. Name this type of migration, give two reasons for it and two problems it causes in the town.
questions.answer: It is rural–urban migration. Reasons: to look for jobs and better pay; to get better schools, hospitals and other services (also town attractions such as electricity). Problems in town: unemployment and crime; overcrowding, slums, pressure on housing, water and health services.

questions.question: A new group settles in an area where people already live. Give two things that may bring conflict and two things that may bring peaceful living together.
questions.answer: Conflict: competition for land, water and pasture; differences in language and customs; loss of grazing land and cattle raids. Peaceful living: intermarriage and trade between the groups; sharing schools, markets and other services; learning one another's languages; respecting each other's culture and settling disputes through local leaders.

questions.question: Why do people in Karamoja often live in manyattas (homes built close together with a fence around them)?
questions.answer: For security. Living close together behind one fence makes it easier to protect people and cattle from raiders and wild animals, and it helps the community share water and pasture.

questions.question: Draw the map of Africa and show, using arrows, the direction of the Bantu migration.
questions.answer: Learner's map. Arrows should start from the Congo–Cameroon region and point eastwards into East Africa and southwards into Southern Africa.

items.subject: Social Studies
subtopics: 1. THE FOREIGN GROUPS THAT CAME TO AFRICA
3. EUROPEAN TRADERS AND THE TRIANGULAR TRADE
5. COLONIALISTS: THE SCRAMBLE AND PARTITION OF AFRICA
6. EUROPEAN SETTLERS AND THE GREAT TREK
7. EFFECTS OF FOREIGN INFLUENCE ON AFRICA
8. HOW AFRICANS REACTED TO COLONIAL RULE

questions.question: An explorer
questions.answer: An explorer is a person who travels to an unknown place in order to find out about it.

questions.question: A colony
questions.answer: A colony is a country or area ruled by a foreign power.

questions.question: The Scramble for Africa
questions.answer: The Scramble for Africa was the rush by European powers to take control of parts of Africa in the late 1800s.

questions.question: Assimilation
questions.answer: Assimilation was the French method of ruling colonies by making Africans adopt French language, culture and citizenship.

questions.question: Any four groups of foreigners who came to Africa.
questions.answer: Any four of: Arab traders, Persian traders, Indian traders, European explorers, European traders, missionaries, colonialists, settlers.

questions.question: Any four European explorers and one thing each is remembered for.
questions.answer: Any four, for example: Bartholomew Diaz — reached the Cape of Good Hope; Vasco da Gama — sailed to India round Africa; Mungo Park — explored the River Niger; David Livingstone — explored Central Africa and fought the slave trade; Speke and Grant — reached the source of the Nile.

questions.question: Any four European countries that colonised parts of Africa and one colony of each.
questions.answer: Britain — Uganda; France — Senegal; Portugal — Angola; Belgium — Congo; Germany — Tanganyika; Italy — Libya. (Any four pairs.)

questions.question: The three items exchanged at each corner of the Triangular Trade.
questions.answer: Europe to Africa — guns, cloth, beads and alcohol. Africa to America — enslaved people. America to Europe — sugar, cotton, tobacco and coffee.

questions.question: The conference that partitioned Africa and the year it began.
questions.answer: The Berlin Conference, which began in 1884 (1884–1885).

questions.question: The two African countries that were not colonised.
questions.answer: Ethiopia and Liberia.

questions.question: The colonial power that used indirect rule.
questions.answer: Britain.

questions.question: The year Britain abolished the slave trade.
The battle where Ethiopia defeated the Italians.
questions.answer: The Battle of Adowa, in 1896.

questions.question: Give four reasons why European explorers came to Africa.
questions.answer: Any four of: to find the sources of the great rivers, to find a sea route to India, to map the interior, to look for raw materials and markets, to look for land for settlement, adventure and fame, to spread Christianity, to see how the slave trade could be stopped.

questions.question: Give four problems the explorers faced.
questions.answer: Any four of: tropical diseases, attacks by hostile people, wild animals, difficult terrain, language barriers, shortage of food and clean water, poor transport, desertion by porters, harsh climate.

questions.question: Give three causes and three effects of the Great Trek.
questions.answer: Causes: dislike of British rule; the abolition of slavery in 1833; unfair compensation for freed slaves; the use of English instead of Dutch; the search for more land. Effects: the Boer republics of Transvaal, Orange Free State and Natal were founded; wars with African peoples such as the Zulu; Africans lost land; minerals were discovered inland; the Anglo-Boer wars followed; apartheid attitudes took root. (Any three each.)

questions.question: Give two political, two economic and two social effects of foreign influence in Africa.
questions.answer: Political: Africans lost independence; traditional rulers lost power; new boundaries split tribes. Economic: raw materials were exploited; roads, railways and towns were built; new cash crops and taxes were introduced. Social: Christianity and Islam spread; schools and hospitals were started; African culture was distorted and foreign languages introduced. (Any two each.)

questions.question: Why did some African leaders collaborate with Europeans while others resisted?
questions.answer: Some collaborated because they wanted guns, protection against stronger neighbours, trade goods, or a stronger position for their own kingdom, and some did not understand the treaties they signed. Others resisted because they wanted to keep their independence, their land, their cattle and their culture, and because they saw the foreigners as invaders.

questions.question: The borders drawn in Berlin were straight lines. Explain two problems this has caused Africa up to today.
questions.answer: The straight borders split single tribes between two or more countries (for example, the Maasai between Kenya and Tanzania), which weakens communities and causes cross-border problems. They also joined together groups that had never lived together, which has led to conflict, and they left some countries landlocked with no coastline of their own.

questions.question: Draw the map of Africa and shade the areas that were ruled by Britain and by France.
questions.answer: Learner's map. British areas should include Egypt, Sudan, Uganda, Kenya, Nigeria, Ghana, Zimbabwe and South Africa; French areas should include most of West Africa (Senegal, Mali, Niger, Ivory Coast, Chad) and Algeria.

items.subject: Social Studies
items.topic: Nationalism and the Road to Independence of Africa
subtopics: 3. THE COUNTRIES THAT WERE NOT COLONISED

questions.question: Pan-Africanism
questions.answer: Pan-Africanism is the feeling and movement of uniting all African people and promoting the political, economic and social interests of Africa.

questions.question: Nationalism
questions.answer: Nationalism is a deep love and pride for one's country and the desire to see it free and self-governing.

questions.question: Patriotism
questions.answer: Patriotism is love for and loyalty to one's country, shown through good actions.

questions.question: A multiparty system of government
questions.answer: A multiparty system is a system of government in which many political parties are allowed to compete for power.

questions.question: Any four leading Pan-Africanists and their countries of origin.
questions.answer: Any four of: Henry Sylvester Williams (Trinidad), W. E. B. Du Bois (America), Marcus Garvey (Jamaica), Booker T. Washington (America), Edward Blyden (Liberia), J. E. K. Aggrey (Ghana), Leopold Senghor (Senegal), Kwame Nkrumah (Ghana).

questions.question: Any four leading African nationalists and their countries.
questions.answer: Any four of: Kwame Nkrumah (Ghana), Nnamdi Azikiwe (Nigeria), Hastings Kamuzu Banda (Malawi), Nelson Mandela (South Africa), Patrice Lumumba (D.R. Congo), Abdul Nasser (Egypt), Samora Machel (Mozambique), Julius Nyerere (Tanzania), Jomo Kenyatta (Kenya), Milton Obote (Uganda).

questions.question: Any four methods used by nationalists in the struggle for independence.
questions.answer: Any four of: forming political parties, forming trade unions, organising strikes, boycotts, petitions and delegations, writing in newspapers, holding rallies, armed struggle.

questions.question: Any four problems faced by nationalists.
questions.answer: Any four of: death, imprisonment, detention, harsh laws, loss of property, intimidation, oppression, lack of funds, disunity, illiteracy among the people.

questions.question: The two African countries that were not colonised.
questions.answer: Ethiopia and Liberia.

questions.question: The first country in sub-Saharan Africa to gain independence and the year.
questions.answer: Ghana, in 1957.

questions.question: The date Uganda got its independence.
questions.answer: 9 October 1962.

questions.question: The battle in which Ethiopia defeated Italy.
questions.answer: The Battle of Adowa (1896).

questions.question: The city where the first Pan-African Conference was held.
questions.answer: London.

questions.question: Give four reasons why Africans wanted independence.
questions.answer: Any four of: to control their national resources, to stop exploitation, to revive African culture, to regain land taken by settlers, to stop oppression, to gain social freedom and rights, to regain African dignity, to ensure human equality, to end racial discrimination.

questions.question: Give three reasons why Ethiopia was not colonised.
questions.answer: It had a strong united government under Menelik II; it had modern weapons; its mountainous terrain made invasion difficult; the people were united by religion and history; it defeated Italy at Adowa in 1896. (Any three.)

questions.question: Give three advantages and three disadvantages of a single party system.
questions.answer: Advantages: leadership is respected; there is less conflict; there is less rigging and few petitions; elections are cheaper; decisions are taken quickly. Disadvantages: it encourages dictatorship; there is less accountability; new ideas are not accepted; people have no choice of leaders; human rights may be abused. (Any three each.)

questions.question: Your school is choosing head prefects. Give two ways in which this election is like a multiparty election and two ways of making sure it is free and fair.
questions.answer: Like a multiparty election: several candidates stand and campaign for the same post, and the pupils vote and choose the one they prefer. Making it free and fair: allow every candidate equal time to campaign; use a secret ballot; have neutral teachers or prefects count the votes in the open; announce the results publicly and allow complaints to be heard.

questions.question: Why did the Second World War help to speed up the independence of African countries?
questions.answer: African soldiers who fought in the war saw that Europeans were not superior, learnt to use modern weapons and returned with new ideas about freedom. The war also weakened the colonial powers economically, and the fight against dictatorship in Europe made it hard for the same powers to defend colonial rule. The United Nations, formed after the war, also encouraged self-rule.

questions.question: Give two reasons why Pan-Africanists found it hard to unite Africa.
questions.answer: Any two of: lack of unity and different political ideologies among the leaders; lack of enough funds; language barriers between English-speaking and French-speaking Africans; long distances between members; opposition and arrests by colonial governments.

questions.question: Draw the map of Africa and shade Ethiopia, Liberia and Ghana. Label each one with what it is remembered for.
questions.answer: Learner's map. Ethiopia — "never colonised, defeated Italy at Adowa 1896"; Liberia — "never colonised, home for freed slaves"; Ghana — "first in sub-Saharan Africa to be independent, 1957".

questions.question: OAU
questions.answer: OAU — the Organisation of African Unity.

questions.question: AU
questions.answer: AU — the African Union.

questions.question: COMESA
questions.answer: COMESA — the Common Market for Eastern and Southern Africa.

questions.question: ECOWAS
questions.answer: ECOWAS — the Economic Community of West African States.

questions.question: Four objectives of the OAU.
questions.answer: Any four of: to promote unity and solidarity of African states; to coordinate cooperation for a better life; to defend the independence and sovereignty of members; to remove all forms of colonialism from Africa; to promote international cooperation in line with the UN Charter.

questions.question: Four organs of the AU.
questions.answer: Any four of: the Assembly of Heads of State and Government, the Executive Council, the AU Commission, the Pan-African Parliament, the Peace and Security Council, the Court of Justice, ECOSOCC, the Permanent Representatives Committee.

questions.question: Five regional economic groupings in Africa.
questions.answer: EAC, COMESA, ECOWAS, SADC and IGAD.

questions.question: Four member states of the East African Community.
questions.answer: Any four of: Uganda, Kenya, Tanzania, Rwanda, Burundi, South Sudan, D.R. Congo, Somalia.

questions.question: The date and place where the OAU was formed.
questions.answer: 25 May 1963, in Addis Ababa, Ethiopia.

questions.question: The number of founder members of the OAU.
questions.answer: 32 member states.

questions.question: The headquarters of the African Union.
questions.answer: Addis Ababa, Ethiopia.

questions.question: The year the African Union was launched and the city where this happened.
questions.answer: 2002, in Durban, South Africa.

questions.question: The day on which Africa Day is celebrated.
questions.answer: 25 May.

questions.question: Give three achievements and three failures of the OAU.
questions.answer: Achievements: it helped end colonialism in Africa; it helped end apartheid in South Africa; it solved some border conflicts such as Morocco and Algeria; it united Africa's voice; it gave birth to the AU. Failures: it failed to stop civil wars in Sudan, Somalia, Liberia and Rwanda; it failed to stop military coups; it failed to end poverty; it had limited funds; it could not interfere in members' internal affairs. (Any three each.)

questions.question: Give four challenges facing the AU and two solutions to them.
questions.answer: Challenges: limited funds; constant civil wars; different political ideologies; dependence on developed countries; poor governance and corruption; poor transport and communication. Solutions: members should pay their contributions on time; strengthen the Peace and Security Council; promote democracy and good governance; increase trade among African states. (Any four and any two.)

questions.question: Give four advantages and three disadvantages of economic cooperation.
questions.answer: Advantages: a wider market; free movement of people and goods; cheaper goods; joint projects; employment; peace and security; sharing of skills; stronger bargaining power. Disadvantages: loss of tax revenue; stronger members benefit more; spread of crime, smuggling and diseases; infant industries are killed by competition; loss of some independence; members produce similar goods. (Any four and any three.)

questions.question: A trader from Kampala sells maize in Kigali without paying import tax. Name the grouping that makes this possible and give two other benefits it brings to the trader.
questions.answer: The East African Community (EAC). Other benefits: he can move freely and work in the other member states without difficulty; he reaches a much bigger market of customers; transport and border procedures are simpler and cheaper, and a common currency and standards are being worked on.

questions.question: The EAC collapsed in 1977. Give two possible reasons why regional groupings break up and two things members can do to keep them alive.
questions.answer: Reasons for breaking up: political differences and quarrels among leaders; unequal sharing of benefits, where one member gains more than the others; different economic systems and ideologies; wars and changes of government. Keeping them alive: share the benefits fairly and help weaker members; settle political differences peacefully through dialogue; honour agreements and pay contributions; build joint projects that all members own.

questions.question: Why does the African Union find it hard to stop wars in member states?
questions.answer: Because it depends on member contributions and donor money, so it has limited funds for peacekeeping; because its old principle of non-interference in the internal affairs of members makes action difficult; because members have different interests and ideologies and do not always agree; and because some governments ignore AU decisions and there is little power to punish them.

questions.question: Draw the map of Africa and shade the member states of the East African Community.
questions.answer: Learner's map. Uganda, Kenya, Tanzania, Rwanda, Burundi, South Sudan, D.R. Congo and Somalia should be shaded.

items.subject: Social Studies
subtopics: 6. CASE STUDY: DEMOCRATIC REPUBLIC OF CONGO (Central Africa)
8. CHALLENGES AFFECTING ECONOMIC DEVELOPMENT IN AFRICA

questions.question: A natural resource
questions.answer: A natural resource is a resource provided by nature, such as land, water, minerals, vegetation, animals and climate.

questions.question: Irrigation
questions.answer: Irrigation is the supplying of water to crops artificially.

questions.question: Nomadism
questions.answer: Nomadism is the practice of moving from place to place with animals in search of pasture and water.

questions.question: Brain drain
questions.answer: Brain drain is the movement of skilled people out of a country to work in other countries.

questions.question: The seven major economic resources of Africa.
questions.answer: Land and soils, minerals, animals, people, vegetation, climate and water.

questions.question: Four problems faced in the utilisation of resources in Africa.
questions.answer: Any four of: low level of technology, shortage of capital, poor transport and communication, remote locations, political instability, over-exploitation, corruption, pollution, unreliable world prices.

questions.question: Four ways of caring for our natural resources.
questions.answer: Any four of: afforestation and reafforestation, crop rotation and terracing, controlled grazing, protecting wetlands and rivers, gazetting parks and reserves, recycling, public education, adding value to raw materials.

questions.question: The six case-study countries in this topic and the main economic activity of each.
questions.answer: Nigeria — oil drilling; Libya — oil mining and irrigation farming; Sudan — irrigation farming (cotton at Gezira); South Africa — mining and industry; D.R. Congo — mining and lumbering; Uganda — farming (coffee).

questions.question: The main mineral mined in Libya.
questions.answer: Oil (petroleum), together with natural gas.

questions.question: The irrigation scheme found between the Blue Nile and the White Nile.
questions.answer: The Gezira Irrigation Scheme.

questions.question: The main crop grown in the Gezira Scheme.
questions.answer: Cotton.

questions.question: The dam built on the River Niger.
questions.answer: The Kainji Dam.

questions.question: The leading export crop of Uganda.
questions.answer: Coffee.

questions.question: Give three social, three economic and three political challenges affecting economic development in Africa.
questions.answer: Social: illiteracy, poverty, diseases, high mortality, famine, early marriages. Economic: poor transport, lack of capital, low technology, unemployment, corruption, brain drain. Political: wars and coups, political instability, refugees, poor governance. (Any three each.)

questions.question: Why is South Africa the most industrialised country in Africa?
questions.answer: Because it has plenty of minerals such as gold, coal, iron ore and platinum to feed its factories; it has capital and skilled labour; it has good transport and busy ports; it has plenty of electricity and a large market; and industries were developed there over a long period.

questions.question: Why must Libya use irrigation in order to farm?
questions.answer: Because most of Libya lies in the Sahara Desert and receives less than 250 mm of rain a year. Without irrigation water from underground and from the Great Man-Made River, there would not be enough water for crops to grow.

questions.question: Uganda exports raw coffee beans. Explain why processing the coffee before export would earn Uganda more money, and give two things needed to make this possible.
questions.answer: Processing (roasting, grinding and packing) adds value, so the coffee sells at a much higher price than raw beans; it also creates jobs, saves the country from unstable raw-material prices and keeps the profit at home. To make this possible Uganda needs processing factories and reliable electricity, and skilled workers, capital and markets for the finished product.

questions.question: Give two ways in which being landlocked affects Uganda's trade and two solutions to the problem.
questions.answer: Effects: goods take longer and cost more to reach the sea, which raises the price of imports and lowers the profit on exports; Uganda depends on the goodwill, roads and politics of neighbouring countries. Solutions: improve regional cooperation through the EAC so that transit is smooth; improve railway, road and air transport, use pipelines, and develop industries at home so that fewer heavy goods need to be imported.

questions.question: A district has fertile soil but the people are still poor. Suggest three reasons and three solutions.
questions.answer: Reasons: poor farming methods and low technology; lack of capital and credit; poor roads and no access to markets; small fragmented land holdings; crops sold raw and cheaply; lack of skills and education. Solutions: train farmers in modern methods; form cooperatives and provide credit; improve feeder roads and market information; add value by processing produce locally. (Any three each.)

questions.question: Draw the map of Africa and mark on it Nigeria, Sudan, South Africa and Uganda, writing the main economic activity of each.
questions.answer: Learner's map. Nigeria — oil drilling; Sudan — irrigation farming (cotton); South Africa — mining and industry; Uganda — farming (coffee).

items.subject: Social Studies
subtopics: 2. MEMBERSHIP AND ORGANS OF THE UN
3. AGENCIES OF THE UN AND THEIR FUNCTIONS
4. HUMAN RIGHTS IN THE UN CHARTER

questions.question: UN
questions.answer: UN — the United Nations.

questions.question: UNICEF
questions.answer: UNICEF — the United Nations Children's Fund.

questions.question: Human rights
questions.answer: Human rights are the basic freedoms and entitlements that every person is born with.

questions.question: CHOGM
questions.answer: CHOGM — the Commonwealth Heads of Government Meeting.

questions.question: The six main organs of the United Nations.
questions.answer: The General Assembly, the Security Council, the Secretariat, the Economic and Social Council, the International Court of Justice and the Trusteeship Council.

questions.question: The five permanent members of the Security Council.
questions.answer: The United States of America, the United Kingdom, France, Russia and China.

questions.question: Any six agencies of the UN and one function of each.
questions.answer: Any six, for example: UNESCO — education, science and culture; UNICEF — children's welfare; WHO — health and fighting diseases; ILO — workers' rights; UNDP — development projects; UNHCR — refugees; FAO — food and agriculture; WFP — food relief.

questions.question: Any four functions of the Commonwealth of Nations.
questions.answer: Any four of: promoting democracy and good governance; giving technical assistance and scholarships; promoting trade among members; settling disputes and observing elections; organising the Commonwealth Games; supporting small states.

questions.question: The date the United Nations was formed.
questions.answer: 24 October 1945.

questions.question: The city where the UN headquarters is found.
questions.answer: New York, in the United States of America.

questions.question: The place where the International Court of Justice sits.
questions.answer: The Hague, in the Netherlands.

questions.question: The date the Universal Declaration of Human Rights was adopted.
questions.answer: 10 December 1948.

questions.question: The number of member countries of the Commonwealth.
Explain how the two world wars led to the formation of the United Nations.
questions.answer: The First World War (1914–1918) caused terrible destruction, so the League of Nations was formed in 1919 to keep peace — but it was weak and failed to stop aggression. The Second World War (1939–1945) killed even more people and destroyed whole cities. The nations therefore met at San Francisco and formed a stronger organisation, the United Nations, in 1945, with a Security Council and peacekeeping powers, so that such wars would never happen again.

questions.question: Give four ways in which human rights are violated and four ways of respecting them.
questions.answer: Violations: torture and inhuman punishment; detention without trial; child labour and child marriage; denying children education; discrimination; domestic violence; denying freedom of speech or worship. Respect: make and enforce protective laws; teach people their rights; set up human rights commissions and courts; give everyone a fair trial; provide education and health services; treat all people equally; report abuse. (Any four each.)

questions.question: Give four challenges faced by the UN and the Commonwealth.
questions.answer: Any four of: insecurity and political instability in member states; limited funding because members do not pay contributions; world dictators who ignore decisions; conflicts among member states; the veto power blocking UN decisions; decisions of the Commonwealth not being binding; domination by big powers.

questions.question: A school in your village receives desks, textbooks and a water tank from a UN agency. Name two agencies that could have done this and say what each one does.
questions.answer: UNICEF — it provides for children's education, health, nutrition and protection, and often supplies desks, books and water facilities to schools. UNESCO — it promotes education, science and culture and supports schools with learning materials and teacher training. (UNDP or WFP would also be acceptable, with their correct work.)

questions.question: Compare the UN and the Commonwealth: give two similarities and two differences.
questions.answer: Similarities: both promote peace, human rights and development; both give technical assistance and scholarships; both hold regular meetings of member states; Uganda is a member of both. Differences: the UN has 193 members from the whole world while the Commonwealth has 56, mostly former British territories; the UN has peacekeeping forces while the Commonwealth has none; the UN is headquartered in New York and the Commonwealth in London; UN Security Council decisions can be binding, while Commonwealth decisions depend on goodwill.

questions.question: Some people say the veto power makes the Security Council unfair. Explain what the veto is and why people complain about it.
questions.answer: The veto is the power held by each of the five permanent members of the Security Council — the USA, the UK, France, Russia and China — to block any decision, even when all the other members support it. People complain because it means one country can stop the whole world from acting, the five have not changed since 1945, Africa has no permanent seat, and important decisions about wars and peace can be blocked to protect a friend of one big power.

questions.question: Give three ways in which Uganda has benefited from the United Nations.
questions.answer: Any three of: peacekeeping and support during conflicts; help for refugees through UNHCR; immunisation and health programmes through WHO and UNICEF; food relief through WFP and FAO; funding for schools, roads and other projects through UNDP and the World Bank; loans and economic advice from the IMF; scholarships and training for Ugandans.
